paragraph:
Asbestos has been extensively used in industry for over a century due to its properties. Its harmful pulmonary effects, including asbestosis, were recognized in the early 1900s and, in 1973, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified all types of asbestos as carcinogenic, a designation confirmed in 2012 [ 1 , 2 ].

Despite the well-established link between asbestos exposure and several cancers, including mesothelioma, only 72 countries had banned all forms of asbestos by early 2025 [ 3 ]. Italy—historically one of the largest consumers—implemented a national ban in 1992 (Law 257/92).

Mesothelioma incidence and mortality at the small-area level (i.e. municipality or census tract) are widely accepted as indicators of asbestos exposure, considering the high etiological fraction due to asbestos (>80% of cases) and the poor prognosis (at the population level in Italy, 50% of the patients survive for <10 months from diagnosis) [ 4–7 ]. Mesothelioma has a long latency (30–50 years since the first asbestos exposure) and affects the pleura in ∼90% of cases, even if other anatomic sites could be affected (i.e. peritoneum, pericardium, vaginal tunic of testis). While occupational exposure remains the primary source of risk, environmental and domestic exposures also contribute.

Since the 1980s, a national epidemiological surveillance plan monitoring mortality from mesothelioma has been updated in Italy. Despite the ban, high mortality persists: between 2010 and 2016, ∼4400 people per year died from asbestos-related diseases and, in the 2010–20 period, an average of 1545 people per year died from mesothelioma (3.79 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants, 35% of all asbestos-related diseases), making Italy one of the most severely impacted countries [ 7 , 8 ]. The latest report from the National Registry of Mesothelioma, which has been operating at the national level since 2003, estimated in Italy a total of 37 003 mesothelioma diagnoses between 1993 and 2021 [ 6 ].

This study aims to contribute to the national surveillance plan for mesothelioma by analysing the mortality trends for pleural mesothelioma (PM) in Italy over 40 years (1980–2020), focusing on calendar periods and birth cohorts. Furthermore, relative risks (RRs) are modelled in space and time by using hierarchical Bayesian methods. We analysed PM because it makes up a high proportion of all mesothelioma (>90%) and there was no specific nosological code before 2003.
### Mortality data

Data on deaths caused by pleural malignant tumours [International Classification of Diseases, 9th edition (ICD-9): 163] and PM [International Classification of Diseases, 10th edition (ICD-10): C45.0] were extracted by using the Statistical Service of the Italian National Institute of Health from the National Mortality Database of the National Census Bureau (ISTAT) for the period 1980–2020, at both the national and regional levels, and separately for the sex assigned at birth. For the period from 1995 (the year in which the multiple-cause-of-death registries became available) to 2002 (the last year in which the ICD-9 classification was in force), we used two sources of data: the multiple-cause-of-death registries and the National Mortality Database, both maintained by ISTAT. The multiple-cause-of-death registries are single, anonymous electronic registries that contain all the causes of death exactly as typed in full by the coroner on the death certificate. To identify the cause of death of the 8508 classified people who died with code 163.9 ‘Malignant neoplasm of pleura, unspecified’, we examined individual entries in the database of multiple causes of death and we identified all people for whom the term ‘mesothelioma’ and the term ‘pleura’ were written as the underlying cause. We obtained information on 6242 people who died with PM. We then used the same proportion of mesothelioma out of the total number of pleural cancers observed in 1995 to adjust for previous years back to 1980.

The data were grouped into 18 5-year age classes (0–4 to 85+ years) and 8 calendar periods (1980–4, …, 2015–20). Over time, we followed 15 birth cohorts (1905–14, …, 1975–84), highlighted in the Lexis diagram ( Supplementary Table 1 ).

### Descriptive analyses

We performed descriptive analyses on the calendar period, evaluating direct standardized rates (using the 2013 European standard population as the reference) and standardized mortality ratios (SMRs, using the Italian population of 1980–2020 as the reference) for PM. We computed cumulative risks and SMRs for people aged 20–84 years by using the 1935–44 birth cohort as the reference. For the computational details, refer to the Supplementary Material .

Age-period-cohort (APC) models were fitted to national data to estimate the adjusted mortality rate ratios for calendar periods and birth cohorts, and the model fit was assessed by using deviance and Pearson chi-square statistics.

### Space-cohort Bayesian model

We modelled PM mortality risk across Italian regions and birth cohorts by using hierarchical Bayesian models with structured random effects for space and time, following Knorr–Held’s approach [ 9 ]. The death counts in each region ( i = 1, …, 20) and cohort ( j = 1905–14 to 1960–9) were assumed to follow a Poisson distribution with mean E i j θ i j ⁠ , where E i j represents the number of expected cases (calculated by using as reference the 1935–44 birth cohort) and θ i j denotes the RR.

The logarithm of RR was decomposed as:

where u i captures the unstructured heterogeneity and v i the spatial structure (via Besag York Mollié priors), p j is a cohort effect (first-order random walk), and ξ i j is a space–time interaction term, modelled as a Markov Random Field with second-order spatial neighbours [ 10 , 11 ]. We assumed both the spatial and temporal structures for the interaction term [ 9 ].

We used WinBUGS32 to perform the Monte Carlo Markov chain analyses and STATA18 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX) for statistical analyses.
In Italy, between 1980 and 2020, a total of 40 702 people died from malignant tumours of the pleura (28 117 males and 12 585 females); of these—after correction for the absence of a specific ICD-9 code for PM—35 134 had PM (24 380 males and 10 754 females), averaging 878 deaths per year. In Table 1 , we report previous adjusted estimates, ICD-9 codes for malignant pleural tumours, and our adjusted estimates (see ‘Methods’ section) [ 12 ]. The last observation period of 2015–20 registered the highest number of deaths.

Table 2 presents the absolute number of deaths and age-specific rates (per 100 000 individuals) by calendar period, stratified by sex. The age group with the highest mortality was 75–79 years, with 4716 deaths among males and 2089 among females during the entire period. The male/female ratio over the whole observation period was 2.27.

These rates seemed to be decreasing, or in some cases reaching a plateau, in the last periods for age classes of between 50 and 75 years. The same rates are plotted by calendar periods and birth cohorts in Fig. 1 (graphs are reported on a logarithmic scale in Supplementary Figure 1 ). The direct standardized rates for males, displayed in Fig. 2 (dark red represents males, sand represents females) alongside SMRs, showed a stable increase until 2014, reaching a plateau in the last period of observation, with a slight decrease. This trend was not as evident for the female population. The increase for males was also consistent with the calendar-period SMR, reaching a peak again in the period of 2010–14. Females experienced a less linear trend, with higher ratios than males until 1999. Nonetheless, their SMR was still above the national standard at the end of the observation period. The analysis by birth cohort, represented here by the cumulative SMR, showed that the most affected cohorts were born between 1935 and 1949 for both males and females. Indeed, the two increasing trends differed: although females reached lower SMR values, they remained above the reference level among the younger cohorts. For cohorts born after the peak, a clear and consistent decrease was observed for both sexes. These same figures are reported for the specific regional profiles of the most affected regions (Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Liguria, Lombardy, Piedmont) in the Supplementary Material ( Supplementary Figures 2–5 ).

Fig. 3 shows the regional profiles for males and females of the RRs obtained from the spatio-temporal model for each birth cohort from the first in 1905–14 to the one in 1960–69. The cohorts after 1960–69 were excluded as too few cases were observed. The region with the highest risk for males was Liguria, with an RR of 3.22 (95% credibility interval: 2.98, 3.52), followed by Friuli-Venezia Giulia, with 2.27 (95% credibility interval: 1.96, 2.61). Notably, these regions reached their risk peaks in different cohorts: 1935–44 for Liguria and 1940–9 for Friuli-Venezia Giulia. The Piedmont region exhibited the highest risk among females, with an RR of 2.45 (95% credibility interval: 2.16, 2.76), followed by Lombardy, with 1.82 (95% credibility interval: 1.66, 1.98), and Liguria, with 1.80 (95% credibility interval: 1.56, 2.06). Both sexes exhibited an increasing trend, reaching their peaks in the cohorts between 1935 and 1949, as observed from the cumulative SMR, with some regional differences. Supplementary Table 3 reports the RRs for each region stratified by birth cohort and sex.

Fig. 4 presents maps of the RR distribution obtained from the spatio-temporal model for males and females. A well-known north–south gradient was evident, with the northern regions consistently showing higher risks than the southern ones. Among all areas, only Liguria exhibited consistently elevated risks in the youngest birth cohorts for both males and females. Maps of the regional SMRs and the posterior probabilities P (RR > 1) are reported in Supplementary Figures 6 and 7 .
We analysed 40 years of PM mortality data in Italy, enabling risk assessment by birth cohort (1905–84).

Our results update previous investigations estimating a decreasing risk of mortality in male cohorts born after 1945 in Italy [ 13 , 14 ].

In absolute terms, in Italy, the burden of mortality for PM was relevant, summing to 35 134 deaths between 1980 and 2020. The birth cohorts contributing more were those in 1935–49. We confirm previous observations of a higher risk of PM among women compared with those in other countries [ 6 , 8 ]. Women’s asbestos exposures, in our country, were reported mainly in the context of textile [ 6 , 15 , 16 ], domestic (i.e. wives of asbestos-cement workers), and environmental settings [ 6 , 8 , 17–19 ].

Asbestos was banned in 1992, contributing to the decrease in occupational exposure that dated back to the late 1970s, as shown by the risk profile of the birth cohorts [ 20 ].

Indeed, trends in the mortality of asbestos-related diseases by birth cohort reflect almost perfectly those of asbestos consumption, with a lag that is roughly proportional to the latency period. People born between 1935 and 1949 in Italy entered the workforce approximately two to three decades later, between 1955 and 1980—a period during which Italy was among the major asbestos producers and users in Europe (our country reached the peak of consumption in 1980, at >180 000 metric tons) [ 3 ].

There were 7 cases in males and 13 in females below ages 20–24 vs 10 years in the pre-asbestos-ban periods (see Table 2 ) [ 6 , 8 ]. PM in young people could have been due to domestic and/or environmental asbestos exposures since their early-life years [ 4 ]. However, in the literature, asbestos exposure was documented in <5% of paediatric mesothelioma [ 21 ]. Misclassification cannot be excluded, as we were able to use death certificate descriptions from 1995 onward to adjust the ICD-9 codes for pleural tumours. We have no explanation for the gender difference.

We cannot exclude an effect of improved survival on the decrease in mortality in the more recent decade. However, access to modern treatments would have resulted in a significant period effect in APC modelling, but we did not find evidence of that. Also, improved median survival was up to <20 months—a time that is too short to have caused differences in the data aggregated in 5-year classes [ 22 ].

The trend in Italy appeared similar to those in other Western countries that have banned asbestos, with the highest risks in individuals who lived or started working before the total ban. Northern European countries—where the first restrictions on asbestos use began in the mid-1970s and total bans were implemented in the early 1980s (except in Finland, where the ban occurred in 1992)—showed a peak in PM risk for the birth cohorts of 1937–47 corresponding to occupational histories aligning with the peak of asbestos use (1960–75) [ 23 ]. A similar figure was observed in the UK, where the use of blue and brown asbestos was banned in 1985 [ 24 ]. In Spain, where asbestos was banned more recently (2002), an increasing risk of mortality from pleural cancers was observed, rising to a maximum in the 1944–8 birth cohorts [ 25 ]. In the USA, an analysis based on nine cancer registries showed a peak of PM risk for the 1921–30 birth cohorts [ 26 ]. All studies agree that mesothelioma risk trends reflect asbestos consumption, which peaked around World War II and the post-war reconstruction in the USA and in the 1970s in industrialized European countries [ 13 , 26 ].

One of the most interesting aspects of our work relies on specific regional analyses. We found a strong heterogeneity among Italian regions that was consistent with historical patterns of asbestos exposure within Italy. For males, Liguria emerged as the region with the highest risk values, reaching its maximum for the earlier birth cohort. Liguria has a long history of shipbuilding—e.g. in the navy and military arsenal in La Spezia and with the navy and steel industry in Genoa—which dates back to the period from the end of the nineteenth century to the beginning of the twentieth century, with an important phase in the post-war period. Similar figures apply to Friuli-Venezia Giulia, which showed the second-highest risks for males and is home to well-known shipbuilding and naval engineering [ 6 ]. Lombardy and Piedmont follow and showed a birth-cohort curve of RRs for PM that peaked later than those of the previous regions of Liguria and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Several investigations reported the high risk of asbestos exposure in these regions, particularly corresponding to former asbestos-cement plants (Broni in Lombardy and Casale Monferrato in Piedmont) and the largest European chrysotile mine (Balangero, Piedmont) [ 6 , 8 , 16 , 17 , 27 ].

For females, the situation differed due to distinct exposure patterns compared with males. An exceeding risk was observed in Liguria for older birth cohorts, and in Piedmont and Lombardy, where females were frequently employed in textile factories—one of the work sectors most involved in asbestos-exposure risks [ 6 , 15 ]—and domestic and environmental exposures in the female population were reported in the areas in which asbestos-cement plants were located [ 18 , 19 ]. Moreover, elevated risk in females was observed in Aosta Valley, where two mines of chrysotile and tremolite were active, and potential environmental exposure to asbestos-bearing rocks was reported [ 6 , 28 ].

In the literature, we found a description of spatio-temporal patterns of PM risk for a few regions only, mostly based on incidence data from local cancer registries [ 29 , 30 ].

Fine-scale spatial analysis could have been affected by misclassification, as the residence at death may not have reflected where the exposure was suffered, due to migration after retirement. In contrast, the method used for the estimates of PM mortality before the ICD-10 code, based on multiple-cause-of-death, is more accurate than earlier methods [ 31 ].

These findings, showing in Italy a persistent mesothelioma mortality risk, even if decreasing in young generations, underscore the need to address the legacy of asbestos exposure and to trace new exposure contexts in Italy. Cohort-based surveillance, highlighting the subpopulations with higher risk, is critical for public health planning and compensation schemes, and can serve as a model for countries in which asbestos is still used. Coordinated action is essential to ensure environmental justice and global efforts towards a world ban.

category.Description: Explains how exposure arises across settings, covering behavioral, environmental, occupational, and social determinants; delineates canonical transmission routes and contact structures; interprets exposure-response with attention to measurement methods, units, detection limits, and thresholds; and situates risks within One Health interfaces involving reservoirs and vectors.
category.Rationale: The passage is fundamentally focused on identifying, characterizing, and analyzing the determinants and patterns of asbestos exposure across time, space, and population subgroups in Italy. It systematically examines how occupational (e.g., shipbuilding, asbestos-cement plants, textile industries), environmental (e.g., living near asbestos mines or industrial sites), and domestic (e.g., exposure via family members working with asbestos) sources contributed to mesothelioma risk. The study uses advanced spatio-temporal modeling to map regional disparities in exposure risk, linking them to historical industrial activity and geographic clusters of asbestos use. The analysis of birth cohorts and calendar periods directly reflects the long latency of asbestos-related disease and the temporal dynamics of exposure, which is a core aspect of exposure-response relationships. The passage also discusses methodological challenges in exposure assessment (e.g., misclassification due to migration, use of death certificate data to infer exposure), further emphasizing its focus on exposure measurement and interpretation. While the study includes surveillance and descriptive elements, its primary aim is to elucidate the sources, distribution, and consequences of asbestos exposure—making Class 3 the most appropriate for generating multi-step inference questions about exposure pathways, regional risk gradients, and the interplay between historical industrial activity and disease outcomes.

topic.Description: Integrates individual behaviours with environmental, occupational, and social/structural conditions that shape exposure probability and inequities.
topic.Rationale: The passage centers on the long-term health consequences of asbestos exposure, particularly pleural mesothelioma, in Italy, with a detailed analysis of how historical patterns of industrial use, regional occupational structures, and social contexts shaped exposure risk across birth cohorts and geographic areas. The study explicitly links mesothelioma mortality trends to asbestos consumption patterns, occupational histories (e.g., shipbuilding in Liguria, asbestos-cement plants in Piedmont and Lombardy), and non-occupational exposures (domestic and environmental). It highlights regional disparities—such as the elevated risk in northern industrial regions—and gender-specific exposure pathways (e.g., women in textile industries or exposed via domestic contact with workers). The analysis of birth cohorts reflects how structural factors like industrialization timing, labor market participation, and regulatory delays (e.g., 1992 ban) created differential exposure windows. These elements collectively illustrate how exposure is not random but shaped by deep-rooted socio-structural and environmental conditions. This makes Topic 1—the contextual determinants of exposure—the most appropriate for guiding multi-step inference questions that require reasoning about how historical, occupational, and geographic factors interact to produce health inequities, even decades after exposure cessation.

external_info: Pleural cancer is classified as a type of connective tissue cancer. It is associated with several drugs, including asbestos and its various forms—amosite, amphibole, crocidolite, and serpentine—along with cisplatin, doxorubicin, tamoxifen, and fluor-edenite. Malignant mesothelioma presents with a range of symptoms such as acute abdomen, abdominal pain, anorexia, chest pain, coma, cough, dyspnea, fever, fever of unknown origin, hemoptysis, nausea, pain, pelvic pain, and weight loss. This condition is linked to multiple drugs, including arsenic trioxide, various asbestos types, clofarabine, interleukin 1 receptor antagonist protein, itraconazole, resveratrol, and fluor-edenite. Malignant mesothelioma is categorized as a cell type cancer and shares characteristics with mediastinal cancer, muscle cancer, ovarian cancer, peritoneum cancer, retroperitoneal cancer, sarcoma, testicular cancer, and thymus cancer. Malignant epithelial mesothelioma is a subtype of malignant mesothelioma, while malignant visceral pleura tumor is classified as a form of pleural cancer. Asbestosis, which is a type of pneumoconiosis, is associated with exposure to asbestos, amphibole asbestos, crocidolite asbestos, serpentine asbestos, iron, reactive oxygen species, and vermiculite.

ori_question.Question: How might the observed regional differences in pleural mesothelioma mortality among birth cohorts in Italy reflect the interplay between historical industrial activity and social exposure patterns?

ori_question.Rationale: The question requires multi-step reasoning that integrates occupational, environmental, and social determinants of exposure across time and geography. The first piece of evidence identifies Liguria’s historical shipbuilding and steel industries as key sources of occupational asbestos exposure, linking industrial activity to male cohort risk. The second evidence highlights that female cohorts in Piedmont and Lombardy faced elevated risk due to employment in textile factories—another occupational exposure context. The third evidence expands the scope to include domestic and environmental exposures, particularly for women, which are social and household-level determinants. The fourth evidence provides the temporal context: the 1935–49 birth cohorts entered the workforce during the peak asbestos use period (1955–1980), directly linking exposure timing to industrial demand. Together, these pieces show that regional mortality patterns are not solely due to occupational exposure but are shaped by the intersection of industrial history (shipbuilding, textiles, cement plants), gendered labor roles, and household-level exposure (e.g., wives of workers). The reasoning chain moves from specific regional industries to broader social structures (gendered work), then to exposure pathways (occupational, domestic, environmental), and finally to the timing of exposure relative to industrial peaks. This synthesis reflects the topic of contextual determinants of exposure, which emphasizes how structural and social conditions shape exposure risk. The external domain knowledge, while listing asbestos types and associated drugs, does not provide new insight into the social or structural context of exposure. It confirms asbestos as a cause but does not address the interplay of industrial history, gender, or geography. Therefore, it is not incorporated into the evidence.

paragraph:
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) continues to be a deadly infection. In 2022, there were an estimated 630 000 (480 000–880 000) deaths worldwide and 1.3 million new infections globally, of which more than half occurred in Eastern and Southern Africa (ESA) [ 1 ]. Combination antiretroviral treatment (ART) suppresses HIV viraemia and is highly effective in reducing HIV-associated mortality [ 2–4 ] and preventing onward HIV transmission [ 5 , 6 ]. Consequently, treatment has been adopted as a public health strategy to prevent new HIV infections (treatment-as-prevention, TasP) [ 1 , 7 , 8 ]. Progress in implementing TasP programs is primarily measured through the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) ‘95–95–95’ targets, with the aim that 95% of people living with HIV (PLHIV) are aware of their status, 95% of those aware are on antiretroviral therapy, and 95% of those on ART achieve viral suppression. All countries in ESA committed to attaining these targets by 2025 [ 9 ] as part of achieving UN Sustainable Development Goals [ 10 , 11 ].

By January 2025, and prior to sudden cuts in global aid funding by the US government [ 12 ], many countries in ESA either attained or had been close to attaining 95–95–95 targets at a population level [ 13 , 14 ]. Maintaining HIV epidemic decline remains a central public health priority across ESA countries and novel methods to measure HIV epidemic control could help to direct future prevention efforts more efficiently. One such approach focuses on stratifying 95–95–95 targets by age and gender, which highlights inequalities in treatment coverage [ 19 ]. However, these metrics do not quantify how HIV viraemia is distributed across populations or in which populations viraemia is concentrated, and may not be predictive of incidence declines [ 15–18 ]. Consequently, they may not provide a complete understanding of the people most at risk of HIV-related mortality and onward transmission, which is necessary to tailor effective prevention interventions.

In this study, we consider a complementary metric for assessing HIV control: the ‘profile’ of how infection burden and HIV viraemia are distributed across age- and gender-specific population subgroups. We compute infection and viraemia profiles and compare the implied priority populations for targeted prevention to those obtained from evaluating 95–95–95 targets on population-based, longitudinal data from the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS)—a large population-based HIV surveillance cohort in southern Uganda. Our analyses were conducted across two distinct settings: in agrarian villages and semi-urban trading centres with population pyramids typical of most ESA communities and in Lake Victoria fishing communities with atypical population structures and very high HIV prevalence. The study time frame of 2013–19 coincided with the national expansion of ART programs.
### Study population

The RCCS is a population-based cohort of individuals aged 15–49 years in communities in and around Rakai District [ 20 ] that was established in 1994 by the Rakai Health Sciences Program (RHSP). Between July 2013 and May 2019, four survey rounds [ 16–19 ] were conducted in four Lake Victoria fishing and 36 inland agrarian and semi-urban communities [ 21 ]. In brief, at each survey round, the RCCS conducted a household census and subsequently invited all individuals aged 15–49 years and residing in the communities with intention to stay for ≥1 month to participate. Consent was obtained privately by a trained interviewer. Following consent, participants were interviewed in a private location—typically a tent—for demographic characteristics as well as behavioural and healthcare behaviour, and asked to provide a blood sample for HIV testing and future laboratory studies. All participants were offered free tests, pretest and post-test counselling, and referrals to ART services if living with HIV.

### Population sizes

Age- and gender-specific population sizes in each survey round were estimated from line-list data of census-eligible individuals reported by household heads during the census. Reported ages tended to reflect grouping patterns around multiples of five, which we disaggregated by smoothing population sizes over age [ 22 ] ( Supplementary Text ).

### Measurement of HIV serostatus and viraemia

Testing was performed through a combination of three rapid tests with confirmation of positive, faintly positive, and discordant results by at least two Enzyme Immunoasays (EIAs) and Western blot or DNA PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) [ 23 ]. Overall, 99.7% of participants accepted HIV testing across survey rounds. Among participants with HIV, HIV-1 viral load was measured on stored serum samples by using the Abbott real-time m2000 assay (Abbott Laboratories, IL, USA). Viral loads were obtained from 99.4% of participants with HIV [ 24–26 ]. Viral suppression was defined as a viral load of <1000 HIV RNA copies/ml plasma, following the recommendations of the World Health Organization [ 27 ] at the time. People who did not achieve viral suppression were defined as viraemic. We estimated population-level HIV seroprevalence (i.e. probability for an individual to have HIV) with a non-parametric Bayesian model over the age of individuals stratified by gender, survey round, and community type (i.e. fishing vs. inland) by using the data from first-time participants as a proxy for non-participating individuals [ 22 ] ( Supplementary Text and Supplementary Fig. S1 ). We used the same model to estimate the proportion of individuals exhibiting viraemia among people with HIV and among all individuals ( Supplementary Text ).

### HIV infection burden and burden of viraemia profiles

The HIV burden profile was defined as the contribution of each gender and age subgroup to all PLHIV. We first estimated the number I g , a of individuals of gender g and age a with HIV in the population by multiplying the estimated age- and gender-specific HIV seroprevalence, π g , a HIV - pop ⁠ , by the estimated number of census-eligible individuals, N g , a ⁠ , ie I g , a = N g , a π g , a HIV - pop . We then computed the HIV burden profile through:

We analogously defined the viraemia profile as the contribution of each gender and age subgroup to all individuals with (unsuppressed) viraemia. We first estimated the number V g , a of individuals of gender g and age a exhibiting viraemia by multiplying the age- and gender-specific viraemia prevalence, π g , a vir - pop ⁠ , by the estimated number of census-eligible individuals N g , a ⁠ , i.e. V g , a = N g , a π g , a vir - pop . We then computed the viraemia profile through:
### Age and gender burden profiles of HIV infection

From July 2013 to May 2019, 37 743 individuals participated at least once across four RCCS survey rounds ( Fig. 1 ). Of these, 22 215 (58.86%) participated for the first time ( Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Inland communities had expansive population pyramids with a predominantly young population, consistently with the rapid population growth across Uganda and ESA [ 28 ]. In contrast, fishing communities had constrictive population pyramids comprising primarily working-age adults (20–40 years) and substantially fewer children or women than in inland communities ( Table 1 and Fig. 2b ).

To describe the burden of HIV infection, we initially followed the typical approach to reporting HIV seroprevalence and estimated the proportion of individuals in each 1-year age band who had HIV, i.e. positive HIV serostatus within age bands ( Fig. 2c , and Supplementary Fig. S3 ). The distinct population pyramids of these communities also prompted us to characterize the infection profile ( Fig. 2c , black). The infection profile centred more strongly on younger populations than the statistics of HIV seroprevalence within each 1-year age band might suggest. For example, by 2019, in inland communities, half of the women with HIV were 28–40 years old and half of the men with HIV were 31–42 years old ( Table 2 ). We also found substantial differences in infection burden by gender. In inland communities, women contributed 66.2% (63.8%–68.4%) to HIV infections, as the higher seroprevalence of women might suggest, but, in fishing communities, women contributed only 55.2% (53.1%–57.3%) due to gender imbalance in the population structures, contrary to what the higher seroprevalence in women compared with that in men might suggest ( Table 1 ).

### Progress towards 95–95–95 targets

We next characterized progress towards 95–95–95 targets in the fishing communities in which TasP has been prioritized since 2013 and in the inland communities in which Universal Test and Treat was implemented in late 2016. We performed 13 844 viral load measurements in 6677 of 6705 (99.6%) participants with HIV. Notably, the proportion of people with HIV exhibiting viraemia decreased from 40.6% (38.4%–42.8%) in 2013 to 17.6% (15.8%–19.6%) in 2019 in inland communities and from 53.5% (51.1%–56.0%) in 2013 to 14.4% (12.4%–16.7%) in 2019 in fishing communities. Gender-specific trends are reported in Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. S4 .

### Trends in population-level viraemia

Considering viraemia at a population level, the proportion of individuals with unsuppressed viraemia decreased from 4.9% (4.6%–5.3%) in 2013 to 1.9% (1.7%–2.2%) in 2019 in inland communities and from 19.1% (18.0%–20.4%) in 2013 to 4.7% (4.0%–5.5%) in 2019 in fishing communities, with gender-specific results reported in Table 2 . Thus, while suppression levels among PLHIV were higher in fishing communities compared with inland communities, suppression levels in the population were lower in fishing communities rather than inland communities due to a higher HIV prevalence in fishing communities.

### Age and gender profiles of HIV viraemia

To characterize the age- and gender-specific populations in whom viraemia was concentrated, we first considered the proportion of age- and gender-stratified PLHIV who had unsuppressed HIV. By 2019, in inland communities, the proportion of PLHIV exhibiting viraemia was highest in men aged 23–27 years [49.8% (39.9%–60.3%)] and in fishing communities in men aged 28–32 years [28.2% (20.0%–41.2%)] ( Fig. 3 ). Among women, this proportion was the highest in women aged 15–17 years in inland communities [30.3% (18.7%–44.0%)] and in women aged 18–22 years in fishing communities [23.9% (16.2%–34.0%)]. The proportion of PLHIV exhibiting viraemia was larger in first-time participants ( Supplementary Figures S4 and S5 ).

Then, we characterized the population subgroups in which viraemia was concentrated. Figure 4a compares the proportion of women and men with HIV in each age band who had unsuppressed viraemia to the viraemia profiles. Viraemia was not centred in the age groups furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets. In inland communities, women aged 15–19 years were the furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets in 2019, but we estimate that they contributed only 4.9% (3.0%–7.3%) to people with unsuppressed viraemia. Instead, women aged 20–24 and 25–29 years each contributed ∼10% to people with viraemia in 2019, although these age groups were either close to or had already exceeded the 95–95–95 targets. Similarly, in inland communities, men aged 20–24 years were furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets in 2019, but we estimate that they contributed only 5.4% (3.9%–7.4%) to the unsuppressed viraemia. Rather, men aged 25–29 and 30–34 years each contributed ∼10% to viraemia in 2019. Similar patterns were observed in fishing communities ( Fig. 4a ).

Figure 4b depicts temporal changes in absolute suppression levels, as well as shifts in the viraemia profile. Even though we found a steady increase in the median age of PLHIV in both genders and locations, the age profile of people exhibiting viraemia remained relatively stable over time ( Supplementary Table S2 ).
This study documents remarkable achievements in reducing unsuppressed HIV viraemia in southern Uganda in 2013–19 and identifies the age- and gender-specific populations in whom unsuppressed viraemia is concentrated by using population-based surveillance data from the RCCS in Uganda. Following expanding TasP programs, fishing communities witnessed faster increases in suppression levels among PLHIV than inland communities, with overall levels surpassing the 95–95–95 targets by 2019. Yet, HIV incidence remained higher in fishing communities despite additional interventions such as Pre Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) [ 29 ]. This may be explained by our finding that the burden of unsuppressed viraemia in the population remained ∼2.5 times larger in fishing communities, reflecting a higher HIV prevalence, and suggests that reaching 95–95–95 metrics may be insufficient to lower the incidence to below the elimination thresholds [ 30 ], especially in countries with elevated HIV burdens [ 31 ]. Furthermore, current UNAIDS targets recommend that the 95–95–95 targets are met within subpopulations stratified by age and gender [ 32 ], thereby supporting the prioritization of interventions to those subgroups that are the furthest from achieving the targets and improving barriers and inequalities in treatment coverage [ 19 ]. However, these subgroups may not predominantly contribute to unsuppressed viraemia in the population. For example, we found that most individuals exhibiting unsuppressed viraemia were men in both inland and fishing communities, although fewer men had HIV than women. In addition, the age groups that contributed the most to unsuppressed viraemia in the population were not those that were furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets. In RCCS inland communities, young individuals aged 15–24 years constituted approximately two-fifths of the census-eligible population, but only one-fifth of the population exhibiting viraemia. In fact, the lower suppression levels commonly reported among young PLHIV [ 13 , 33–40 ] are counterbalanced by the small absolute number of young PLHIV. This observation is typically missing from studies supporting the prioritization of younger age groups in ESA based on 95–95–95 targets [ 45 ]. The viraemia profiles that we estimate provide evidence for reaching and treating a wide subset of the population—men aged 25–34 years and women aged 20–39 years, who predominantly contribute to unsuppressed viraemia in the population.

While we assessed age- and gender-specific profiles of both HIV infection and viraemia in this study, the latter metric provides a cross-sectional description of individuals most at risk of HIV mortality and onward transmission. Hence, we propose the viraemia profile as a new metric for HIV control. We observed that the viraemia profiles revealed similar relative contributions of men and women, and larger relative contributions of middle-aged individuals [ 25–34 ] than younger individuals [ 15–24 ], whereas these important observations were obscured in age- and gender-stratified 95–95–95 targets. Furthermore, unlike the 95–95–95 targets [ 15 , 16 ], the population burden of HIV viraemia has been shown to be strongly predictive of population HIV incidence [ 18 , 41 ].

The findings of this study need to be considered in the context of several limitations. First, following the survey protocol in place during the study period, our study population was limited to individuals aged 15–49 years. Accordingly, we are not able to quantify HIV prevalence among individuals aged ≥50 years or viral suppression outcomes in children (<15 years old) with HIV. Thus, the reported age- and gender-specific percentages in the burden profiles in the population aged 15–49 years should not be interpreted as fractions of the entire population. Second, this study only considered RCCS data. However, the demographic and epidemiological patterns seen in Rakai are typical of rural and semi-urban populations across ESA, including expansive population pyramids [ 28 ], age and gender trends in HIV prevalence [ 42 ], and gender gaps in suppression levels [ 13 , 33–40 ]. It seems likely that individuals aged 25–34 years may be predominantly contributing to HIV viraemia across the subcontinent. Third, to generalize our results from study participants to the population, we assumed that first-time study participants were representative of non-participants by age- and gender-specific prevalence and viral suppression levels. If viral suppression among non-participants is lower than among first-time participants, then the reported viral suppression levels could be overestimates. Fourth, considering HIV prevention, the age profiles in onward HIV transmission correspond only approximately to those of viraemia and, in particular, men tend to contribute more to heterosexual transmission than viraemia may suggest [ 22 , 43 , 44 ]. Additionally, transmission risk factors such as sexual behaviour are highly heterogeneous across individuals of the same age and gender [ 45–47 ]. This supports complementing population-based metrics such as the viraemia profiles with individual-level metrics, e.g. HIV acquisition risk scores [ 48 , 49 ], to further guide the next generation of targeted prevention policies.

As of December 2024, the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) program had supported >20 million PLHIV with lifesaving treatment corresponding to approximately two-thirds of all PLHIV accessing ART globally [ 50 ] and has over the past two decades saved >26 million lives through HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support programs, and averted almost 5 million HIV infections in children [ 12 ]. In early 2025, the USA abruptly cut PEPFAR funding, causing service disruptions, HIV clinic closures, and fear among people who depend on wide-ranging PEPFAR-supported services [ 51 ]. It is now critical to monitor and mitigate the impacts of these unprecedented funding cuts on people affected by HIV. This must include population-based surveillance of HIV incidence and viral suppression as key determinants of prospective morbidity, mortality, and transmission risk, to guide the global HIV response through a looming, man-made global health emergency. Future surveillance efforts should include population-level measures of HIV viraemia to help direct HIV control and elimination efforts more effectively.
The study was independently reviewed and approved by the Ugandan Virus Research Institute, Research and Ethics Committee, protocol GC/127/13/01/16; the Ugandan National Council for Science and Technology; and the Western Institutional Review Board, protocol 200313317. All study participants provided written informed consent at baseline and follow-up visits by using institutional review board-approved forms. This project was reviewed in accordance with Centers for Disease Control (CDC) human research protection procedures and was determined to be research, but CDC investigators did not interact with human subjects or have access to identifiable data or specimens for research purposes. RCCS participants received 10 000UGX (∼2.50USD) in compensation for their time and costs to participate in each survey.

category.Rationale: The passage presents a methodological innovation in HIV surveillance by introducing and evaluating a new metric—the 'viraemia profile'—to assess HIV epidemic control. The core of the study lies in the development and application of statistical models to estimate age- and gender-specific HIV infection and viraemia burdens using population-based longitudinal data from the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS). The authors employ non-parametric Bayesian modeling to estimate seroprevalence and viraemia prevalence, account for population structure (e.g., age pyramids in fishing vs. inland communities), and adjust for potential biases (e.g., non-participation, age misreporting). They compare this novel metric to the standard 95–95–95 targets, demonstrating how traditional indicators may obscure the true distribution of viraemia and thus mislead prevention priorities. The study rigorously evaluates the performance of different metrics in predicting transmission risk and identifies limitations in current surveillance approaches. This focus on methodological design, model selection, bias correction, and evaluation of surveillance metrics aligns precisely with Class 5. Multi-step inference questions could explore how model assumptions affect burden estimates, how different metrics perform under varying population structures, or how measurement error in viral load testing might influence the viraemia profile—requiring integration of epidemiological principles with statistical reasoning.

topic.Description: Assesses coverage and implementation fidelity, audits routine data quality, evaluates real-world effectiveness, and estimates disease burden.
topic.Rationale: The passage centers on evaluating the performance and impact of HIV treatment-as-prevention (TasP) programs in Eastern and Southern Africa (ESA) using population-based surveillance data from the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS). It critically examines the extent to which the UNAIDS 95–95–95 targets—used as a proxy for program success—align with actual population-level outcomes, particularly the burden of unsuppressed HIV viraemia, which is a direct determinant of transmission and mortality. The study goes beyond simple measurement of coverage by introducing a novel metric—the 'viraemia profile'—to assess where HIV-related risk is concentrated in the population, thereby evaluating the real-world effectiveness of TasP in reducing epidemic drivers. The analysis compares program outcomes across different community types (fishing vs. inland), evaluates temporal trends in viral suppression, and identifies gaps between achieving targets and reducing actual viraemia burden. These findings directly inform public health decision-making about where to target interventions, making this a quintessential example of program performance and impact evaluation. While the passage touches on measurement (e.g., viral load testing) and study design, the overarching goal is to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of large-scale HIV control programs, which aligns most closely with Topic 5.

An outbreak of HIV infection-AIDS occurred in Pakistan on April 25, 2019, with 876 confirmed cases. 

HIV infection is associated with the biological pathway of Human immunodeficiency virus 1 infection. The condition is classified as a viral infectious disease. Several drugs are associated with HIV infection, including Abacavir, Adefovir dipivoxil, Didanosine, Efavirenz, Emtricitabine, Enfuvirtide, Etravirine, Fosamprenavir, Indinavir, Lamivudine, Maraviroc, Nevirapine, Ritonavir, Tenofovir, Zidovudine, and various drug combinations such as Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate, lamivudine/abacavir, and lopinavir-ritonavir. Additional substances linked to the disease include Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors, HIV Core Protein p24, and various compounds such as 3,4,5-trihydroxybenzamidoxime, (2,8-dioxabicyclo(3.3.0)oct-6-yl)-N-(4-((3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)sulfonyl-(2-methylpropyl)amino)-3-hydroxy-1-phenylbutan-2-yl) carbamate, arzanol, heminordihydroguaiaretic acid, and plant extracts. Other associated agents include amphetamines, cocaine, methadone, nicotine, tobacco smoke pollution, vitamin A, beta carotene, resveratrol, thalidomide, and metal exposure such as nickel.

ori_question.Question: In the context of evaluating the real-world impact of HIV treatment programs, which metric would most accurately identify the population subgroups that are most critical to target for interventions aimed at reducing onward transmission and mortality?
Evidence: Passage: 'We estimated population-level HIV seroprevalence ... by using the data from first-time participants as a proxy for non-participating individuals.'

Passage: 'In inland communities, women aged 15–19 years were the furthest from achieving the 95–95–95 targets in 2019, but we estimate that they contributed only 4.9% (3.0%–7.3%) to people with unsuppressed viraemia.'

Passage: 'The viraemia profiles revealed similar relative contributions of men and women, and larger relative contributions of middle-aged individuals [25–34] than younger individuals [15–24], whereas these important observations were obscured in age- and gender-stratified 95–95–95 targets.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to answer a question about program impact evaluation. Evidence 1 establishes that the study used first-time participants as a proxy for non-participants to estimate population-level HIV seroprevalence, which introduces a methodological assumption about representativeness. This is critical because it implies that the data used to assess program performance may be subject to selection bias if non-participants differ systematically in their HIV status or viral suppression. Evidence 2 presents a key finding: despite being furthest from the 95–95–95 targets, young women (15–19 years) contributed minimally to the burden of unsuppressed viraemia. This contradicts the intuitive assumption that subgroups furthest from targets are the most critical to target for intervention. Evidence 3 directly states that the viraemia profile—unlike the 95–95–95 targets—reveals that middle-aged individuals (25–34 years) and men are the primary contributors to unsuppressed viraemia, even though they may not be the furthest from the targets. The inference is that metrics based on coverage and treatment access (like 95–95–95) may mislead program planners about where to focus interventions, while the viraemia profile better identifies those most responsible for transmission and mortality. The external domain knowledge lists antiretroviral drugs and biological agents associated with HIV, but does not provide information on program evaluation metrics, data quality, or real-world effectiveness assessment. Therefore, it is not substantively relevant to the reasoning chain and was not incorporated. The question requires multi-step reasoning: one must recognize that program performance is often assessed via coverage targets, but the study shows these may not align with actual disease burden; then, one must infer that a metric reflecting the actual distribution of viraemia—rather than treatment access—is more predictive of transmission risk; and finally, conclude that this metric is superior for guiding intervention priorities. The question is not answered by any single piece of evidence and cannot be answered by paraphrasing a passage statement.

choices.Option: The HIV seroprevalence profile, which shows the proportion of individuals in each age- and gender-specific subgroup who are infected with HIV, to identify populations with the highest number of new infections and potential for onward transmission

The proportion of people with HIV who are not virally suppressed, stratified by age and gender, to identify subgroups with the highest rates of treatment failure and prioritize interventions to improve adherence and retention in care

The viraemia profile, which quantifies the contribution of each age- and gender-specific subgroup to the total population burden of unsuppressed HIV, is the most accurate metric for identifying high-risk populations for transmission and mortality

The age- and gender-specific incidence rate of new HIV infections, calculated from longitudinal data, to identify populations with the highest risk of acquiring HIV and target prevention efforts accordingly

The 95–95–95 targets stratified by age and gender, which identify subgroups with the lowest treatment coverage and highest gaps in viral suppression, to prioritize interventions for those furthest from achieving program goals

paragraph:
Periodic counts of deaths are essential for monitoring population health [ 1 , 2 ]. In high-income countries, this information is extracted from civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems that operate continuously [ 3 ]. It allows the detection of periods of excess mortality, such as those that occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, in near real time [ 3–5 ]. In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), CRVS systems are incomplete [ 6 ]. Representative mortality data are only generated every few years from retrospective household surveys and/or censuses [ 7 ]. Some of these inquiries ask respondents to list all of the deaths that have recently occurred in their household [ 8 ] and to indicate the demographic characteristics of the deceased [ 9 ]. By comparing the list of reported deaths to the list of current household members, they allow estimations of the sex- and age-specific mortality rates for a reference period that covers one or several years before data collection.

The retrospective mortality data collected during surveys and censuses might also help to better ascertain the magnitude of recent mortality fluctuations in LMICs caused on a month-to-month basis by epidemics, conflicts, or natural disasters [ 10 ]. However, not all surveys and censuses that collect data on recent household deaths also ascertain the dates of reported deaths. Furthermore, when questions about dates of events are included in a survey or census, they might generate imprecise data [ 11 ] .

To improve the reporting of dates of demographic events, surveys and censuses that are conducted in LMICs often use calendars of local events [ 12 ]. These tools allow respondents to anchor their answers to events with known dates that have happened in close temporal proximity to the event of interest. Such calendars have referenced local elections, festivities, or weather-related disasters (e.g. droughts, floods). These time markers might help to reduce the proportion of reported events with unknown dates. They might also ensure that the reported date is more consistent with the true date of an event.

Calendars of local events used in surveys and censuses predominantly employ annual scales, e.g. to better assess the age of respondents [ 13 , 14 ]. Except for a few studies that were conducted in the wake of conflicts or natural disasters [ 15–17 ], they have seldom been used to improve the reporting of recent household deaths on a monthly scale. We conducted a multi-arm randomized trial of the use of calendars of local events in interviews about recent household deaths. We hypothesized that, compared with standard close-ended questions about the month and year of death, the use of calendars would yield more accurate data on the dates of recent household deaths.
### Study setting

We worked in Guinea-Bissau—a low-income country in west Africa ( Fig. 1 ). The country has a population of ∼2 million and an estimated life expectancy at birth of 60 years [ 18 ]. Leading causes of death include neonatal conditions, lower respiratory infections, HIV/AIDS, and tuberculosis [ 19 ]. The COVID-19 pandemic has also spread among various population groups and disrupted daily activities [ 20 , 21 ].

The trial was conducted in five neighborhoods of Bissau, the capital city [ 22 , 23 ]. These areas are covered by a Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS), which follows >100 000 people [ 24 ]. HDSS fieldworkers conduct household visits every 2 months to detect and monitor pregnancies, births, and deaths. Young children are followed up every 3–4 months, from birth until their third birthday, to gather data on vaccinations and other health behaviors [ 24 , 25 ]. Among the rest of the population, deaths are recorded periodically during censuses, with the most recent taking place between September 2019 and October 2020. Evaluations of health interventions conducted in HDSS neighborhoods also routinely include the collection of mortality data. In 2020–21, fieldworkers recorded deaths among participants in assessments of the role of face masks and Oral Polio Vaccines in limiting the impact of COVID-19 on population health [ 26 , 27 ].

We used records generated by these HDSS activities as a sampling frame to recruit participants and as a common benchmark against which we compared the data obtained from different versions of questionnaires about recent household deaths. Despite frequent follow-up, some deaths might be missed by HDSS fieldworkers and characteristics of recorded deaths (e.g. dates, ages) might be misreported. We thus acknowledge that HDSS data are not a perfect source of information on recent mortality [ 28–30 ] but also believe that, thanks to its features, including shorter recall, it provides a good standard against which to evaluate the trial arms.

### Participants

We selected households in which at least one death had occurred among regular household members between January 2020 and May 2022, according to HDSS records. Households were located by using the numbering system established by the HDSS and were visited in person. In each household, a regular member aged 18+ years and who spoke Crioulo (the vernacular language) was invited to serve as the informant. Households in which no eligible informant was available or an informant asked to reschedule the interview were revisited later. Each household was visited up to three times.

### Data collection instruments

We asked informants to describe their own sociodemographic background and the characteristics of their households. They were then asked whether there had been any death among regular household members since January 2020. Following recommendations [ 31 ], we anchored this question to the occurrence of an event of national relevance, i.e. the second round of the last presidential elections held on 29 December 2019. If the informant reported deaths during this period, then s/he was asked to report the number of deaths, list the deceased members by name, and provide details about each of them.

We implemented three approaches to asking about dates of reported deaths. The control arm of the trial followed the standard questionnaire (‘SQ’) used in surveys and census. For each listed death, data collectors asked informants: ‘In what month and year did [NAME] die?’ The experimental arms also included this question, but interviewers and respondents were aided by a calendar of local events. To devise this calendar, we drew a preliminary list of events that included COVID-related events (e.g. the national mandate for mask use in May 2020), political happenings (e.g. an attempted coup in February 2022), festivities (e.g. a popular music festival in May 2022), and annual holidays (e.g. Christmas Day). We then asked some residents from one of the HDSS neighborhoods whether they knew of these events. Events that were not recalled were excluded. Other events that were suggested by local residents and corroborated by HDSS data collectors were added. The final calendar only included public events ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ) [See online supplementary material for a color version of this figure.]

In the first experimental arm (‘physical calendar’, PC), the calendar was displayed on an A4 sheet of paper. It was bracketed by months in columns and years in rows, thus defining cells that covered the period from January 2020 to the month of the interview. Events were listed in relevant cells, with some cells containing multiple events. Interviewers used the PC to confirm or correct the dates of deaths that were spontaneously reported by respondents or to determine the date for which respondents stated not knowing the month and/or year of death.

In the second experimental arm, a ‘digital calendar’ (DC) was designed to address concerns that interviewers might not systematically use the PC in ascertaining dates of deaths. Following the initial question about month and year of death, the DC progressed to one of three screens. If respondents had reported a month and year of death, then the application displayed a portion of the calendar covering ±6 months around the initial report. Interviewers used events displayed on this screen to confirm or correct the reported date. If respondents had only reported the year of death, then the application displayed the monthly calendar for the reported year and interviewers used that information to locate the month. If respondents only recalled the month of death, then the application showed a list of events and interviewers asked whether the death had happened around the time of one of those events. If the respondent identified an event close to the date of death, then the application showed a portion of the calendar covering ±6 months from the selected event to determine the month/year.

In both experimental arms, if respondents remained unable to recall both the month and the year of death, then they were asked to indicate another event (not included in the calendar) that had occurred around its time. Study investigators looked up the date of the reported event and imputed it as the date of death.

### Randomization

Selected households were randomized 1:2:2 to an interview with SQ (control arm), PC, or DC (experimental arms). The randomization was stratified by neighborhood of residence and time elapsed since the most recent household death recorded by the HDSS. All randomization procedures were conducted on the list of selected households, using random numbers generated in Stata, v.18 [ 32 ].

### Primary outcome

The main study outcome was the proportion of deaths reported to have occurred in the same month and year as indicated by the HDSS. To assess this outcome, we attempted to link each reported death to its HDSS record by using a manual approach [ 33 ]. We did not use information about dates of deaths to establish links. We planned to compare each experimental arm to the control arm of the trial. We used the multiarm R package to perform sample size calculations [ 34 ]. Assuming that 65% of deaths in the control arm were reported to have occurred on the same date as indicated by the HDSS, we sought to detect whether each type of (experimental) calendar increased concordance with the HDSS-recorded date by 15%age points. We accounted for multiple comparisons with the control arm by using Dunnett’s correction, setting the significance level at α = 0.03. Under the 1:2:2 allocation ratio, and with the power set to 0.8 for each comparison, we required linked reports of 101 deaths in the control arm and 202 deaths in each of the experimental arms.

### Data collection

Three interviewers and one team supervisor conducted the trial from April to June 2023. All interviewers had prior data collection experience, but not in the study areas. They were trained to conduct interviews by using each of the trial’s instruments. All data were collected on tablets using SurveyCTO [ 35 ]—a common data collection platform in LMICs. To prevent crossovers, we created separate data collection forms with preloaded lists of assignments for each arm. Data collectors did not have access to any mortality-related data from the HDSS. This study was approved by the institutional review board of New York University-Abu Dhabi (Protocol HRPP-2023–39) and by the Comité Nacional de Ética na Saúde, in Guinea-Bissau (ref: 026/CNES/INASA/2023).

### Analytical methods

In each arm of the trial, we described participation rates and the characteristics of participating households. We then tested null hypotheses in which we assumed that there was no difference in outcomes between the control arm and each experimental arm. We used a χ 2 test to compare the distribution of households by number of reported deaths between study arms. To evaluate our primary outcome, as well as the proportion of reported deaths with missing date components, we used logistic regressions, controlling for stratification variables (i.e. time since death and neighborhood of residence), as recommended for the analysis of stratified randomized trials [ 36 ]. Among linked deaths with complete dates, we measured absolute differences (in months) between the reported date of death and the HDSS-recorded date. To test for differences between arms in such error patterns, we used nonparametric Kruskal–Wallis tests. In each arm, we also assessed the correlation between monthly series of deaths obtained from retrospective reports and from HDSS records. Finally, we estimated the amount of time required to complete each questionnaire (in minutes). If the PC or DC required significantly more time to complete than the SQ, then it may be impractical to adopt them in surveys and censuses. All standard errors were adjusted for clustering of deaths within households. Supplementary Table S1 presents the CONSORT checklist for the trial [ 37 , 38 ]. [See online supplementary material for a color version of this table.]
We identified 578 households with at least one death between January 2020 and May 2022 according to HDSS records. Among those, 508 were interviewed (87.9%). Participation was slightly lower among households assigned to PC. Table 1 presents the sociodemographic characteristics of the participating households.

In 448 of the 508 interviewed households (88.2%), informants reported that at least one death had occurred among regular members since January 2020. Characteristics of the deceased are shown in Supplementary Table S2 . [See online supplementary material for a color version of this table.] There were no differences between each experimental arm and the control arm in whether respondents reported at least one death (SQ versus PC P = 0.48; SQ versus DC P = 0.62) or in the number of deaths reported to have occurred during the reference period (SQ versus PC P = 0.16; SQ versus DC P = 0.49, Fig. 2 ).

Informants reported that 574 deaths had occurred since January 2020. We linked 82% ( n = 472/574) of those deaths to HDSS records, without differences in linkage rates between control and experimental arms (SQ versus PC P = 0.28; SQ versus DC P = 0.32). Deaths among individuals who had recently joined the household and deaths due to accidents were overrepresented among unlinked deaths (see Supplementary Table S3 ). [See online supplementary material for a color version of this table]. Fourteen linkages pertain to individuals who had migrated out of the study areas prior to death and for whom the HDSS did not include death records.

In total, we evaluated the reported dates of 458 deaths. Among those, 50.0% of deaths elicited by the SQ had the same month and year of death as recorded by the HDSS ( Fig. 3 ). In the experimental arms, the estimated proportions were 52.6% in the PC arm ( P = 0.74) and 48.0% in the DC arm ( P = 0.73).

Household informants did not report the month or year for 39 out of 574 reported deaths (6.8%). In the control arm, an estimated 13.1% of reported deaths had missing data on one of these components ( Fig. 4 ). In the experimental arms, the estimated proportion was 6.1% with PC (SQ versus PC P = 0.04) and 3.2% with DC (SQ versus DC P = 0.002).

When deaths were not reported in the same month and year as recorded by the HDSS, the median absolute difference from the HDSS records ( Fig. 5 ) was 9 months in the control arm [inter quartile range (IQR): 1–12], 11 months in the PC arm (IQR: 3–12, SQ versus PC P = 0.16), and 12 months in the DC arm (IQR: 2–12, SQ versus DC P = 0.13). Among the observed discrepancies, 25.7% of deaths were displaced by 12 months in the control arm versus 32.9% in the PC arm (SQ versus PC P = 0.45) and 33.0% in the DC arm (SQ versus DC P = 0.43).

We observed similar levels of correlation between the monthly series of deaths obtained from the HDSS data and the retrospective data generated by SQ or PC ( Fig. 6 , r = 0.57 and r = 0.60, respectively). The monthly series generated by DC yielded a lower level of correlation with the HDSS series ( r = 0.40).

Interview durations ( Fig. 7 ) were similar in the SQ (median: 13’20’’, IQR: 9’20’’ to 16’49’’) and PC arms (median: 13’01’’, IQR: 10’08’’ to 19’01’’; SQ versus PC P = 0.39). Relative to the control SQ arm, interviews aided by DC were longer (median: 14’29’’, IQR: 10’34’’ to 19’48’’; SQ versus DC P = 0.01).
In this trial, the use of calendars of local events did not improve the reporting of dates of recent deaths collected during surveys or censuses typically conducted in LMICs. Although calendar tools reduced the extent of missing data on dates of death, the proportion of deaths reported to have occurred in the same month and year as recorded by the HDSS did not vary between control and experimental arms.

Our study has several limitations. First, our comparisons between control and experimental arms might have lacked sufficient power to reject various null hypotheses, in large part because (i) we assumed higher levels of concordance with HDSS records than attained during the study and (ii) more households than expected did not report any recent household death. Limited statistical power might have prevented us from detecting differences between study arms, e.g. in the magnitude of errors in reported dates. Second, participation was slightly lower in households assigned to interviews with the physical calendar. This might have confounded our comparison between trial arms. However, the observed characteristics of participating households were similar across all arms. Third, we did not investigate whether the effects of calendars might vary with the characteristics of households and recent deaths. Knowledge of dates of deaths might depend on factors such as the age of the deceased or the underlying cause of death. The dates of accidental deaths, for instance, might be better known because they are more frequently reported to local authorities (e.g. police). Detailed subgroup analyses of the use of calendars would, however, require larger sample sizes [ 39 ]. Fourth, our questionnaires asked informants to report household deaths that occurred over a long reference period (>3 years). While this is not uncommon [ 40 ], in many LMICs, surveys and censuses often only elicit deaths of the past 12 months, as recommended by the United Nations [ 41 ]. Our sample of households included too few deaths in the 12 months before the trial to investigate the effectiveness of calendars for such a recent period. Fifth, the reference HDSS dataset remains affected by errors and omissions. Some of the discrepancies observed in our trial might thus be attributable to limitations of HDSS records rather than to errors in retrospectively collected data. Finally, it is unclear whether our results might extend to other populations in Guinea-Bissau or other LMICs. We conducted our study in urban areas, where residents often have higher numeracy levels than residents of more rural areas. They might also be more accustomed to reporting dates of events because of frequent interactions with HDSS data collectors or with formal institutions such as governmental offices. The effectiveness of calendars of local events in improving dates of death reporting might thus differ in other LMIC settings.

Nevertheless, this study has multiple implications. First, our results do not support the use of a digital calendar to improve the reporting of dates of deaths. Not only did this approach fail to improve reported dates, but it also increased the interviewing time relative to standard close-ended questions about dates of death. Second, studies are needed to determine the optimal design and use of a physical calendar of local events in collecting data on recent household deaths. Indeed, while the physical calendar at times led to larger errors in reported dates than the standard approach, it also fostered higher levels of data completeness without increasing interviewing times. Future studies could thus explore whether excluding annual events from those listed in the calendar might reduce the proportion of deaths displaced by exactly 12 months in interviews aided by a physical calendar. These studies might also investigate protocols in which interviewers do not systematically use the physical calendar to verify the date of every reported death, but instead only use it when respondents do not know the month and/or year of death. Finally, the high levels of omissions and errors documented in retrospective data on recent household deaths further stress the need for large investments in strengthening CRVS systems in LMICs [ 42 ].
The trial was approved by the institutional review board of New York University-Abu Dhabi (Protocol HRPP-2023–39) and by the Comité Nacional de Ética na Saúde in Guinea-Bissau (Guinean-Bissau National Ethics Committee) (ref: 026/CNES/INASA/2023).

category.Rationale: The passage describes a multi-arm randomized trial designed to evaluate the effectiveness of different data collection instruments—specifically, physical and digital calendars of local events—in improving the accuracy of reported dates of recent household deaths in a low- and middle-income country setting. The study focuses on methodological rigor, including randomization, stratification, control of confounding variables, statistical analysis (logistic regression, Kruskal–Wallis tests), handling of clustering, and use of a benchmark (HDSS data) to assess validity. The primary outcome is measured by concordance between retrospective reports and a reference dataset, and the analysis includes evaluation of bias, missing data, error patterns, and time efficiency. These elements fall squarely within the scope of Class 5, which emphasizes methodological evaluation, study design, measurement quality, and bias assessment. The passage does not primarily focus on surveillance, outbreak response, determinants of disease, immunity, or forecasting. Instead, it centers on evaluating a novel data collection method using robust epidemiological methods, making it the most appropriate class for generating multi-step inference questions that require reasoning about study design, validity, bias, and measurement error in public health data systems.
