paragraph:
Endometrial (EC), epithelial ovarian (EOC), and cervical cancers (CC) are among the most common cancers in females, and substantial causes of cancer-related mortality [ 1 ].

Statins, widely used to treat and prevent cardiovascular diseases, inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMGCoA) reductase, leading to reduced cholesterol levels and inhibition of proteins involved in the development and progression of several cancers, including gynecological cancers [ 2 , 3 ]. Previous studies on statin use and gynecological cancer risk have reported conflicting results [ 3 , 4 ]. These studies have often been impaired by small sample size and limited data on associations by type of statin (e.g. lipophilic, hydrophilic) and in disease subgroups (e.g. histological subtypes).

We used a large population-based cohort (>1 million women) to assess the association between use of statins and the risk of EC, EOC, and CC, including stratified analyses by type of statin, strength of statin, age, histology, and body mass index (BMI).
### Study design, population, and data sources

We used the Population Registry from Statistics Norway [ 5 ] to identify women born between 1925 and 1986 who lived in Norway at any time in 2004–18, forming the underlying cohort. Women entered the analytic cohort for the current study on the latest of: 1 January 2004, the date they turned 49.5 years old, or their first immigration date. Women born in 1968 or later did not turn 50 before end of follow-up, and therefore could not enter the analytic cohort. Follow-up started 6 months after cohort entry to ensure 6 months of medication history. Statin use is uncommon among women <50 years in Norway, thus we included only women aged ≥50 years at the start of follow-up. We excluded women with a history of invasive cancer prior to the start of follow-up {except invasive non-melanoma skin cancer [International Classification of Diseases (ICD) version 10 code: C44]}. Women were followed until they were diagnosed with EC, EOC, or CC (the outcomes of interest in the separate analyses), diagnosed with a different invasive cancer, died, emigrated, or on 31 December 2018, whichever occurred first.

Medication data were obtained from the Norwegian Prescription Database, which have detailed information on all dispensed prescriptions from community pharmacies since January 2004 [ 6 ] including: date, Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) code, amount (number of tablets), strength (e.g. mg per tablet), and number of defined daily doses (DDD). One DDD is the average dose associated with one day of use if the medication is prescribed for its main indication to an adult [ 7 ]. Data on cancer diagnoses were obtained from the Cancer Registry of Norway [ 8 ]. Date of birth, migration, educational level, income, marital status, country of origin/birth, and the number of children were obtained from Statistics Norway [ 9 ]. Date of death was obtained from the Cause of Death Registry [ 10 ]. BMI was available for a subset of women who participated in selected health surveys, as described previously [ 11 ]. We used the BMI measurement closest to the start of follow-up, with a maximum of 5 years before or after the start of follow-up (92% of the measurements are pre-diagnostic).

### Consent to participate

Informed consent is not needed for use of registry data. Informed consent for the health surveys was collected by the team collecting the data for the health surveys.

### Exposure assessment

Statin use (ATC code: C10AA, C10BA02, C10BA05 as these are marketed in Norway) was based on dispensed prescriptions. Treatment days were calculated using the number of DDDs, assuming one DDD per day. To account for use beyond the estimated treatment days (i.e. use <1 DDD per day), we added a 4-month grace period to the initially estimated duration of statin use. We analyzed the exposure to statins as a time-dependent variable. Women contributed person-time as never, current, or past users. Women with no statin dispensation during the 6 months before start of follow-up contributed time as never users from the start of follow-up until the date of the first dispensed statin prescription ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Women contributed person-time as current users from the date of dispensation until the end of the estimated duration of statin use. In cases where there were gaps between the end of the estimated duration of use and the next dispensation of statin, women contributed person-time as past users from the end of the estimated duration until the next dispensation of statin or end of follow-up. Women with a period of current use that covered the start of follow-up began contributing person-time as current users from the start of follow-up. Women who were dispensed a prescription of statin in the 6 months before the start of follow-up, with an estimated duration not covering the start of follow-up, contributed person-time as past users from the start of follow-up. Women who were dispensed a statin between cohort entry and start of follow-up were defined as prevalent users, while women who were dispensed their first statin after start of follow-up were defined as incident users. To limit reverse causation, we applied a 6-month lag-time period to all prescriptions [ 12 ].

Statin use was assessed overall and by type (lipophilic and hydrophilic; Supplementary Table S1 ) and strength (low, medium, high [ 13 ]). Women could be users of different types and strengths of statins (i.e. they are not censored for the previous type or strength when starting a new type or strength of statin, and the statistical models are mutually adjusted for the different types and strengths of statins).

### Outcome assessment

The outcomes were diagnoses of EC (ICD-10: C54), EOC (including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancers) (C48.2, C56, C57.0–C57.4), or CC (C53). Non-carcinomatous cancers, such as sarcomas, lymphomas, and neuroendocrine tumors were excluded. Histologic subgroups were categorized using morphology codes ( Supplementary Table S2 ).

### Nested-case control study

In addition to the cohort design, we conducted a nested-case control study to evaluate duration of statin use and time since cessation and risk of EC, EOC, and CC. To accurately estimate the cumulative DDDs and time since cessation in the nested-case control study, we excluded prevalent statin users (see “Exposure assessment”) at baseline from the original cohort. Each case was matched with 10 controls who were at risk of an incident cancer diagnosis at the age and date when the corresponding case was diagnosed (index date). We defined the exposure based on status at the index date ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) and created a variable with 7 categories: never use, 3 levels of time since cessation (<1, 1–2.9, and ≥3 years since last period of current use), and 3 levels of current use (based on cumulative DDD; <548 DDDs, 548–1824, and ≥1825 DDDs).

### Statistical analysis

Cox proportional hazard models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) in the cohort design. Age was the underlying time scale. Conditional logistic regression models were used to estimate associations in the nested-cased control study. Estimates were adjusted for a priori selected covariates registered at cohort entry in the cohort design and at index date in the nested-case control design: age in years (underlying time scale in the cohort design and matching variable in the nested-case control design), education (none/primary school only, secondary school, higher education, missing), income (quartiles), marital status (married/partnered, not married/partnered, missing), country of origin/birth (Norway, other countries), number of children (0, 1, 2, ≥3). All estimates were also adjusted for use of other individual medications during follow-up (≥1 dispensed prescription of the specific medication), including beta-blockers (ATC code: C07), calcium channel blockers (C08), agents acting on the renin–angiotensin system (C09), diuretics (C03), low-dose aspirin (B01AC06, B01AC56), antidiabetics (A10), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; M01A), and menopausal hormone therapy (G03C, G03F). The women were defined as never users until their first dispensed prescription of the specific medication, from that date onwards they were defined as ever users. Missing information on covariates was handled as a separate category in the variable.

We evaluated risk of EC, EOC, and CC overall, and in subgroups defined by type and strength of statin, age (attained age or age at index: 50–64.9 years, 65–94 years, in the cohort analysis the follow-up time was left truncated at the lower age interval and censored at the upper age interval for the two age categories), histology, and BMI (<25, ≥25 kg/m 2 ). The cutoff level for BMI was set as it represents the definition of overweight and can therefore give clinically relevant information using a readily available metric. We also performed an analysis in the subset of women with a BMI measurement adjusting for BMI as a continuous variable. Prevalent users, as described previously, were excluded from the cohort analysis in a sensitivity analysis.

All tests were two-sided with a 5% significance level. Statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.2.3 ( http://cran.r-project.org/ ).
We identified 1 872 600 women who resided in Norway at any point between 2004 and 2018. After excluding women who lived in Norway <6 months ( n = 15 311), those with a history of cancer ( n = 64 064), and those not reaching age 50 by the end of 2018 ( n = 709 596), 1 083 629 women were included. During median follow-up of 11.6 years, 334 582 (31%) women used statins at least once (90% did not switch between hydrophilic and lipophilic statins), and 7709 EC cases, 4415 EOC cases, and 1603 CC cases were identified. At the start of follow-up, women who used statins at least once were generally older, and more likely to have only mandatory education, low income, be born in Norway, have children, and use other medications compared to women who had never used statins ( Table 1 ). BMI was available for 450 143 (42%) women; among those, a higher proportion of women with BMI ≥ 25 was found among statin users (60.7%), as compared to non-users (47.3%). The cumulative time as a user of statins during the study period was longer among the women categorized as current users at the end of follow-up (median = 7.12 years, Quartile 1 = 3.05 and Quartile 3 = 11.50) as compared to those categorized as past users (median = 2.96 years, Quartile 1 = 1.02 and Quartile 3 = 6.95).

Inverse associations were observed between statin use, compared to no use, and EC risk [current: HR = 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85–0.96), past: HR = 0.79 (0.71–0.88)] ( Fig. 1 ). Associations were similar in analyses stratified by age and histology. In analyses by statin type, associations were observed for lipophilic [e.g. current: HR = 0.90 (0.85–0.96)] but not hydrophilic statins [current: HR = 1.09 (0.92–1.29)]. No consistent pattern was observed by strength. When considering the subset of women with BMI data, the estimate for the association between statin use and EC risk was similar to that observed in the full cohort [current: HR = 0.90 (0.82–0.99); past: HR = 0.85 (0.72–1.00)], and was not impacted by adjustment for BMI [current: HR = 0.90 (0.82–0.99); past: HR = 0.84 (0.71–1.00)].

No significant association was observed between statin use and EOC risk overall [current: HR = 1.07 (0.99–1.16); past: HR = 1.04 (0.91–1.19)] ( Fig. 2 ). The estimates were consistent across different subgroups defined by type and strength of statin, age, and histology, with the exception of a significant inverse association observed between past use and risk of high-grade serous EOC [HR = 0.78 (0.62–0.99)].

Current statin use was not associated with CC risk [HR = 1.02 (0.89–1.18)], but past use was [HR = 0.71 (0.53–0.94)] ( Fig. 3 ). Overall, estimates in subgroups defined by type of statin, strength of the statin, age, and histology did not differ substantially, though significant inverse associations were observed with past use, but not current use, of medium-strength statins, and past use among women ages 50–64 years [e.g. medium-strength statins, current use: HR = 1.04 (0.89–1.22); past use: HR = 0.68 (0.53–0.88)].

When stratified by BMI (<25, ≥25 kg/m 2 ) the estimates for all three cancers were similar to those for the overall populations ( Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ). Findings were similar when restricting the cohort to only those categorized as non-users at baseline (i.e. excluding past and current users; data not shown).

Overall results for current and past use were similar in the cohort and nested-case control designs. In the nested-case control studies evaluating cumulative DDDs for current users and time since cessation among past users, we included 7642 women with EC and 76 420 controls ( Supplementary Tables S6 and S7 ), 4379 women with EOC and 43 790 controls ( Supplementary Tables S8 and S9 ), and 1576 women with CC and 15 760 controls ( Supplementary Tables S10 and S11 ). We found no trends in the association with cumulative DDDs or time since cessation for any cancer type in the overall population or in any of the subgroups ( Supplementary Tables S7, S9 , and S11 ).
In this large population-based cohort, statin use was associated with lower EC risk. These associations were observed only for lipophilic statins, and associations were similar across subgroups defined by age, histology, and BMI. We observed no trend in the association by cumulative DDDs or time since last use. We found limited evidence of associations between statin use and EOC or CC.

A proposed mechanism supporting the hypothesis that statins may reduce cancer risk involves their inhibition of HMGCoA-reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the mevalonate pathway. This inhibition lowers cholesterol levels and interferes with the synthesis of other proteins known to be implicated in carcinogenesis [ 2 , 3 ]. Additionally, statins might exert an anticancer effect through a mechanism independent of the mevalonate pathway by disrupting the interaction between integrin LFA-1 and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1) and thereby affecting the invasion, migration, and cell adhesion [ 2 ]. Specific to EC, statins may be associated with decreased risk via reductions in total cholesterol, and downstream reductions in estrogen receptor-modulating cholesterol metabolites such as 27-hydroxycholesterol [ 14 ], which has agonist activity in the normal corpus uteri [ 15 , 16 ], and has been linked to EC in experimental models [ 17 ].

Current statin use was associated with a 10% lower EC risk and past use with a 21% lower risk. These associations were consistent when adjusted for and stratified by BMI, and across age and histology subgroups. Our findings align with results from previous studies using data from population-based databases [ 18–20 ], as well as large prospective cohorts [ 21 , 22 ]. These studies reported risk reductions ranging from 22% to 85%. While we found an association for both short-term and long-term statin use, prior studies have reported a reduced EC risk only for longer-term use of statins [ 20 , 22 ]. Further, while we observed associations predominantly for lipophilic statins (the predominant type prescribed in our study), others evaluating associations for lipophilic and hydrophilic statins have found no difference in association by statin type [ 20 , 21 ]. Lipophilic statins have been shown to decrease endometrial stromal cell proliferation [ 23 ] and inversely impact inflammation-related pathways [ 24 ], while the investigated hydrophilic statins (pravastatin [ 23 ]; rosuvastatin [ 24 ]) did not induce these effects. Further studies, all evaluating ever vs. never statin use, have observed no associations with EC risk, which might be due to differences in population characteristics, and patterns of prescribing and use of statins [ 25–28 ].

We found limited evidence of an association between statins and EOC risk. This is consistent with most previous studies [ 21 , 25 , 26 , 28–30 ], though some studies have suggested a protective effect of statins against EOC [ 20 , 31 ]. The only significant associations observed in the current study were between past use of statins and high-grade serous EOC. Though these findings were not fully consistent, they align with the associations observed for EC, and notably for type II (primarily serous) EC, and with the potential common origins of a subset of high-grade serous EOC and EC in the fallopian tube [ 32 ]. While there are commonalities in risk factors for endometrioid EOC and EC [ 33 , 34 ], we observed a lack of agreement in the associations between statins and these subtypes, though the number of endometrioid EOCs was limited ( n = 50 exposed cases).

We found no clear evidence for an association between statin use and CC risk, with associations only observed for past use. Current research on statins and CC is limited, with conflicting results. A cohort study in the USA ( n = 2 145 593 women) reported no association [ 25 ], while a South Korean cohort study ( n = 587 705 women) found a 64% reduced CC risk among long-term users and no difference by statin type [ 20 ]. In contrast, a study in the UK Biobank ( n = 180 855 women) reported a 55% increased CC risk associated with statin use [ 28 ].

The main strength of this study is the large population, allowing evaluations in subgroups defined by statin type, and individual and cancer characteristics. However, even in this study of >1 million women, the number of cases in some subgroups (e.g. non-serous EOC histologies) was limited. The linkage with the Norwegian Prescription Database ensured no recall bias, though a limitation is the lack of data on actual use of the medications, and medications used in nursing homes was not available. An important further limitation is the lack of information on comorbid conditions associated with gynecological cancer risk. We addressed this by adjusting for medication use related to treatment of comorbid conditions. BMI is arguably the most important confounder of the association between statins and EC. BMI data were available for 42% of the study population, and BMI-adjustment did not alter the results. Another limitation was that we did not have information on the exact duration of statin use. To estimate this, we used the total number of DDDs dispensed, assuming one DDD per day. By definition DDDs are the average maintenance dose per day for a drug used for its primary indication thus DDDs are expected to be a reasonable estimate of the duration of use. We consistently observed stronger associations for past use compared to current use. Past users had shorter overall duration of use during the study period than current users, though duration of use prior to the beginning of follow-up was not quantified, and findings were similar in a sensitivity analysis where the study population excluded prevalent statin users at baseline. Given these observations, the stronger associations observed in past users may be a consequence of residual confounding or total longer-term statin use not captured during the study period.
Our study found that statin use is associated with a reduced risk EC, and provides no, or very little, evidence to support associations with EOC or CC. The reduced risk for EC was evident across various subgroups defined by individual (e.g. age, BMI) characteristics and tumor histology. Further studies to clarify (or confirm) associations by tumor histotype are needed for both EOC and EC.
This study has a legal basis in accordance with Articles 6(1)(e) and 9(2)(j) of the GDPR. The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics Sør-Øst (S-09113b 2009/2062, 2009/594, 2014/1854/REK sør-øst B) and by the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (17/00222-4/GRA). The data were disclosed with legal basis in the Cancer Registry Regulations section 3–1 and the Personal Health Data Filing System Act section 19 a to 19h and regulations on population-based health surveys 6–1.

category.Rationale: The passage investigates the association between statin use—a pharmacological exposure—and the risk of three gynecological cancers (endometrial, epithelial ovarian, and cervical). The core of the study is to characterize the exposure (statin use) in detail, including its type (lipophilic vs. hydrophilic), strength, duration (via DDDs), timing (current, past, never use), and patterns of use (including lag periods and time since cessation). The analysis explicitly evaluates exposure-response relationships by stratifying on multiple factors such as age, BMI, histology, and duration of use, which aligns with the class's focus on interpreting exposure-response dynamics. The study also addresses methodological aspects of exposure measurement (e.g., using dispensed prescriptions, DDDs, grace periods, and time-dependent definitions), which reflects a rigorous approach to exposure assessment. Furthermore, the discussion of biological mechanisms (e.g., inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase, mevalonate pathway, and integrin-ICAM1 interactions) situates the exposure within a biological pathway that explains how statins may influence cancer development. This makes the primary focus of the passage not just on disease occurrence (which would fall under surveillance), but on understanding how a specific exposure (statin use) is linked to cancer risk across subgroups and over time—making Class 3 the most appropriate. Multi-step inference questions could explore how different exposure metrics (e.g., DDDs vs. duration) affect risk estimates, why associations differ by statin type, or how residual confounding might influence observed exposure-response patterns.

topic.Description: Describes protection after vaccination or prior infection, its change over time, risks of reinfection, hybrid immunity, and variant-related escape. Considers how vaccine dose number and dose intervals influence vaccine effectiveness and its waning over time.
topic.Rationale: The passage evaluates the association between statin use (a pharmacological intervention) and the risk of developing gynecological cancers (EC, EOC, CC), with a focus on estimating protective effects over time. The study uses a large cohort and nested case-control design to assess the impact of statin use—categorized as current, past, or never use—on cancer incidence, including stratified analyses by duration of use (cumulative DDDs), time since cessation, and other subgroups. The key findings show that past statin use is associated with a 21% lower risk of endometrial cancer (EC), while current use is associated with a 10% reduction, suggesting a potential time-dependent protective effect. The absence of a dose-response trend with cumulative DDDs or time since cessation raises important questions about the nature of protection—whether it is sustained, waning, or influenced by residual confounding. This pattern invites multi-step inference questions about the durability of protection, the potential for delayed or cumulative effects of statins, and whether the observed associations reflect true biological protection or confounding by unmeasured factors (e.g., longer-term statin use preceding the study period). Although statins are not vaccines, the core epidemiological concept of 'protection' over time, its variation by duration and timing of exposure, and the interpretation of waning or persistent effect aligns most closely with Topic 3. This topic best supports inference-based questions that go beyond the reported hazard ratios to explore mechanisms, timing, and the implications of non-linear or paradoxical associations (e.g., stronger effect in past vs. current users).

external_info:
Lymphoma is classified as a hematologic cancer. It is associated with a wide range of drugs, including anthracyclines, alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and cisplatin, and chemotherapeutic regimens like CHOP, MACOP-B, and CTVP protocols. Other drugs linked to lymphoma include calcitriol, dexamethasone, doxorubicin, idelalisib, thalidomide, and various compounds such as 2',3-dimethyl-4-aminobiphenyl, benzo(a)pyrene, and radioactive pollutants.  

Neuroendocrine tumors are categorized as a type of endocrine gland cancer. They are associated with drugs including octreotide, sandostatinLAR, interferon alfacon-1, everolimus, sunitinib, carboplatin, paclitaxel, and the FDE protocol.  

Carcinogenesis is linked to multiple agents that play a role in disease pathogenesis, including carbon, reactive oxygen species, and various environmental and chemical carcinogens such as benzo(a)pyrene, 1,3-butadiene, and chromium hexavalent ion. Other substances associated with carcinogenesis include dimethoxon, norathyriol, phosphates, usnic acid, and protein-bound polysaccharide K.  

Sarcoma is a type of cell type cancer and shares clinical similarities with skin cancer, spinal cancer, testicular cancer, tracheal cancer, uterine cancer, uterine fibroid, vaginal cancer, vascular cancer, and vulva cancer. It presents with a broad range of symptoms, including abdominal pain, back pain, chest pain, fever, fatigue, cachexia, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, pain, paralysis, paresis, paresthesia, edema, ecchymosis, purpura, jaundice, and neurologic manifestations.  

Cancer is broadly defined as a disease of cellular proliferation. It is associated with numerous drugs, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, imatinib mesylate, erlotinib hydrochloride, paclitaxel, and various chemotherapeutics such as doxorubicin, cisplatin, and methotrexate. Some drugs are implicated in disease pathogenesis, including amines, glycine, kynurenic acid, ethyl arachidonate, and trimethionine.  

Cervical cancer is a type of female reproductive organ cancer and shares characteristics with fallopian tube cancer, ovarian cancer, penile cancer, rectum cancer, uterine cancer, uterine fibroid, vaginal cancer, and vulva cancer. It is associated with symptoms such as pelvic pain, abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, dysmenorrhea, constipation, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence. Drugs used in its treatment include 5-FU-CDDP, carboplatin, cisplatin, paclitaxel, gemcitabine, tamoxifen, and various natural compounds like resveratrol and sulforaphane. The disease is linked to the human papillomavirus infection and viral carcinogenesis pathways.  

Cervix carcinoma is classified as a subtype of cervical cancer.

ori_question.Question: In this large cohort study, what would be the most appropriate method to evaluate whether the protective effect of statin use against endometrial cancer diminishes over time after discontinuation, while accounting for potential confounding by duration of use and time since last exposure?
Evidence: Passage: 'We found no trend in the association with cumulative DDDs or time since cessation for any cancer type in the overall population or in any of the subgroups (Supplementary Tables S7, S9, and S11).'

Passage: 'In the nested-case control study, we included 7642 women with EC and 76,420 controls... We defined the exposure based on status at the index date (Supplementary Fig. S2) and created a variable with 7 categories: never use, 3 levels of time since cessation (<1, 1–2.9, and ≥3 years since last period of current use), and 3 levels of current use (based on cumulative DDD; <548 DDDs, 548–1824, and ≥1825 DDDs).'

Passage: 'The estimates were consistent across different subgroups defined by type and strength of statin, age, and histology, with the exception of a significant inverse association observed between past use and risk of high-grade serous EOC [HR = 0.78 (0.62–0.99)].'
ori_question.Rationale: The question requires multi-step reasoning that integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the passage. First, Evidence 1 states that no trend was observed in the association between time since cessation and endometrial cancer risk, which directly addresses the core question of whether protection wanes after discontinuation. However, this finding alone does not explain how the study was designed to assess this. Evidence 2 reveals the methodological approach: the nested-case control study used a stratified exposure variable that explicitly categorized time since cessation into three levels, allowing for a direct test of whether the protective effect changes over time. This shows that the study was designed to evaluate waning protection. Evidence 3, while not directly about endometrial cancer, provides context on the robustness of the findings across subgroups, reinforcing that the lack of trend was consistent across strata. The combination of these pieces—methodological design (Evidence 2), observed result (Evidence 1), and consistency across subgroups (Evidence 3)—is necessary to conclude that the study was appropriately designed to assess waning protection and found no evidence of it. The external domain knowledge, while rich in drug-cancer associations, does not provide relevant information about the temporal dynamics of drug effects or study design for evaluating waning protection. Therefore, it is not incorporated. The question is not answerable from any single piece of evidence and requires integration of study design, results, and context to assess the validity of the methodological approach.

paragraph:
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are proposed to influence systemic inflammation [ 1 ]. There are two families of PUFAs that are essential for many metabolic processes: omega-3 (n-3) [ 2 , 3 ] and omega-6 (n-6) [ 3 ]. Some PUFAs, like docosahexaenoic acid [DHA; an n-3 PUFA (22:6-n3)] can come from both exogenous sources (such as meat, egg products, and seafood) and endogenous sources (synthesized from their metabolomic precursors through desaturation and elongation reactions) [ 4 ]. However, linoleic acid [LA: an n-6 PUFA (18:2-n6)] can only be acquired through dietary consumption [ 5 ].

Evidence suggests that n-3 PUFAs have anti-inflammatory effects and subsequently reduce the severity/occurrence of inflammation-related conditions [ 6 , 7 ] given that cytokines and acute-phase proteins are implicated in the pathophysiology of many non-communicable diseases (NCDs) [ 8–16 ]. A meta-analysis of 14 clinical trials ( n = 135 291) suggested that n-3 supplementation reduced the risk of adverse cardiovascular events/death [ 17 ]. However, a randomised control trial (RCT) investigating dietary intake and mortality in 3114 men with angina found that risk of cardiac death was higher among individuals advised to eat oily fish/take fish oil compared with a control group [ 18 ]. Additionally, studies have reported that the consumption of n-6 PUFAs had no effect on concentrations of inflammatory biomarkers, despite reports that they were pro-inflammatory [ 19–22 ]. However, these studies do not directly assess the impact of FAs on inflammation and the contradictory results raise questions of whether PUFAs ‘causally’ affect inflammation or whether changes to inflammatory biomarker levels are the result of residual confounding.

Both n-3 and n-6 PUFAs are metabolized by the same enzymes and compete for desaturation and elongation. Therefore, n-6 PUFAs act as competitive inhibitors of n-3 PUFAs and thus reduce the amount of end-product n-3 PUFAs that can be synthesized [ 23 ]. Therefore, the plasma n-6:n-3 ratio may also impact the concentration of inflammatory makers and subsequent health [ 24–27 ]. Research to understand the importance of the n-6:n-3 ratio on levels of inflammation and its impact on the occurrence of NCDs is of public health concern.

We investigated the effect of specific n-3 and n-6 PUFAs, which play a role in key metabolic processes on inflammatory markers, by using (i) traditional observational epidemiological analyses and (ii) Mendelian randomization (MR) [ 28 ].

Our exposures were DHA and LA, positioned at opposite ends of the biosynthesis pathways ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). To further interrogate the PUFA–inflammation relationship, we included total n-3 PUFAs, total n-6 PUFAs, and the ratio of total n-6:total n-3 PUFAs. Outcomes included C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6)—commonly used biomarkers of systemic inflammation and glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA). GlycA are derived from multiple proteins involved in the acute-phase response and consequently is thought to be a more stable marker of inflammation compared with single proteins such as CRP [ 29–31 ]. Our aim was to assess how PUFAs affect inflammation by using specific and broad measures.
### Observational epidemiological analyses

The primary analysis used the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) birth cohort that recruited a total of 14, 541 pregnant women residing in South-West England [ 32–34 ]. For eligibility criteria, see the study flowchart ( Supplementary Figure S2 ). Participants were included if they had exposure (DHA, LA, total n-3, and total n-6) and outcome (CRP, IL-6, and GlycA levels) data available at 24 years.

We used maternal self-reported highest educational qualification and highest occupation of either parent [measures of social economic position (SEP)], maternal and paternal smoking pattern during pregnancy (measures of pregnancy health), participants’ sex, smoking status, alcohol-drinking status, and triglyceride, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL cholesterol), saturated fatty acid (SFA), and monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) levels at 24 years as covariates.

For additional information on ALSPAC, blood sampling, and data collection/processing, see Supplementary Materials .

Linear regression analyses were used to examine the cross-sectional associations of PUFA levels with GlycA, CRP, and IL-6 levels at age 24 years. We ran an unadjusted model; a model adjusted for sex, age, maternal and paternal smoking patterns during pregnancy and SEP (Model 2); a model including all covariates from Model 2 and triglycerides and LDL cholesterol (Model 3); and finally a model that included all covariates from Model 3 and SFAs and MUFAs (Model 4). Due to high correlations between PUFAs, lipids, MUFAs, and SFAs, results from Model 2 were used as our main findings. Results from Models 3 and 4 should be interpreted with multicollinearity in mind (variance inflation factors are presented in Supplementary Figure S3 ). Details about data cleaning are presented in the Supplementary Materials . Analyses were run by using the whole sample and sex-stratified.

We used multiple imputation (described in detail in the Supplementary Materials ) to impute missing exposure, outcome, and covariate data in the eligible sample ( N = 2802).

We replicated the analysis by using data from UK Biobank (UKB) ( N = 12 401)—a community-based, prospective study ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk ) [ 35 ]. Despite, the larger sample size, UKB served as replication because it was used in the MR analysis. To strengthen confidence in the results (triangulation), we used different methods in different cohorts [ 36 ]. Information about UKB and the replication analysis is presented in the eMethods.

### Two-sample MR analysis

We conducted two-sample MR by using genome-wide significant single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs; P < 5.0 ×10 −8 ) as instrumental variables (IVs) from European Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS) of PUFAs [ 37 ], GlycA [ 38 ], CRP [ 39 ], and IL-6 [ 40 ]. SNPs were harmonized, aligning the genetic association for exposure and outcome on the effect allele by using the effect allele frequency. See Supplementary Materials for details on instrument selection and the number of remaining instruments.

The inverse-variance weighted [ 41 ] method was the primary analysis used to calculate the effect estimates. MR–Egger, weighted median, and weighted mode methods were used as sensitivity analyses. As these methods make different assumptions about instrument validity, consistency across primary and sensitivity analyses increased the confidence that findings were robust. Methods to investigate pleiotropy and heterogeneity are described in the Supplementary Materials .

We replicated the MR analysis by using different outcome datasets and the results were consistent with those of the primary analysis. The GWAS used in this secondary analysis and results are discussed in the Supplementary Materials .

### MR analysis focusing on specific PUFA genes

The FADS gene cluster and ELOVL2 gene encode key desaturase and elongase enzymes, respectively, and are involved in the n-3 and n-6 FA biosynthesis pathways. Therefore, we conducted a complementary and mechanistically informative MR analysis by using only SNPs from within or close to (±500 kb) the FADS gene cluster ( FADS1 , FADS2 , and FADS3 ; chromosome 11:61 560 452–61 659 523) and the ELOVL2 gene (chromosome 6:10 980 992–11 044 624) from the DHA GWAS and the LA GWAS. SNPs were selected and harmonized by using the same method as in the primary analysis. Details are presented in the Supplementary Materials .

### Multivariable MR analysis

We conducted a multivariable MR (MVMR) analysis [ 42 ] (MVMR-1) to estimate the independent direct causal effects of n-3 and n-6 PUFAs on the biomarkers of inflammation. Although SNPs within the FADS region should be reliable instruments of PUFAs due to their proximal relation to PUFA biosynthesis, results may be biased because the SNPs can also be associated with non-fatty acid traits, such as LDL cholesterol and triglycerides [ 43 ]. Therefore, we ran two further MVMR analyses: MVMR-2—as in MVMR-1 but also accounting for triglycerides and LDL cholesterol; and MVMR-3—as in MVMR-2 but also accounting for MUFAs and SFAs. Diagrams representing the intertwined metabolic pathway of LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and FAs, and their effects on inflammation are presented in Supplementary Figure S4 .

MVMR analyses are further discussed in the Supplementary Materials .

We used MR-Lap to assess potential bias in effect estimates due to sample overlap, winner’s curse, or weak instruments [ 44 ]. Given that SNPs can influence the outcome in distinct ways via discrete biological mechanisms [ 45 ], we explored heterogeneity by using MR-Clust [ 45 ]. Greater details about MR-Lap and MR-Clust are provided in the Supplementary Materials .
Table 1 presents the median/range for PUFA levels and inflammatory biomarker levels in ALSPAC and UKB. Results are discussed in detail in the Supplementary Materials . A summary of all results is presented in Figure 1 .

### Results for primary analyses (Model 2) using ALSPAC cohort data

Results for all models are presented in Figure 1 and Table 2 .

DHA and LA were associated with higher CRP and GlycA levels, but lower IL-6 levels after adjusting for Model 2 confounders.

Total n-3 and n-6 PUFAs were associated with higher GlycA levels, but lower IL-6 levels after adjusting for Model 2 confounders. Total n-6 was associated with higher CRP levels and there was no strong evidence of an association between total n-3 PUFAs and CRP after adjusting for Model 2 confounders. The total n-6:n-3 ratio was associated with higher levels of all three biomarkers after adjusting for Model 2 confounders.

In the sex-stratified analyses, the n-6:n-3 ratio was associated with higher levels of all three biomarkers in both sexes ( Figure 3 and Supplementary Table S1 ). PUFAs were associated with higher GlycA in both sexes. The effects of all PUFAs on CRP and IL-6 levels attenuated to the null in males. In females, findings mirrored the results from the whole cohort.

Results when including all listed covariates are presented in the Supplementary Materials and Figure 2 . In all analyses, the inclusion of triglycerides and LDL cholesterol (Model 3) and SFAs and MUFAs (Model 4) shifted the effect size towards the negative. With the exception of the n-6:n-3 ratio, the Model 4 shift of effect changed the direction of the effect of all PUFA measures on the CRP and GlycA levels ( Figure 2 ). Given that MUFAs and PUFAs are highly correlated, these results should be interpreted with multicollinearity in mind.

Results when using UKB cohort data are presented in the Supplementary Materials . Results for Model 2 are consistent with findings when using ALSPAC data; however, when including the additional covariates (triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, SFAs, and MUFAs), the findings diverged.

### Results from MR analyses

Tests investigating instrument validity indicated that instruments were unlikely to be subject to weak instrument bias (see Supplementary Materials ). MR results are presented in Supplementary Figure S5 .

We observed no strong evidence of an effect of DHA levels on CRP, GlycA, or IL-6. These results were largely consistent across sensitivity analyses.

We observed no strong evidence of an effect of LA levels on CRP or IL-6. However, estimates suggest that higher LA levels cause higher GlycA levels, which is consistent with results from the cohort analyses. Other than in the analysis investigating the effect of LA levels on CRP, results were consistent across the MR sensitivity methods.

Higher total n-3 PUFA levels were associated with higher GlycA levels (consistently with the cohort analyses). There was also evidence to suggest that higher total n-3 PUFA levels were associated with higher CRP and this was replicated in the secondary MR analysis. We found no effect of total n-3 on IL-6. Results attenuated to the null for sensitivity analyses of total n-3 PUFA levels on GlycA.

We observed no strong evidence of an effect of total n-6 PUFA levels on CRP or IL-6. However, estimates did suggest that higher n-6 PUFA levels cause higher GlycA levels (consistently with the cohort analyses). The MR effect estimates were fairly consistent with the main MR analysis.

Pleiotropy and heterogeneity tests are discussed in the Supplementary Materials , along with the replication analysis. In short, there was no strong evidence of pleiotropy, but there was evidence of heterogeneity. Replication was fairly consistent with the main MR analysis.

### Results from the MVMR analyses

MVMR analyses suggested that total n-6 PUFA levels independently increased both GlycA and CRP levels, but not IL-6 levels, after controlling for the effect of n-3 PUFAs. There was no direct independent effect of total n-3 PUFA levels on GlycA, CRP, or IL-6 after controlling for the effect of n-6 PUFAs ( Figure 4 ), suggesting that pleiotropy may have biased the univariable MR. After further accounting for the effect of triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, we found that total n-6 PUFA levels independently increased the levels of GlycA, but not CRP levels. There was no independent effect of total n-3 PUFAs on any biomarker ( Figure 5 ). A further description of the results, including the third MVMR, in which triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, SFAs, and MUFAs ( Figure 6 ) were also included, is presented in the Supplementary Materials along with results from MR-Lap.

### Results for MR analyses focusing on specific PUFA genes

MR analyses using SNPs from the FADS gene region suggested that DHA increased CRP levels, but that LA decreased CRP levels. FADS instrumented DHA and LA had no effect on GlycA or, where testable, IL-6. There was no evidence of a causal effect of any SNPs from the ELOVL2 gene on GlycA, CRP, or IL-6. See the Supplementary Materials for further information.

### Results from the MR-Clust analysis

As SNPs can influence outcomes in distinct ways and associations between PUFAs and GlycA were consistent across the cohort and MR analyses, we used MR-Clust [ 45 ] to identify SNP clusters driving heterogeneity. For LA, total n-3, and total n-6 PUFAs, all clusters showed positive associations with GlycA, aligning with the main result ( Supplementary Figures S6–S8 ). For DHA, two clusters were positively associated with GlycA whereas one showed a negative association ( Supplementary Figure S9 ). All three showed gene enrichment in lipid pathways/lipid-related GWAS. No cluster-related differentially expressed gene sets met statistical significance for tissue enrichment ( Supplementary Tables S2–S6 and Supplementary Figure S10 ). Detailed results are presented in the Supplementary Materials .
By combining cohort and genetic analyses, we provide insight into the relationships between PUFAs and systemic inflammation. Using multivariable linear regression, we found evidence that DHA, LA, total n-3, and total n-6 increased levels of GlycA (in ALSPAC and UKB). However, results between cohorts were less consistent for the effect of FAs on CRP. When using the ALSPAC cohort, we found a consistent positive association between the n-6:n-3 ratio and all three biomarkers, although this was not replicated in UKB.

Subsequent genetic analyses shed light on the complex nature of these associations. First, consistently with the cohort analyses, LA, total n-3, and total n-6 potentially causally increased the levels of circulating GlycA, which suggests a pro-inflammatory effect of these FAs. Further, as with GlycA, the MR results show that total n-3 PUFAs causally increased the circulating CRP levels. This contrasts with the presumed anti-inflammatory effect of n-3 PUFAs. We also replicated this finding by using secondary, independent GWAS data, which increases the confidence in this result.

Our MVMR analyses highlight the potential importance of total n-6 FAs above total n-3 FAs regarding their effect on systemic inflammation. We found, consistent with the cohort and univariable MR analysis, that higher total n-6 FAs increased GlycA levels after accounting for the effect of n-3 FA levels, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol. Therefore, as suggested by previous literature, n-6 FAs may increase levels of inflammation. In contrast, total n-3 FAs had no effect on GlycA or CRP after accounting for total n-6 FAs, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol. This brings into question the use of n-3 supplementation as a method to reduce systemic inflammation. Despite this, biomarkers measure different aspects of inflammation (acute versus low-grade chronic inflammation) and the PUFAs affect them differentially. Therefore, by only using three biomarkers of inflammation, we may have missed important effects that PUFAs have on inflammation. Research using additional biomarkers or inflammatory networks is needed to better understand the relationship between PUFA consumption and systemic inflammation.

Results from our MR analyses using genetic variants within/near the FADS gene cluster differed from those of the main analysis, indicating that the original results may have been biased by pleiotropy, rather than reflecting the true effect of FA biosynthesis. Even when using genetic variants that fall within the FADS gene region, which is key for FA metabolism, the instruments may lack specificity because they are also enriched in genes involved in actions such as lipoprotein metabolism [ 43 ]. We aimed to mitigate this problem through the inclusion of lipoproteins in an MVMR, although they too may be impacted by horizontal pleiotropy.

A major strength of our study is that we investigated the association between PUFAs and levels of CRP, IL-6, and GlycA by using two different methods, replicated the methods by using different cohorts, and ran further sensitivity analyses to address potential biases that arise in epidemiological research.

Despite this, we recognize several limitations. Using cross-sectional analyses means that we could not determine the temporal or causal relationship between the exposure and the outcome. However, it does provide useful context and evidence for associations between PUFA levels and biomarkers of inflammation, including GlycA, which is novel.

DHA and LA appear at different ends of FA biosynthesis pathways (DHA is a product of n-3 desaturation/elongation reactions whereas LA is a n-6 precursor), creating difficulties with direct comparisons. Additionally, the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) platform did not measure all FAs, meaning that key inflammatory metabolites may have been missed. Although our results suggest that total n-6 increases inflammation, the limited NMR coverage and pleiotropic nature of FA genetic instruments prevent us from confidently identifying the specific classes of FAs that were driving these associations. Conditioning on total fatty acid levels could introduce collider bias and therefore we did not use FAs reported as a proportion of total FAs. Subsequently, the relative abundance of each FA may have been obscured and it is harder to interpret the significance of individual FAs. Further, in some cases, reporting FAs individually may not have provided enough context regarding the overall composition of the individual’s blood, such as the overall lipid profile. Despite this, reporting individual FAs was informative, as this is the first study on their causal link with inflammation.

Another limitation is that inflammation is a latent trait that is inferred through various markers. Circulatory protein levels may not fully capture its biological complexity. Although we failed to observe anti-inflammatory properties, our findings do not rule out anti-inflammatory effects of n-3 PUFAs and work is needed to understand this multifaceted relationship. However, given that the focus of this work was to examine the relationship between PUFAs and systemic inflammation, CRP, IL-6, and GlycA are appropriate, as they reflect broad inflammatory activity.

Lastly, although the FADS gene cluster encodes enzymes that are fundamental to PUFA biosynthesis, suggesting that IVs within this region are more likely to satisfy MR assumptions, FADS variants have been shown to be highly pleiotropic [ 46 ] and do not differentiate n-3 or n-6 effects. As such, our gene-based analyses may have captured pathways to inflammation through factors other than PUFAs, thus violating the exclusion–restriction assumption [28] .

Given the popularity of n-3 PUFAs supplements [ 47–49 ], our results are of public health importance. Replication could shift messaging toward reducing total n-6 PUFA consumption and promoting a healthy, balanced n-6:n-3 ratio to lower inflammation. However, we acknowledge that n-3 PUFAs have benefits beyond their posited anti-inflammatory effects, e.g. hypotriglyceridaemic properties [ 50 ], and that some anti-inflammatory effects may not have been captured by our biomarkers. A better understanding of n-6 and n-3 interactions is needed before policy change.
Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the ALSPAC Ethics and Law Committee and the Local Research Ethics Committee and can be found here at http://www.bristol.ac.uk/alspac/researchers/research-ethics/ . Informed consent for the use of data collected via questionnaires and clinics was obtained from participants following the recommendations of the ALSPAC Ethics and Law Committee at the time. Consent for biological samples has been collected in accordance with the Human Tissue Act (2004). UKB has approval from the North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee as a Research Tissue Bank. Code for data management and statistical analysis has been made available in daisycrick (github.com) . Cohort analyses were performed by using STATA version 17.0. All other analyses were performed by using R Software version 4.1.0.

category.Rationale: The passage presents a comprehensive epidemiological investigation that integrates multiple advanced analytical methods to assess the relationship between polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and systemic inflammation. The study employs a multi-method approach, including traditional observational epidemiological analyses (linear regression in ALSPAC and UK Biobank cohorts), Mendelian randomization (MR) with multiple sensitivity methods (inverse-variance weighted, MR-Egger, weighted median), multivariable MR (MVMR) to account for confounding by lipids, and gene-based MR focusing on the FADS and ELOVL2 loci. Additionally, the authors use MR-Clust to explore heterogeneity and MR-Lap to assess bias from sample overlap and weak instruments. These methods are explicitly designed to infer causal effects, handle confounding and pleiotropy, and evaluate the robustness of findings—hallmarks of advanced methodological evaluation in epidemiology. The passage emphasizes methodological rigor, replication across cohorts, and sensitivity analyses, all of which fall squarely within the scope of Class 5. The primary goal is not to describe population occurrence or determine susceptibility, but to critically evaluate the validity and reliability of causal inferences using sophisticated statistical and genetic methods. This makes Class 5 the most appropriate for guiding multi-step inference questions that require reasoning about study design, bias mitigation, method selection, and interpretation of causal estimates across different analytical frameworks.

topic.Description: Selects designs and identification strategies and defines effect measures for causal estimation.
topic.Rationale: The passage presents a comprehensive epidemiological investigation into the causal relationship between polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and systemic inflammation, using a multi-method approach that integrates observational cohort analyses with advanced genetic methods, particularly Mendelian randomization (MR) and multivariable MR (MVMR). The study explicitly aims to move beyond correlation to infer causality, addressing key challenges such as confounding, reverse causation, and pleiotropy. The use of instrumental variables (SNPs) from GWAS, sensitivity analyses (MR-Egger, weighted median), and MVMR to isolate independent effects of n-3 and n-6 PUFAs—while adjusting for lipids and other metabolic factors—demonstrates a deliberate and sophisticated selection of causal inference strategies. The authors also critically evaluate the validity of their instruments, assess potential biases (e.g., pleiotropy, sample overlap), and use triangulation across cohorts (ALSPAC and UK Biobank) to strengthen causal claims. This focus on methodological rigor in causal estimation—choosing appropriate designs, defining effect measures, and justifying identification assumptions—aligns most closely with Topic 3. While the passage touches on measurement (e.g., biomarker selection) and bias handling, the central theme is the systematic evaluation of causal effects, making Topic 3 the most appropriate and richest source for generating multi-step inference questions about study design choices, assumptions in MR, and the interpretation of causal estimates in the presence of complex biological pathways.

ori_question.Question: In this study, what methodological approach was most critical for distinguishing the independent effects of n-6 and n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids on inflammation, given their shared metabolic pathways and overlapping genetic influences?
Evidence: Passage: 'Both n-3 and n-6 PUFAs are metabolized by the same enzymes and compete for desaturation and elongation. Therefore, n-6 PUFAs act as competitive inhibitors of n-3 PUFAs and thus reduce the amount of end-product n-3 PUFAs that can be synthesized.'

Passage: 'We conducted a multivariable MR (MVMR) analysis [ 42 ] (MVMR-1) to estimate the independent direct causal effects of n-3 and n-6 PUFAs on the biomarkers of inflammation. Although SNPs within the FADS region should be reliable instruments of PUFAs due to their proximal relation to PUFA biosynthesis, results may be biased because the SNPs can also be associated with non-fatty acid traits, such as LDL cholesterol and triglycerides [ 43 ]. Therefore, we ran two further MVMR analyses: MVMR-2—as in MVMR-1 but also accounting for triglycerides and LDL cholesterol; and MVMR-3—as in MVMR-2 but also accounting for MUFAs and SFAs.'

Passage: 'In contrast, total n-3 FAs had no effect on GlycA or CRP after accounting for total n-6 FAs, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol. This brings into question the use of n-3 supplementation as a method to reduce systemic inflammation.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to identify the methodological approach that enabled isolation of independent causal effects. Evidence 1 establishes the biological basis for confounding: n-3 and n-6 PUFAs share metabolic pathways and compete, meaning their levels are correlated and confounding is likely. Evidence 2 introduces the multivariable Mendelian randomization (MVMR) framework as the primary method designed to address this—by adjusting for the effects of one PUFA while estimating the causal effect of the other, and further controlling for related metabolic traits (triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, MUFAs, SFAs). Evidence 3 provides the outcome of this method: after adjusting for n-6 PUFAs and other lipids, n-3 PUFAs showed no independent effect on inflammation, which would not have been detectable using univariable methods. This demonstrates that MVMR was critical for disentangling the effects. The external domain knowledge discusses drugs and inflammatory markers in angina, but does not provide relevant information about causal inference methods, genetic instruments, or metabolic pathway interactions. Therefore, it is not incorporated. The question requires multi-step reasoning: understanding biological confounding, recognizing the need for a method that controls for multiple exposures, and identifying MVMR as the solution—none of which is directly stated in any single evidence piece.
