paragraph:
In sub-Saharan Africa, the burdens of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and reproductive tract infections (RTIs) are among the highest globally. Each year, an estimated 12.4 million pregnant women are exposed to malaria infection [ 1 ] and 3 million are diagnosed with an STI or RTI [ 2 ]. Most STIs/RTIs are asymptomatic, and go undetected and untreated, yet can trigger inflammation that can increase stillbirth, preterm delivery, and low birthweight (LBW) risk [ 3 ]. To prevent malaria in pregnancy, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends monthly intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) starting in the second trimester of pregnancy [ 4 ]. No comparable intervention exists for STIs/RTIs. In sub-Saharan Africa, the WHO recommends routine screening for syphilis and HIV, while other STIs/RTIs are managed syndromically [ 5 ], potentially missing 40%–70% of the infections [ 6 ].

Over the past two decades, the spread of P. falciparum resistance to SP in Africa [ 7 ] has motivated efforts to identify alternative IPTp regimens. Dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (DP) is the leading candidate, given its potent antimalarial activity. In a recent meta-analysis [ 8 ], IPTp-DP was markedly more effective than IPTp-SP at preventing malaria, yet it did not yield superior birth outcomes. This unexpected finding raised the possibility that SP confers non-malarial benefits. Several observational studies support this hypothesis, suggesting a dose–response relationship between increased IPTp-SP doses and lower LBW risk, even in areas with very low malaria transmission [ 9 , 10 ] or high-level P. falciparum resistance to SP [ 11 ].

One possible non-malarial mechanism of SP is through its potential activity against STIs/RTIs [ 12 ]. The sulfadoxine component of SP belongs to the sulfonamide class of antibiotics, which have shown in vitro activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae , Chlamydia trachomatis , and Group B Streptococcus (GBS) [ 13–16 ]. Historically, sulfonamides were used to treat N. gonorrhoeae [ 17 , 18 ] and C. trachomatis [ 19 ], but were abandoned following the rapid emergence of resistance. Triple-sulfa vaginal cream was evaluated for bacterial vaginosis (BV) in the 1990s, but showed inferior cure rates compared with metronidazole [ 20 ]. Pyrimethamine has also been shown to inhibit Gardnerella vaginalis —a key organism implicated in BV [ 21 ]. While sulfonamides are no longer used clinically for STIs/RTIs and contemporary resistance patterns are not well characterized, these findings suggest the possible activity of SP against select STIs/RTIs.

In a recent randomized–controlled trial of IPTp among pregnant women from Kenya, Malawi, and Tanzania, monthly IPTp-SP reduced the C. trachomatis prevalence by 76% compared with IPTp-DP, despite IPTp-DP demonstrating superior malaria protection [ 3 ]. However, the trial did not assess GBS, despite prior in vitro evidence suggesting intermediate activity [ 13 ]. In light of this evidence, we hypothesized that IPTp-SP would be associated with reduced risks of STIs/RTIs and, consequently, improved birth outcomes. To evaluate this, we conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized–controlled trial of pregnant women that compared IPTp with SP, DP, or a combination of DP and SP (DP+SP).
### Study population and design

We conducted a secondary analysis of a three-arm, double-blinded, placebo-controlled randomized–controlled trial (NCT04336189) that compared monthly IPTp with SP, DP, or DP+SP for the prevention of adverse birth outcomes [ 22 ]. The trial was conducted in Busia, Uganda—an area of intense, perennial malaria transmission.

Between December 2020 and December 2023, 2757 participants were enrolled. Eligibility criteria included: age ≥16 years, HIV-negative status, viable singleton pregnancy at between 12 and 20 gestational weeks confirmed by ultrasound, and agreement to receive antenatal care and deliver at the study clinic. Participants were excluded if they reported a history of serious adverse events to study drugs or had previously received IPTp-SP in their current pregnancy. We further restricted our analyses to participants who had had a vaginal swab collected.

Intervention randomization was conducted at a 1:1:1 ratio. Study drugs were initiated at 16 or 20 gestational weeks, depending on the gestational age at enrollment, and administered every 4 weeks until delivery. SP was administered as a single dose consisting of three tablets containing 500 mg of sulfadoxine and 25 mg pyrimethamine (Kamsidar, Kampala Pharmaceutical Industries). DP was administered as three consecutive daily doses; each dose consisted of three tablets containing 40 mg of dihydroartemisinin and 320 mg of piperaquine (Duo-Cotexcin, Holley-Cotec). The first dose of the study drugs was directly observed; the second and third were taken at home. Placebo pills were given to ensure that all participants received the same number and color of tablets for each IPTp course.

### Study procedures

At enrollment, participants underwent a standardized examination, were tested for syphilis and, if positive, treated with penicillin. Home visits were conducted to collect baseline data on household characteristics and malaria-prevention measures. Routine antenatal care visits were scheduled every 4 weeks for IPTp administration, clinical assessment, and blood collection. Symptomatic STIs/RTIs were managed according to national guidelines.

At delivery, standardized procedures were used to document the delivery details, collect vaginal swabs, and assess newborn outcomes. Participants were strongly encouraged to deliver at the hospital adjacent to the study clinic; those delivering elsewhere were visited by study staff at or shortly after delivery. Swabs were rotated against the vaginal wall two to three times, rolled onto microscope slides to perform Nugent scoring for BV, and placed into an Xpert® Vaginal/Endocervical Specimen Collection Kit (SWAB/A-50, Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) for storage at –80°C. Per protocol, swabs were collected at delivery. When this was not possible due to active labor or delivery outside of the study clinic, swabs were obtained at the earliest postpartum visit (1 week post-delivery) or when swab collection could be performed safely and comfortably [ 22 ]. Additional details of the study procedures are provided in Supplementary Materials Section 2 and elsewhere [ 22 ].

### STI/RTI diagnosis

Vaginal swabs were tested for C. trachomatis , N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , and GBS by using GeneXpert qPCR (Xpert® CT/NG, Xpert® TV, and Xpert® Xpress GBS; Cepheid). Due to budgetary constraints, GBS testing was discontinued midway through the trial. BV was defined as a Nugent score of 7–10, assessed by trained, blinded microscopists [ 23 , 24 ].

### Birth outcomes

Birth outcomes included: preterm delivery (<37 gestational weeks), LBW (birthweight <2500 grams), term LBW (LBW among term infants), and small-for-gestational age (SGA; <10th percentile of birthweight-for-gestational age based on INTERGROWTH-21st standards [ 25 ]. Preterm delivery included live births and fetal losses (i.e. stillbirths and miscarriages). Due to missing birthweights for fetal losses, the LBW- and SGA-based outcomes only included live births. Stillbirths and miscarriages were rare (<2%) and not separately evaluated.

### Covariates

We used a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to guide our decisions on covariate adjustment ( Fig. 1 ). Maternal age, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), weight, and gravidity at enrollment were modeled as continuous variables. Maternal education was categorized into three levels and household-wealth tertiles were derived by using principal components analysis of common household items [ 26 ]. Current/recent alcohol use and history of any adverse delivery outcome (preterm delivery, miscarriage, or stillbirth) were assessed as binary variables at enrollment.

### Statistical analysis

This study had three objectives: (i) to compare the prevalence of STIs/RTIs between IPTp arms, (ii) to estimate associations between STIs/RTIs and adverse birth outcomes, and (iii) for STIs/RTIs associated with both IPTp-SP and adverse birth outcomes, quantify the extent to which the effects of IPTp-SP on birth outcomes are mediated through STI/RTI prevention. For Objective (i), we conducted intention-to-treat analyses by using randomized IPTp assignment. IPTp-DP served as the reference arm, assuming that DP has no antibacterial activity, and was compared with the IPTp-SP, IPTp-SP+DP, and combined IPTp-SP and IPTp-SP+DP arms. Unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated by using log-binomial regression. Prevalence differences and numbers needed to treat (NNT) were computed by using the Stata ‘margins’ command. Differences in the distribution of IPTp courses across the study arms were assessed by using the Kruskal–Wallis test.

To determine the associations between STIs/RTIs and adverse birth outcomes, we fitted multivariable Poisson regression models with robust standard errors, adjusting for the IPTp arm, household wealth, maternal age, weight, MUAC, education, current/recent alcohol use, history of adverse delivery outcome, and gravidity. Continuous variables were modeled as three-knot restricted cubic splines.

We used causal mediation analyses to estimate the effect of IPTp-SP on birth outcomes mediated through STI/RTI prevention. Analyses were conducted via the ‘CMAverse’ R package [ 27 ] using the parametric g-formula [ 28 ]. To ensure that the mediation analyses focused on biologically and statistically plausible pathways, analyses were limited to STI/RTIs that demonstrated associations with IPTp-SP and the birth outcome of interest. These decisions were guided by the magnitude of the estimated effects, supported by 95% CIs that excluded the null. Logistic regression was used for mediator and outcome models, and included an exposure–mediator interaction term, regardless of a statistically significant interaction [ 29 ]. We report the total (overall) effect and the natural indirect (mediated) and direct (non-mediated) effects. Mediation analyses excluded the IPTp-DP+SP arm to ensure that the comparisons were not affected by drug–drug interactions [ 30 ]. Percentile bootstrapped 95% CIs were computed based on 1000 simulations.

Analyses were performed by using Stata 16.1 (Stata Corp, College Station, Texas) and R (version 4.4.0, R Project for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

### Sensitivity analyses

Several sensitivity analyses were conducted. First, although it was intended that vaginal swabs would be collected at delivery, 28% ( n = 705) were obtained at delivery, 59% ( n = 1509) were obtained postpartum, and 13% ( n = 324) were missing or of unknown timing. The participant characteristics differed between samples collected at delivery vs postpartum ( Supplementary Material Section 1 ). To account for potential bias, we treated nondelivery samples as missing and performed multiple imputation (MI) by using chained equations with the ‘MISL’ R package [ 31 ], which employs an ensemble machine-learning approach (SuperLearner) for flexible model estimation. Imputed estimates were combined by using Rubin’s combining rules [ 32 ]. As an additional approach, inverse probability of selection weighting (IPSW) was used. Further methodological details are provided in Supplementary Material Section 2 .

Second, causal interpretation of the estimated effects assumes no unmeasured confounding. While randomization supports this assumption for estimating the effects of IPTp-SP, it may not hold for STI/RTI–birth outcome associations and mediation analyses. We therefore report E-values [ 27 , 33 , 34 ] to quantify the minimum strength that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the exposure and the outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to fully explain the observed effects.

Third, as fetal losses may involve different pathophysiological pathways compared with live births, we repeated STI/RTI-preterm analysis outcomes restricting to live births.
Among the 2757 participants enrolled in the parent trial, 2538 (92%) were followed to delivery and 2265 (82%) had a vaginal swab collected ( Fig. 2 ). Of these 2265 swabs, 705 (31%) were collected before delivery, 1509 (66.7%) were collected postpartum, and, for 51 (2.3%) the time of collection was unknown. Among the postpartum samples, the mean time from delivery to collection was 28 days (SD = 5). The mean age at enrollment was 24.7 years (SD = 6.3), 96% completed primary school, and 8.5% reported a prior adverse delivery outcome. Fourteen participants (0.6%) tested positive for syphilis at enrollment. Baseline characteristics were balanced across the IPTp arms ( Table 1 ). The number of IPTp courses received was comparable across the arms (median = 6 in all arms; P = .46) and compliance was high ( Supplementary Material Section 3 ).

### Effect of IPTp regimen on STI/RTI risk

During the study period, there were no syndromic diagnoses of C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae ; two participants were diagnosed with symptomatic T. vaginalis and four with BV. At delivery, the prevalence of C. trachomatis , N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , BV, and GBS colonization at or near delivery in the IPTp-DP arm (reference) was 12.4%, 2.7%, 8.3%, 43.6%, and 11.7%, respectively. Compared with the IPTp-DP arm, the IPTp-SP arm had a markedly lower prevalence of C. trachomatis at delivery [2.5% vs 12.4%; PR = 0.20 (95% CI: 0.12–0.33)], corresponding to NNT  = 10 (95% CI: 8–14) ( Fig. 3 ). Similar reductions were observed when the IPTp-DP arm was compared to the IPTp-DP+SP arm [PR = 0.26 (95% CI: 0.17–0.41)] and the combined IPTp-SP and IPTp-DP+SP arms [PR = 0.23 (95% CI: 0.16–0.33)].

The GBS prevalence was lower among participants randomized to SP-containing IPTp regimens compared to IPTp-DP [8.7% vs 11.7%, any SP: PR = 0.74 (95% CI: 0.53–1.03); NNT = 32 (95% CI: 15–200)], with the largest reduction in the IPTp-SP arm [PR = 0.65 (95% CI: 0.43–0.99); NNT = 24 (95% CI: 13–500)]. The effect sizes for N. gonorrhoeae and T. vaginalis were modest, with wide CIs that included the null. The IPTp effects on BV were attenuated after accounting for the timing of swab collection [PR MI = 1.09 (95% CI: 0.88–1.35) and PR IPSW = 1.09 (95% CI: 0.85–1.40) vs primary estimate PR = 1.17 (95% CI: 1.05–1.30)] ( Supplementary Material Section 4 ). Sensitivity analyses for other STI/RTIs were consistent with the primary results.

### Effect of STIs/RTIs on birth outcomes

In adjusted models, C. trachomatis was associated with a higher risk of preterm delivery [PR = 1.86 (95% CI: 1.07–3.25)] ( Fig. 4 ). The point estimates for N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , and GBS suggested an increased risk of preterm delivery, but were highly imprecise. For LBW-based outcomes, the associations were generally null and imprecise, except for GBS, which was associated with a 2.08-fold (95% CI: 1.06–4.08) increase in the term-LBW risk and LBW overall [PR = 1.66 (95% CI: 0.94–2.94)]. There was no clear evidence of an association between STIs/RTIs and SGA risk. BV was associated with increased preterm-delivery risk [PR = 1.48 (95% CI: 1.07–2.05)], consistent with the sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Material Section 5 ).

The E-values indicated that, for estimates with 95% CIs that excluded the null, an unmeasured confounder would need to have a PR of ≥2.0 with both the exposure and the outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to fully account for the observed effects ( Fig. 3 ). Sensitivity analyses accounting for the timing of swab collection were consistent with the primary analyses ( Supplementary Material Section 5 ). The preterm-birth estimates (excluding fetal losses) were broadly similar to those for preterm delivery ( Supplementary Material Section 6 ).

### Mediation analyses

Mediation analyses evaluated the extent to which C. trachomatis and GBS contributed to the overall differences in preterm delivery and term LBW between the IPTp arms ( Table 2 ). Compared with IPTp-DP, IPTp-SP was associated with increased preterm-delivery risk [total effect: PR = 1.39 (95% CI: 0.86–2.13)]; however, this effect was partially offset by IPTp-SP’s greater prevention of C. trachomatis [indirect effect: PR = 0.78 (95% CI: 0.57–1.03)]. In contrast, IPTp-SP was associated with lower term-LBW risk compared with IPTp-DP [total effect: PR = 0.28 (95% CI: 0.11–0.56)], which was minimally mediated through GBS prevention [% mediated: 1% (95% CI: –1% to 5%)]. The E-values for indirect effects (1.82 for C. trachomatis and 1.14 for GBS) suggested moderate robustness to unmeasured confounding for the C. trachomatis estimate, but not for GBS.
In this randomized–controlled trial comparing monthly IPTp regimens, the IPTp-SP arm had an 80% lower C. trachomatis prevalence and a 35% lower GBS prevalence at delivery than the IPTp-DP arm. These effects are noteworthy, as C. trachomatis was associated with a 1.86-fold increase in preterm delivery and GBS with a 2.08-fold increase in term LBW. There was no clear evidence to suggest that IPTp-SP influenced N. gonorrhoeae, T. vaginalis , or BV upon correcting for the timing of sample collection. Our results were highly consistent with those of a recent randomized trial that also demonstrated lower C. trachomatis prevalence among women receiving IPTp-SP, but not for N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , or BV [ 3 ]. We found that BV was associated with increased preterm delivery, consistently with prior meta-analytic evidence [ 35 ]. Collectively, our results suggest that, beyond its antimalarial activity, IPTp-SP may reduce the burden of certain STIs/RTIs, with potential downstream impacts on birth outcomes.

Mediation analyses revealed that, although IPTp-DP had a stronger overall effect than IPTp-SP on reducing preterm birth, likely reflecting its superior antimalarial activity [ 8 , 22 ], the greater impact of IPTp-SP on C. trachomatis partially offset this effect. In contrast, GBS prevention accounted for only a small fraction of the effect of IPTp-SP on term LBW, suggesting the potential involvement of other studied mechanisms, including maternal nutrient absorption [ 36 ], reductions in febrile respiratory illnesses [ 37 ], or the modulation of maternal inflammation [ 38 ]. We also cannot rule out that some of the observed differences reflect the antimalarial or non-malarial effects of IPTp-DP.

In most of sub-Saharan Africa, antenatal STI/RTI screening relies on syndromic management due to limited diagnostic capacity [ 5 ], leading to undertreatment and excess adverse pregnancy outcomes. A modeling study from South Africa estimated that 25.5% of HIV-negative and 34.6% of HIV-positive pregnant women had undiagnosed STIs, for which treatment could have prevented ∼6.3% of preterm deliveries, 10.1% of stillbirths, and 9.1% of LBW infants [ 39 ]. Our findings suggest that IPTp-SP may offer a low-cost chemoprevention strategy against C. trachomatis and GBS, which affected 11%–12% of women in our study and 14%–16% of those in other regions of sub-Saharan Africa [ 40 , 41 ]. Notably, the NNT to prevent one C. trachomatis infection was 10—a compelling figure given its associations with adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes [ 42 ]. The 35% reduction in GBS was similarly noteworthy, as GBS is not routinely screened for in resource-limited settings despite its role in neonatal sepsis, morbidity, and mortality [ 43 ]. Thus, even as the antimalarial efficacy of SP declines, its potential STI/RTI-related benefits warrant consideration as continued intervention in addition to more effective malaria-prevention strategies.

Our analysis had limitations. First, most swabs were collected postpartum. However, we do not expect this to have biased our findings, as estimates were highly consistent with those of a recent trial [ 3 ] that evaluated IPTp-SP effects on STIs/RTIs, in which the samples were collected at 32–36 gestational weeks. Moreover, sensitivity analyses, which treated postpartum results as missing and used MI or IPSW, produced estimates that were consistent with the primary results, except for BV, for which the results should be interpreted cautiously. Second, STI/RTI–birth outcome associations and mediation analyses may be subject to unmeasured confounding. However, the E-values suggested that moderately strong unmeasured confounding (RR ≥ 2.0) would be required to fully explain the observed effects. Third, we assessed a limited set of STI/RTI pathogens and the effects on other reproductive tract microbes or pathobionts is unknown. Fourth, we were unable to assess chorioamnionitis or neonatal sepsis, which may be strongly linked to STIs/RTIs. Fifth, we assumed that IPTp-DP had no antibacterial activity. If it does, then the effects of IPTp-SP on STIs/RTIs may have been underestimated. Sixth, STIs/RTIs were not measured at enrollment. Although randomization should have balanced the baseline infection risk across the study arms, the absence of baseline testing prevents distinguishing whether the effects of IPTp-SP reflect the clearance of existing infections or the prevention of incident infections. However, either mechanism is consistent with the chemoprevention role of IPTp-SP. Moreover, assessment of STIs/RTIs at or near delivery may not have fully captured infections during pregnancy, particularly those that would have naturally cleared up by the time of delivery. Lastly, the findings are not generalizable to pregnant women living with HIV, as IPTp-SP is contraindicated for those receiving daily co-trimoxazole, which remains the standard of care in malaria-endemic settings [ 44 ].

The WHO currently recommends IPTp-SP across 34 malaria-endemic African countries despite widespread antifolate resistance [ 1 , 45 ]. Our findings indicate that IPTp-SP reduces C. trachomatis by 80% and GBS by 35%, which could partially explain its positive impacts on newborn outcomes. As alternative IPTp regimens are being considered to replace SP, these ancillary effects should be appreciated, especially in settings with limited STI/RTI screening and treatment.
The study was approved by the Makerere University School of Biomedical Sciences Research Ethics Committee (SBS 714), the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (HS 2746), the Uganda National Drug Authority (CTC 0135/2020), and the University of California San Francisco Human Research Protection Program (19–29105).

category.Description: Explains how exposure arises across settings, covering behavioral, environmental, occupational, and social determinants; delineates canonical transmission routes and contact structures; interprets exposure-response with attention to measurement methods, units, detection limits, and thresholds; and situates risks within One Health interfaces involving reservoirs and vectors.
category.Rationale: The passage investigates the role of sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP), a medication used in intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp), as a potential exposure with non-malarial effects—specifically, its impact on the prevalence of sexually transmitted and reproductive tract infections (STIs/RTIs) such as *Chlamydia trachomatis* and *Group B Streptococcus* (GBS). The study evaluates how this pharmacological exposure (IPTp-SP) influences the burden of specific infections, which are themselves key determinants of adverse birth outcomes. The analysis goes beyond simple association by exploring the biological plausibility of SP’s antibacterial activity (via sulfonamide and pyrimethamine components), linking it to known in vitro effects against STI pathogens. The research also examines exposure-response relationships (e.g., dose-dependent effects, timing of administration, and impact on infection prevalence), and considers how the timing of sample collection (delivery vs. postpartum) may affect exposure assessment. Furthermore, the study situates the exposure within a broader public health context—where limited STI screening in sub-Saharan Africa leads to undetected infections and poor outcomes—highlighting the interplay between medical interventions, health systems, and population-level exposure dynamics. This rich exploration of how a pharmacological exposure (IPTp-SP) modifies the risk of infectious exposures (STIs/RTIs) and their downstream health consequences makes Class 3 the most appropriate, as it best supports multi-step inference questions about exposure mechanisms, biological plausibility, measurement challenges, and the interplay between medical interventions and infection risk in vulnerable populations.

topic.Description: Specifies the exposure metric (what/how measured), determines whether values are above/below assay limits and thresholds, and interprets exposure to infection/severity/transmissibility patterns as reported in the passage.
topic.Rationale: The passage centers on a rigorous secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial evaluating the relationship between IPTp regimen (SP, DP, or DP+SP) and both STI/RTI prevalence and adverse birth outcomes. The core of the analysis involves interpreting the exposure-response relationship between the use of IPTp-SP (a specific pharmacological exposure) and key health outcomes—specifically, the reduction in C. trachomatis and GBS colonization, and the subsequent impact on preterm delivery and low birthweight. The study quantifies these relationships using precise metrics: prevalence ratios (PRs), numbers needed to treat (NNT), and mediation effects, all of which are central to exposure-response interpretation. The passage reports how the magnitude and timing of exposure (e.g., monthly dosing, median number of courses) correlate with measurable biological outcomes, including the 80% reduction in C. trachomatis prevalence (NNT = 10) and the 35% reduction in GBS. These findings are interpreted in the context of both biological plausibility (in vitro activity of SP components) and clinical significance (impact on birth outcomes). While the study touches on mechanisms (e.g., non-malarial benefits), the primary focus is on quantifying and interpreting the strength and pattern of the exposure-response relationship between IPTp-SP and infection burden and birth outcomes. This makes Topic 3 the most appropriate, as it best supports multi-step inference questions that require integrating the exposure metric (timing, regimen, drug components), the response (infection prevalence, birth outcomes), and the interpretation of thresholds (e.g., NNT, CI overlap, mediation percentages) to assess causal pathways and public health implications.

external_info: Malaria has been reported in multiple outbreaks across several countries, including a significant event in Burundi on May 25, 1999, which involved 616,034 confirmed cases and 51 deaths. Additional outbreaks occurred in the United Republic of Tanzania in May 1998 and July 1999, and in Ethiopia in November 2024. A major outbreak was also reported in Pakistan on January 1, 2022, with 3,400,000 confirmed cases. Malaria is classified as a parasitic protozoa infectious disease and is associated with the pathway known as Malaria. The disease presents with a wide range of symptoms, including fever, chills, coma, unconsciousness, jaundice, diarrhea, vomiting, retinal hemorrhage, purpura, oliguria, pallor, pruritus, hypergammaglobulinemia, hemoglobinuria, cerebellar ataxia, birth weight abnormalities, fetal hypoxia, eye hemorrhage, consciousness disorders, neurologic manifestations, and jet lag syndrome. Several drugs are associated with the treatment or study of malaria, including Amodiaquine, Artesunate, Atovaquone, Chloroquine, Mefloquine, Pyrimethamine, Quinine, and Proguanil, among others. Some of these drugs, such as Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine, are also implicated in the disease’s pathogenesis, along with metabolic factors like bilirubin, cholesterol, and glutamic acid. Malaria is further linked to the drug combination mefloquine-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and other compounds such as artemisinin, artesunate, and various antimalarial derivatives. The disease is also associated with the pathogen Plasmodium falciparum, which is itself classified as a form of malaria.

ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to assess how timing of sample collection affects interpretation of exposure-response relationships. Evidence 1 establishes that the majority of swabs (66.7%) were collected postpartum, not at delivery, which introduces potential misclassification of infection status relative to the exposure window. Evidence 2 shows that when the timing of collection was adjusted using multiple imputation and inverse probability weighting, the effect estimate for bacterial vaginosis (BV) was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, indicating that timing can bias results. Evidence 3 reports a strong, statistically significant reduction in C. trachomatis prevalence in the IPTp-SP arm compared to IPTp-DP at delivery. The key inference is that while the primary analysis reports a strong association, the fact that most samples were collected postpartum—after the critical exposure period—raises concerns about whether the observed reduction reflects true prevention of infection during pregnancy or merely detection of clearance of pre-existing infections. The attenuation seen in BV, a condition with known fluctuating prevalence, supports the idea that postpartum sampling may dilute or obscure true treatment effects. Therefore, the interpretation of the exposure-response relationship for C. trachomatis must consider that the timing of swab collection may have introduced bias, potentially overestimating the effect of IPTp-SP if infections were cleared postpartum rather than prevented during pregnancy. The external domain knowledge, while rich in information about malaria and its treatments, does not provide relevant insight into the timing of STI testing, sample collection, or misclassification bias in pregnancy studies. Thus, it was not incorporated into the reasoning chain.

paragraph:
The Covid-19 pandemic caused an estimated 14.8 million deaths globally in 2020 and 2021 [ 1 ]. Aotearoa New Zealand used a combination of border and community control measures to minimize transmission of SARS-CoV-2 until high vaccine coverage was achieved in late 2021 [ 2 , 3 ]. Following the establishment of the B.1.1.529 (Omicron) variant in January 2022 [ 4 ], New Zealand experienced a series of Covid-19 waves [ 5 ]. By 31 December 2023, there had been a total of 750 Covid-19-attributed deaths per million people [ 6 ], one of the lowest rates in the world.

The number of Covid-19-attributed deaths is one measure of the pandemic’s impact on mortality, but it has limitations. It could be influenced by factors such as test availability, how Covid-19-attributed deaths are distinguished from incidental deaths in Covid-19-positive individuals, and processes for recording multiple causes of death. Furthermore, Covid-19-attributed deaths only measure the direct impact of the disease on mortality. This ignores indirect effects, such as deaths that occurred or were prevented as a result of pandemic control measures and deaths that would have occurred due to another cause within a given time period.

Another measure of the pandemic’s impact is excess mortality, i.e. the number of additional deaths relative to the expected number if no pandemic had occurred [ 1 ]. Various methods have been used to estimate the expected number of deaths, known as the baseline. The method of Karlinsky and Kobak [ 7 ], which has been widely used to make international comparisons of excess mortality via the Our World in Data dashboard [ 8 , 9 ], estimated cumulative excess mortality in New Zealand in 2020–23 as 99 per million. Another widely used model developed by the Economist estimated 198 per million [ 10 ], whilst Kung et al. [ 11 ] estimated excess mortality for 2020–22 as 215 per million.

The Karlinsky and Kobak [ 7 ] baseline relies on extrapolating the pre-pandemic trend in raw death counts. This may, in some cases, mainly reflect the trend in total population size if the crude mortality rate (i.e. deaths per capita) does not vary greatly. Gibson [ 12 ] correctly pointed out that, in such cases, if the trend in total population size abruptly changes, then the Karlinsky and Kobak baseline will be systematically biased. There was a sharp drop in the rate of population growth in New Zealand in 2020 due to reduced international travel. Gibson [ 12 ] argued that controlling for population size by fitting to the trend in crude mortality rate, rather than raw deaths, led to a lower baseline than that of Karlinsky and Kobak [ 7 ] and, therefore, a higher estimate of excess mortality.

However, the trend in raw deaths may also be influenced by population ageing, which would generally lead to an upward trend in crude mortality rate. For this reason, where age-stratified data are available, it is preferable to control for age when estimating mortality baselines [ 13 ]. This will limit international comparisons to jurisdictions where age-stratified data are available but will provide more accurate estimates. Neither Gibson [ 12 ] nor Kung et al. [ 11 ] controlled for age. Reliable estimates of pandemic excess mortality in New Zealand that control for the combined effects of population growth and ageing are lacking.

Here, we use age- and sex-stratified data on all-cause mortality in New Zealand to estimate excess mortality in 2020–23 relative to the pre-pandemic baseline. We compare the results of two methods: a quasi-Poisson regression model fitted to monthly age-specific death counts and a linear regression on the age-standardized annual mortality rate.

Both methods account for changes in population size and age structure, which means they provide more reliable estimates of excess mortality than methods that do not. We use the quasi-Poisson regression model as our primary method, as this allows us to disaggregate results by monthly time periods and by age and sex. We compare aggregated yearly results from this method with the standardized mortality rate linear regression to benchmark our results against a simpler model. We then compare the estimated excess to the number of Covid-19-attributed deaths over time and in different subgroups. This enables us to estimate whether there was any net non-Covid-19 excess mortality during this period.
We obtained data on monthly all-cause deaths among New Zealand residents and the Stats NZ estimated resident population [ 14 ], stratified by sex and age, up to the end of 2023. We also obtained data on the number of deaths attributed to Covid-19 [ 6 ]. See online supplementary material Section S1.1 for further details.

We used two methods for constructing a mortality baseline from pre-pandemic data: (i) a generalized linear quasi-Poisson regression model for monthly death counts including age, sex, and month of the year as predictors, based closely on the model of the UK’s Office for National Statistics [ 15 ]; (ii) a linear regression fitted to the age- and sex-standardized annual mortality rate. Quasi-Poisson regression is a natural model for count data whilst allowing for the possibility that the variance may be higher than in a Poisson regression. See online supplementary material Section S1.2 for further details.

We fitted each model to all-cause mortality data from January 2014 to December 2019. Using a 6-year baseline is a compromise between shorter baselines, which are more sensitive to annual fluctuations in death rates, and longer baselines, which are biased by the nonlinear shape of annual mortality rates over time. We conducted a sensitivity analysis with different lengths of baseline ranging from 4 to 10 years.

We used the fitted baseline to estimate expected deaths from January 2020 to December 2023 if pre-pandemic trends had continued. We calculated excess mortality as the difference between actual deaths and expected deaths.
In the pre-pandemic period, all-cause monthly deaths in the New Zealand resident population had a pronounced seasonal pattern, with relatively high deaths during the winter (i.e. June–August) respiratory disease season ( Fig. 1 ). The quasi-Poisson regression model captured the seasonality and the gradually increasing trend in deaths. The age- and sex-standardized yearly all-cause mortality rate varied between 7.0 and 7.9 per 1000 between 2010 and 2019, with a decreasing trend ( Fig. 2 ). The model standardized yearly mortality rate was very similar under the two methods.

The number of excess deaths according to the quasi-Poisson regression model was −2276 [95% confidence interval (CI) (−2663, −1941)] in 2020; −654 (−1144, −228) in 2021; 2735 (2141, 3252) in 2022; and 1235 (531, 1858) in 2023 ( Fig. 3a , red). The cumulative excess for 2020–23 was 1040 (−1134, 2927), which equates to 204 (−222, 573) per million and to 0.7% (−0.8%, 2.0%) of expected mortality. The standardized mortality rate linear regression model gave very similar results ( Fig. 3a , yellow).

Covid-19-attributed deaths were extremely low in 2020 and 2021 (26 in each year). In 2022–23, the number of Covid-19-attributed deaths was close to the central estimate for excess deaths ( Fig. 3a , blue), accounting for 102% of the estimated excess in 2022 and 82% in 2023, and fell within the 95% CI in both years.

Looking at monthly data ( Fig. 3b ), Covid-19 deaths and excess deaths, according to the quasi-Poisson regression model, followed similar trends in 2022–23. The number of Covid-19 deaths was below the 95% CI for excess deaths in February and March 2022, and above it from July to September 2022. The unexplained excess in early 2022 could represent unattributed Covid-19 deaths that occurred when the country’s laboratory testing capacity became overwhelmed [ 16 ]. The monthly discrepancies could also partly reflect temporal displacement of mortality due to disruption of seasonal respiratory disease patterns [ 17 ].

The number of Covid-19 deaths fell within the 95% CI for the number of excess deaths in each age band (0–59 years, 60–69 years, 70–79 years, and 80+ years) and for both sexes in 2022 and 2023 ( Fig. 4 ). Note we used these four age bands because appropriate data on Covid-19 deaths were available for comparison (see online supplementary material, Fig. S1 for results disaggregated into finer age groups). The results in Fig. 4 mirror similar patterns seen in Australia [ 18 ], where there was some positive non-Covid excess in the 70–79-year age band and, despite there being more Covid-19 deaths among men than women, the central estimate for excess deaths was higher for women.

When different pre-pandemic fitting periods were used, the estimated number of excess deaths for 2020–23 according to the quasi-Poisson regression model varied between a low of −1770 (−4973, 924) for the 4-year baseline, and a high of 1995 (500, 3368) for the 9-year baseline ( Table 1 ). Expressed as a percentage of expected deaths, these correspond to a low of −1.2% (−3.4%, 0.6%) and a high of 1.4% (0.4%, 2.4%). The estimate from our default baseline of 6 years (2014–19) ranked third out of the seven baselines investigated. The 95% CI for the quasi-Poisson model contained zero in all cases except for the 9-year baseline. The results of the standardized mortality rate linear regression model showed a similar pattern with respect to baseline length. In both models, the variations in estimated excess seen in Table 1 were mainly driven by whether or not the first year in the fitting period had a relatively high all-cause death rate.

The Karlinksy and Kobak estimate for 2020–23 of 517 excess deaths [ 7 , 9 ] falls within the 95% CI for all seven baselines. The Economist estimate of 1026 excess deaths [ 10 ] is very close to our central estimate of 1040 for the 6-year baseline, is within the 95% CI for five of the seven baselines, and slightly above it for other two. These estimates are therefore largely consistent with our results. In contrast, Gibson estimated +4% excess mortality for the 3-year period of 2020–22 using a 5-year baseline, which translates to ∼4000 excess deaths [ 12 ]. This estimate, which failed to control for changes in population age structure, is 4500 deaths higher than our central estimate for this period using a 5-year baseline, and 2500 deaths higher than the highest upper limit of the 95% CI for ‘any’ baseline length between 4 and 10 years (see online supplementary material, Table S1 ).
We have estimated the number of excess deaths in Aotearoa New Zealand between January 2020 and December 2023 using two different methods. Importantly, both methods controlled for age, sex, and population size (one by including these variables as predictors in a regression model, and one by using an age- and sex-standardized mortality rate). This avoids the potential for systematic biases caused by changes in population size or age structure.

To comprehensively measure the impact of the pandemic on deaths, estimates need to include the period after most non-pharmaceutical interventions were removed and the virus became endemic. However, the longer pre-pandemic baselines are extrapolated forward in time, the greater the uncertainty and potential for bias due to nonlinear trends over time. In New Zealand, most remaining interventions ended in September 2022 [ 19 ], except for mask requirements in healthcare and aged residential care settings and isolation requirements for confirmed cases, which continued until August 2023 [ 20 ]. Choosing the period from January 2020 to December 2023 is a reasonable trade-off that allows enough time for the transmission dynamics to settle into a relatively steady pattern without extrapolating pre-pandemic trends too far. Organizations estimating excess deaths in the UK [ 15 ] and Australia [ 18 ] have adopted a similar approach, moving to a new baseline from 2024 that partly includes the pandemic period.

Consistent with other methods [ 7 , 10 ], both our models estimated negative excess mortality in 2020 and, to a lesser extent, 2021. This was likely due to the effective suppression of Covid-19 (there were only 52 Covid-19 deaths in 2020–21), the elimination of influenza [ 21 ], and the reduction in other respiratory pathogens during this period [ 17 , 22 ].

Our models estimated positive excess mortality in 2022 and 2023, after New Zealand ended its elimination strategy and the Omicron variant became established. The magnitude, timing, and age-distribution of the excess closely matched those of Covid-19-attributed deaths. This suggests that the bulk of the excess in 2022–23 was directly attributable to Covid-19, either as an underlying or a contributory cause of death. This could be because there were relatively few Covid-19 deaths that were not recorded as such. Alternatively, it could be that any undocumented Covid-19 deaths were offset by reduced mortality from other causes, such as non-Covid respiratory disease.

The timing of the excess does not coincide with the timing of the Covid-19 vaccine rollout, the bulk of which occurred between February 2021 and February 2022 (more than 10 million doses were administered in this period). Excess deaths were either negative or close to zero for most of this period. In contrast, the period during which excess deaths were relatively high (March 2022 to April 2023) coincided with a period where far fewer vaccine doses (fewer than 1.7 million) were administered. This suggests that vaccines were not responsible for any substantial portion of the excess mortality, consistent with New Zealand safety data [ 23 ] and international research showing very low risk of severe adverse events following Covid-19 vaccination [ 21 ].

Mortality rates fluctuate from year to year depending on the severity of the winter respiratory illness season and other factors. This means that the fitted baseline for expected mortality can be sensitive to the choice of fitting period. To mitigate this, we ran our model with seven different fitting periods ranging from 4 to 10 years duration. The limits of the 95% CIs for excess mortality for 2020–23 fell between −3.4% and +2.4% and contained zero for all but one choice of fitting period. Thus, our results provide robust evidence that, regardless of the choice of baseline, there was no more than 2.4% cumulative excess mortality between 2020 and 2023, and any net excess that did occur cannot be confidently distinguished from zero.

We have not attempted to apply our method to estimate excess mortality in countries other than New Zealand, as this is beyond the scope of the study. Nevertheless, our estimated excess mortality of 204 (−222, 573) deaths per million people for 2020–23 ranks amongst the lowest in the world. Estimated excess mortality for 2020–23 for most OECD countries (with a few notable exceptions, including Australia) was in the range of 1500–4500 per million [ 7–9 ].

Gibson [ 12 ] argued that, by extrapolating raw death counts and not accounting for the abrupt drop in population growth in 2020, the Karlinksy and Kobak method [ 7 ] systematically overestimated expected mortality and therefore underestimated excess deaths. However, although population growth slowed dramatically during the pandemic, this was largely a result of reduced migration, which occurs predominantly in younger groups [ 24 ]. The population over 65 years of age (which is only around 15% of the total population but accounts for 80% of deaths) continued to grow at a rate similar to before the pandemic (see online supplementary material, Fig. S2 ). By controlling for total population size but not for age, Gibson’s method introduced a systematic bias and consequently underestimated expected mortality for 2020–22 by ∼4%. The main advantage of the method of Karlinsky and Kobak [ 7 ] is that it can be applied to a large set of countries to provide a meaningful and useful basis for international comparisons. Despite not controlling for population size or age, the Karlinksy and Kobak estimate was within the 95% CIs from our model. This is because the pre-pandemic trend in death counts was driven more by population ageing (which continued throughout the pandemic) than by population growth (which did not).

Our study has a number of important limitations. Due to reporting delays, there could be ∼40 deaths that occurred in 2023 that do not yet appear in the data. Hence, our results could underestimate excess deaths for 2023 by around 40, but we note this difference is much smaller than the model CIs.

We have compared estimates of all-cause excess mortality with Covid-19-attributed deaths. It is likely that the pandemic differentially impacted various causes of death at different times. This could be investigated by estimating excess mortality associated with different causes of death [ 18 ]. However, we have not attempted this due to a lack of up-to-date data on causes of death other than Covid-19.

Our model lumped all deaths over 95 years of age into a single age class. This was necessary because population size data were only available at this level. The size of the over-95-year age group increased from 5130 in 2014 (Q1) to 8530 in 2023 (Q4). It is likely that the age-distribution within this group became increasingly elderly over time, which would influence the group-specific mortality rate. This is mitigated by the inclusion of an interaction term in the quasi-Poisson model, which allows a group-specific linear trend in the mortality rate. Nevertheless, the model cannot explicitly account for any shift in the age distribution within the group that may have occurred between 2019 and 2023.

Covid-19 in New Zealand disproportionately affected Māori, Pacific Peoples, and people living with high levels of deprivation [ 25–27 ]. This mirrors well-documented international trends [ 28 , 29 ], whereby social determinants of health intersect with factors affecting people’s ability to take protective measures, such as working from home [ 30 ]. Our analysis did not include socioeconomic variables such as ethnicity or deprivation because the required data were not available. Investigating how excess mortality in 2022 and 2023 was distributed across these axes and how this relates to the distribution of Covid-19 deaths is an important aim for future research.
Ethics approval was not required for this research as it only used routinely collected administrative data, which were de-identified and aggregated prior to use.

category.Rationale: The passage is fundamentally centered on the development, application, and evaluation of statistical methods to estimate excess mortality in New Zealand during the COVID-19 pandemic. It critically compares multiple modeling approaches—specifically, a quasi-Poisson regression model and a linear regression on age- and sex-standardized mortality rates—each designed to account for confounding factors such as population size, age structure, and seasonal trends. The authors conduct sensitivity analyses across different baseline periods (4–10 years), assess model robustness, and evaluate the impact of methodological choices (e.g., controlling for age vs. raw death counts) on the resulting estimates. The discussion explicitly addresses measurement bias, model limitations, and the trade-offs between accuracy and generalizability. These elements align precisely with the core focus of Class 5: the rigorous evaluation of analytical methods, including bias handling, model selection, and causal inference in epidemiological data. The passage does not primarily aim to describe disease occurrence (Surveillance), investigate an outbreak (Outbreak), explore exposures (Determinants), assess immunity (Susceptibility), or generate forecasts (Projections). Instead, it exemplifies methodological evaluation in action—making Class 5 the most appropriate and richest source for generating multi-step inference questions about model validity, bias mitigation, and comparative method performance.

topic.Description: Addresses measurement validity, misclassification and measurement error, confounding and selection, generalizability, survey weighting, and sample size.
topic.Rationale: The passage centers on the methodological challenges and solutions in measuring the true impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on mortality through excess mortality estimation. It critically evaluates different approaches—such as the Karlinsky and Kobak method, Gibson’s adjustment for population size, and Kung et al.’s model—highlighting how each may introduce bias due to uncontrolled factors like population growth, ageing, and changes in data reporting. The authors explicitly address measurement validity by comparing models that control for age, sex, and population size (via quasi-Poisson regression and age-standardized rates) versus those that do not. They conduct sensitivity analyses on baseline length, assess the impact of reporting delays, and discuss limitations related to data granularity (e.g., lumping over-95s into one group, lack of socioeconomic data). These are all core concerns under 'Measurement & bias handling'. While the study also involves estimation of effectiveness (e.g., comparing excess to Covid-19 deaths), the primary focus is on the robustness and validity of the measurement process itself. This makes Topic 4 the most appropriate, as it enables multi-step inference questions about how methodological choices affect estimates, how biases propagate, and how to assess the reliability of different metrics in real-world epidemiological surveillance.

external_info: Respiratory tract diseases are associated with a wide range of environmental and chemical agents, including air pollutants, heavy metals such as arsenic and manganese, industrial chemicals like carbon monoxide and chlorpyrifos, tobacco smoke, particulate matter, and various pesticides. Specific substances such as nicotine, sulfur dioxide, ozone, and vehicle emissions are also linked to these conditions. Additionally, certain drugs including doxorubicin, etomidate, fentanyl, ketamine, midazolam, and disinfecants have been associated with respiratory tract diseases, with bilirubin identified as playing a role in disease pathogenesis. The condition is further related to broader categories such as respiratory system diseases NOS and respiratory system disease, which are classified as diseases of anatomical entities. Influenza, a viral infectious disease, is associated with drugs such as oseltamivir, amantadine, rimantadine, azithromycin, and resveratrol, and is linked to the Influenza A pathway. It shares a classification as a viral infectious disease. COVID-19, which is classified as a coronavirus infectious disease, is associated with a broad spectrum of pharmaceutical agents, including antivirals such as remdesivir, lopinavir-ritonavir, and chloroquine, as well as drugs like baricitinib, hydroxychloroquine, and interferon alfa. Other agents linked to COVID-19 include acalabrutinib, ivermectin, and various compounds such as emodin, galidesivir, and sirolimus.

ori_question.Question: In this study, what methodological choice was most critical to ensuring that the estimated excess mortality was not biased by changes in the population's age structure over time?
Evidence: Passage: 'We used two methods for constructing a mortality baseline from pre-pandemic data: (i) a generalized linear quasi-Poisson regression model for monthly death counts including age, sex, and month of the year as predictors, based closely on the model of the UK’s Office for National Statistics [ 15 ]; (ii) a linear regression fitted to the age- and sex-standardized annual mortality rate.'
Passage: 'Both methods account for changes in population size and age structure, which means they provide more reliable estimates of excess mortality than methods that do not.'

Passage: 'Gibson [ 12 ] argued that, by extrapolating raw death counts and not accounting for the abrupt drop in population growth in 2020, the Karlinksy and Kobak method [ 7 ] systematically overestimated expected mortality and therefore underestimated excess deaths.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to answer a question about methodological bias. Evidence 1 identifies the two primary analytical methods used in the study: a quasi-Poisson regression model that includes age and sex as predictors, and a linear regression on age- and sex-standardized mortality rates. This establishes that the study explicitly incorporated demographic variables into its modeling framework. Evidence 2 states that both methods were designed to account for changes in population size and age structure, which directly addresses the core concern of the question—how to avoid bias from demographic shifts. Evidence 3 provides a counterexample: the Karlinsky and Kobak method, which did not control for age structure, was shown to produce biased estimates due to unaccounted-for changes in population dynamics. This highlights the importance of adjusting for age structure, especially when population growth patterns shift abruptly. The question asks which methodological choice was most critical to avoiding bias from age structure changes. The correct answer must be the inclusion of age and sex as predictors in the regression model or the use of age-standardized rates—both of which are explicitly stated in the passage as the key mechanisms for handling this bias. The external domain knowledge discusses pharmaceutical agents and environmental factors related to respiratory diseases but does not provide any information relevant to measurement bias, confounding, or demographic adjustment in mortality estimation. Therefore, it is not incorporated into the evidence. The question is not answered by a single sentence but requires synthesizing the study’s design with the critique of alternative methods to infer that controlling for age and sex was the critical methodological safeguard.

paragraph:
The cognitive health of older adults is a growing global concern. Cognitive decline, particularly in episodic memory, often represents an early stage in the neurodegenerative process that, if progressive and accompanied by deficits in other cognitive domains, can eventually lead to dementia [ 1 ]. In 2015, approximately 47 million people were living with dementia, with projections indicating a 1.6-fold increase to 75 million by 2030 [ 2 ]. In response to rapidly aging populations, many developed countries are raising their state pension age (SPA). These policy changes may affect cognitive health by delaying retirement, thereby altering individuals’ budgetary constraints and time allocation between work and leisure in later life [ 3 ].

Despite numerous studies using identical datasets, the effects of retirement on cognition remain uncertain, with no clear consensus emerging [ 4 , 5 ]. For example, studies using Health and Retirement Study (HRS) data have yielded contradictory findings, with some demonstrating a detrimental association of retirement with cognitive function [ 6 , 7 ], whereas others show no association [ 8 ]. Similarly, research utilizing data from the English Longitudinal Study on Ageing (ELSA) or the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) has produced inconsistent results. While several studies reported harmful associations [ 9 , 10 ], others found no relationship [ 11–14 ], and some even suggested beneficial associations [ 15 , 16 ].

Several factors may contribute to these inconsistencies in the literature. First, model misspecification can influence effect estimates. A review replicating previous studies demonstrated that the choice of statistical methodologies is a key determinant of findings [ 5 ]. Additionally, effect heterogeneity introduces another source of variation. Studies have shown that the association between retirement and cognitive function varies by individual characteristics such as sex, education, and pre-retirement occupation [ 10 , 12 , 17–20 ]. When adverse effects in one subgroup mask positive effects in others, the overall population treatment effect becomes ambiguous. Nonetheless, the full extent of heterogeneity in this relationship remains poorly understood.

To address these challenges, we applied instrumental variable causal forests (IV forests) [ 21 ] to investigate the conditional average treatment effect (ATE) of retirement on cognitive function. We employed country-specific SPA as an instrument for retirement to address the endogenous nature of retirement decisions. The IV forests method incorporates random-forest-based nonparametric estimation, offering greater robustness against model misspecification compared to conventional parametric approaches. Our analysis utilized harmonized data from 19 countries and incorporated 60 covariates as potential confounders and effect modifiers. This machine learning-based approach enables us to uncover previously hidden effect heterogeneity in the association between retirement and cognitive function.
### Study design and participants

This study used harmonized panel datasets from the HRS, ELSA, and SHARE provided by the Gateway to Global Aging Data project [ 22 ]. Our data encompassed three waves: covariates (excluding age) were obtained from the HRS and ELSA in 2014 and SHARE in 2015; age and labor force status were ascertained via the HRS and ELSA in 2016 and SHARE in 2017; and cognitive function outcomes were assessed in the HRS and ELSA in 2018 and SHARE in 2019. To prevent retirement from influencing covariates, we collected covariate information from the wave preceding retirement status measurement. Furthermore, we measured outcomes at least 2 years after retirement, acknowledging the potential temporal lag in retirement’s impact on cognitive function [ 12 ].

Among 94 824 individuals who participated in the first wave, 49 555 completed all three waves. We included 43 052 individuals aged 50–80 years from the second wave, but excluded 29 519 individuals who were not working in the first wave and 722 individuals who neither worked nor retired in the second wave (e.g. unemployed, disabled, or homemaker). The final sample comprised 12 811 participants for IV forests development ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). To assess the potential impact of attrition, we compared baseline characteristics between included and excluded individuals (12 033 individuals who aged under 78 years and worked in the first wave but were excluded from the analysis). Supplementary Table S1 shows that there was no difference in the baseline cognitive function between included retirees and excluded individuals.

### Cognitive function assessment

Episodic memory was assessed as a measure of cognitive function. Episodic memory involves the ability to recall past experiences, which typically declines with age [ 23 ]. The assessment followed the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD) Battery protocol [ 24 ]. Participants listened to 10 common words and were immediately asked by an interviewer to recall as many words as possible. After approximately 5 minutes, they were asked to recall the words again. Hence, the total number of words recalled, ranging from 0 to 20, represented their episodic memory function, consistent with previous studies [ 5–8 , 10–13 , 15 , 16 ].

### Retirement status classification

Labor force status was self-reported in the surveys ( Supplementary Method S1 ). We focused on individuals who were working during the first wave. In the second wave, we defined retirees as those who self-identified as “retired” or “partly retired,” regardless of current working status, aligning with previous literature ( Supplementary Table S2 ) [ 15 , 17 , 20 , 25 ]. While some studies have defined retirement simply as not working [ 6 , 10 , 11 , 14 ], we tested our findings’ robustness using this narrower definition.

### State pension age implementation

To address potential endogenous retirement decision bias, we employed the SPA as an IV for retirement ( Supplementary Table S3 ). Following previous research [ 11 , 20 , 25 , 26 ], we used joint instruments including the early retirement age (ERA) and official retirement age (ORA). The binary ERA variable indicated whether participants had reached the earliest age for receiving reduced or full pension benefits under specific conditions. The ORA variable denoted whether participants had reached the age for receiving a minimum guaranteed or full pension without conditions. For countries without early retirement schemes, the ERA variable was set to zero.

The SPA serves as a valid IV by increasing retirement probability (relevance condition) without directly affecting cognition (exclusion restriction condition). Assuming monotonicity, the point estimate represents a local ATE among individuals who would retire upon reaching SPA. Our study leverages within-country SPA variations (institutional differences across birth cohorts and sexes) and between-country variations using harmonized data. Retirement rates demonstrably increase around the SPA ( Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 ), supporting the relevance condition.

### Statistical analysis

We compared ATEs using parametric ordinary least squares (OLS), two-stage least squares (2SLS), nonparametric causal forests without IVs (non-IV forests), and IV forests. For parametric methods, we adjusted for 10 covariates selected by importance in trained IV forests. ATEs for nonparametric methods were obtained through residual-on-residual regressions [ 27 ].

The IV forests method combines the generalized method of moments for IV estimation with random forests to identify similar treatment effects ( Supplementary Method S2 ). The IV forests incorporated 60 harmonized covariates from the first wave ( Supplementary Tables S4 and S5 ). To mitigate potential reverse causality, we included the baseline score of cognitive function. Missing values were imputed using a random forests-based algorithm [ 28 ], assuming data missing at random ( Supplementary Table S6 ). After training, we restricted the analysis to 7432 individuals with retirement propensity scores between 0.1 and 0.9 [ 29 ], as extreme scores destabilize estimation. Our estimand of the IV forests represents the conditional local ATE on the overlap population (CLATO).

We then categorized observations into quintiles from Q1 (the lowest CLATO; least retirement benefits) to Q5 (highest CLATO; most retirement benefits), and compared sociodemographic characteristics, health and behaviors, and countries across quintiles. P -values were adjusted using the Bonferroni method. All analyses were performed using R 4.1.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

### Sensitivity analyses

We performed several sensitivity analyses to confirm the robustness of our findings. These included: restricting the sample to ages 55–75, excluding partially retired individuals, analyzing only full-time employees, and excluding US data with the largest number of samples.
### Descriptive statistics

The study population comprised 7432 individuals, of whom 2165 (29.1%) were retirees in the second wave ( Table 1 ). On average, workers could recall 11.1 words, while retirees could recall 10.8 words in the third wave. The outcome showed a normal distribution ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ).

### Association between retirement and cognitive function

Initial analyses using OLS and non-IV forests revealed no evidence of the association between retirement and cognitive function ( Table 2 ). However, 2SLS presented a positive association between retirement and word recall (0.962, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.287–1.637). The validity of our IVs was supported by an F statistic of 163.037 ( P < .0001) and a Sargan statistic of 1.177 ( P = .28). IV forests corroborated these findings, indicating that retirees recalled 1.348 more words than workers (95% CI: 0.313–2.384). Variable importance metrics from the IV forests are presented in the Supplementary Fig. S5 .

### Heterogeneity across individual characteristics and countries

The distribution of conditional ATEs, detailed in the Supplementary Fig. S6 , showed marked differences between non-IV and IV forests. While non-IV forest estimates clustered around zero, IV forest estimates exhibited heterogeneous distribution. The ATEs increased monotonically with CLATO ranking from Q1 to Q5, suggesting that IV forests captured heterogeneity in retirement’s effect on cognitive function ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ).

Analysis of sociodemographic characteristics across CLATO quintiles shown in Fig. 1 revealed distinct patterns. Individuals in the highest CLATO group (Q5) were more likely to be older, female, native-born, and have fewer than three children compared to those in the lowest group (Q1). They also demonstrated higher education levels and greater assets and income. Occupationally, clerks, professionals, and part-time workers were more prevalent in the highest group, whereas service workers, sales personnel, manual laborers, those in physically demanding jobs, and the self-employed were more commonly represented in the lowest group.

Health and well-being metrics also showed variation across CLATO groups ( Fig. 2 ). The highest CLATO group reported better self-rated health, life satisfaction, eyesight, and hearing. Conversely, the lowest CLATO group showed a higher prevalence of various health conditions, including depressive symptoms, hypertension, diabetes, lung and heart diseases, arthritis, psychiatric problems, hyperlipidemia, work limitations, difficulties in activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental ADL (IADL), and pain-related problems. Obesity was more common in the lowest CLATO group, while regular physical activity was associated with the highest group.

In Fig. 3 , geographic analysis revealed that individuals from Denmark and Greece were more likely to fall into higher CLATO groups, whereas those from Estonia and France typically belonged to lower CLATO groups. Age-related analysis showed CLATO estimates increased until age 65 before plateauing. Individuals with average or below-average assets and income showed greater CLATO variations, while those with higher assets and income typically maintained higher CLATO values ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ).

### Sensitivity analyses

Sensitivity analyses maintained the robustness of our findings across various specifications ( Supplementary Table S7 ). These included: restricting the sample to ages 55–75 (Model 1), excluding partially retired individuals (Model 2), analyzing only full-time employees (Model 3), and excluding US data with the largest number of samples (Model 4). ATE estimates remained consistent with our main findings across all specifications.
This study examined the heterogeneous relationship between retirement and cognitive function using harmonized data from 19 countries. Our findings revealed enhanced cognitive function among retirees compared to workers, with conditional ATEs varying according to individual characteristics and countries.

The association observed in our study contrasts with previous research suggesting cognitive decline post-retirement [ 6 , 7 , 9 , 10 ], while aligning with studies indicating beneficial associations [ 15 , 16 ]. The absence of associations in OLS and non-IV forests analyses highlights the importance of methodological choice, suggesting potential negative bias due to health-related selection into retirement. The IV forests method, with its data-driven, nonparametric features, offers greater robustness against model misspecification compared to conventional parametric approaches. The observed improvement of 1.348 words in IV forests represents a substantial effect, corresponding to a 0.42 SD in outcome distribution. According to a systematic review for the effect size of educational interventions on cognition, that of over 0.2 SD is meaningful from a public health perspective [ 30 ]. Several mechanisms may explain cognitive enhancement post-retirement. Job strain, a recognized risk factor for cognitive decline [ 31 ], is eliminated upon retirement, reducing psychosocial stress. Additionally, retirees can dedicate more time to health-promoting behaviors, such as increased physical activity, improved sleep quality, and smoking cessation [ 32 ], which are protective against cognitive decline.

The association between retirement and cognitive function demonstrated notable heterogeneity. Women showed greater cognitive benefits from retirement than men, consistent with evidence indicating women’s higher likelihood of maintaining physical and mental health through post-retirement exercise [ 17 , 20 ]. Similarly, individuals who exercised before retirement were more likely to experience cognitive benefits, suggesting the importance of pre-existing health behaviors maintained into retirement.

Our findings align with the Grossman model [ 3 ], particularly regarding socioeconomic factors. Individuals with higher education, assets, and income demonstrated greater retirement benefits. The model suggests that while retirees have more time but reduced budgets for health investments, those with high socioeconomic status can better afford cognitive health investments. Additionally, better pre-retirement health correlated with enhanced post-retirement cognitive function, consistent with the model’s prediction that healthier individuals have more time for health investments. This relationship between pre-retirement health limitations and post-retirement cognitive function supports previous empirical research [ 33 ].

Occupational characteristics influenced retirement outcomes. Professionals showed greater cognitive benefits compared to those retiring from manual labor and physically demanding jobs, supporting previous research linking retirement from complex, mentally demanding occupations to slower cognitive decline [ 18 , 19 ]. Conversely, retirement from physically demanding jobs showed fewer cognitive benefits, aligning with studies associating such occupations with increased dementia risk [ 34 , 35 ]. This pattern may reflect the combination of high physical demands with low job control, resulting in reduced cognitive stimulation [ 14 ], suggesting workplace cognitive stimulation influences post-retirement cognitive outcomes.

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, our analysis focused on short-term effects, measuring cognitive function two years post-retirement. While previous SHARE research showed early retirement benefits, it also indicated potential negative effects of late [ 16 ]. Further research on long-term effects is needed. Second, our heterogeneity analysis was exploratory, with potential confounding between variables, such as education and occupation. Third, despite including 60 candidate variables, unmeasured factors like traumatic brain injury, social isolation, and air pollution might influence retirement’s effect on cognitive function [ 36 ]. Fourth, self-reported data may introduce measurement errors though word recall tests have demonstrated predictive validity for dementia onset [ 37 ]. Fifth, findings may not generalize beyond Western countries, highlighting the need for comparable studies in rapidly aging Asian nations. Sixth, despite expert harmonization, inter-survey discrepancies may persist. Seventh, our causal inference relies on the validity of the IV. Although the SPA has been widely used as an IV for retirement [ 4 , 5 ], the assumption of exclusion restriction is not testable. The SPA makes individuals anticipate retirement and may affect their behaviors and mental health, such as starting exercise, undergoing preventive care, or experiencing financial stress. A study using data from the SHARE demonstrated that individuals planning to retire in the next two years had a reduced risk of depression compared with other workers [ 26 ]. If such changes in behaviors and mental health before anticipated retirement affect cognitive function, the exclusion restriction assumption can be violated. However, the overidentification test in our 2SLS estimation did not show evidence of its violation.

In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that retirement’s impact on cognitive function varies with individual characteristics and countries. This heterogeneity suggests policymakers should consider incorporating flexible early retirement options into pension systems, allowing individuals to make retirement decisions based on personal circumstances. A machine-learning-based prediction tool could enable individuals to determine optimal retirement timing by evaluating their specific characteristics.
Our study used publicly available data that have obtained with informed consent from all participants and ethical approval from relevant local ethics committees. Thus, the Ethics Committee of Kyoto University exempted this study from review.

Alzheimer's disease is a tauopathy and is classified as a subtype of Alzheimer's disease 1. It is characterized by a range of neurological and cognitive symptoms, including amnesia, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, confusion, delirium, memory disorders, hallucinations, gait disturbances, sleep disorders, and urinary incontinence. The disease shares similarities with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and Parkinson's disease. Pathway analysis indicates an association with the Alzheimer disease pathway. Several drugs are associated with the condition, including acetylcholine, curcumin, resveratrol, and tacrine, while others such as glutathione, hydrogen peroxide, nitrogen, pyruvaldehyde, and alpha-tocopherol are implicated in its pathogenesis. Additionally, environmental and metabolic factors like aluminum, cholesterol, homocysteine, and oxidative stress markers are linked to disease development.

Dementia is classified as a cognitive disorder. It is associated with a range of symptoms and conditions, including memory impairment, confusion, and behavioral changes, though specific symptom details are not provided in the current data.

Hypertension is categorized as a type of artery disease and shares characteristics with abdominal obesity-metabolic syndrome 1, obesity, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It presents with symptoms such as headache, dizziness, edema, proteinuria, albuminuria, hypertension, cardiac output reduction, and various cardiovascular and neurological manifestations. A wide range of drugs are associated with hypertension, including antihypertensives like atenolol, bisoprolol, and perindoprilat, as well as agents such as nicotine, caffeine, and environmental pollutants. Some compounds, including 1-naphthaleneacetic acid, 2,3-epoxypropyl acrylate, and prostaglandins, are implicated in the disease's pathogenesis.

Arthritis is classified as a bone inflammation disease. It is associated with various drugs, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents like ibuprofen, diclofenac, and celecoxib, as well as immunomodulators such as methotrexate and leflunomide. Drugs involved in pathogenesis include arachidonic acid and ethanol, suggesting inflammatory and metabolic contributions to disease progression.

Diabetes mellitus is classified as a glucose metabolism disease. It is associated with drugs such as insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, and various antidiabetic agents, as well as environmental and metabolic factors like lead, mercury, and pesticides. Compounds such as alanine, chemokine CX3CL1, and pyrimidine are implicated in its pathogenesis.

Mental depression is classified as a mood disorder and is associated with the serotonergic synapse pathway, indicating a neurochemical basis involving serotonin signaling.

Obesity is classified as a form of overnutrition and shares features with polycystic ovary syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is characterized by symptoms such as excessive body weight, hyperphagia, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and sleep apnea. Drugs associated with obesity include appetite suppressants like sibutramine and rimonabant, as well as agents such as caffeine, folic acid, and environmental pollutants. Pathway analysis reveals associations with neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, PPAR signaling, oleoyl-phe metabolism, and regulation of lipolysis in adipocytes. Compounds such as eltanolone, nitroprusside, nucleotides, and valproic acid are implicated in its pathogenesis.

Other agents include cobaltiprotoporphyrin, lovastatin-niacin combination, and various pharmaceuticals and natural compounds.

ori_question.Question: In this study, what feature of the instrumental variable approach enables the identification of causal effects despite unmeasured confounding, and how does the method address potential model misspecification?
