Passage: 'The IV forests method incorporates random-forest-based nonparametric estimation, offering greater robustness against model misspecification compared to conventional parametric approaches.'
Passage: 'Our estimand of the IV forests represents the conditional local ATE on the overlap population (CLATO).'
ori_question.Rationale: The question requires multi-step reasoning that integrates three distinct pieces of evidence from the passage. First, Evidence 1 establishes that the state pension age (SPA) is used as an instrumental variable (IV) to address endogenous retirement decisions—this is the core causal identification strategy. The key insight here is that SPA affects retirement status but is assumed not to directly affect cognitive function, satisfying the exclusion restriction. Second, Evidence 2 highlights that the IV forests method uses random-forest-based nonparametric estimation, which is a methodological feature that enhances robustness to model misspecification—a critical concern in causal inference when parametric assumptions may be violated. This directly addresses the challenge of correctly specifying functional forms in complex, high-dimensional data. Third, Evidence 3 identifies the specific estimand (CLATO), which clarifies that the estimated effect is not for the entire population but for a subgroup where the instrument has a meaningful effect (i.e., those with propensity scores in the overlap region). This reflects a nuanced understanding of causal effect heterogeneity and the local nature of IV estimates. The reasoning chain connects these elements: the IV design enables causal identification by isolating exogenous variation in retirement (via SPA), while the nonparametric IV forests method ensures that the estimation is not biased by incorrect model assumptions. The combination of these features allows for valid causal inference even when unmeasured confounders (e.g., health status, motivation) influence both retirement and cognition. External domain knowledge, while rich in disease associations, does not provide relevant information about causal study design, IV methods, or model robustness. Therefore, it is not incorporated. The question is not answerable by referencing any single piece of evidence—each contributes a distinct component to the reasoning, and the correct answer must synthesize all three.

paragraph:
Adiposity and diabetes are major causes of premature death and disability worldwide, and both are particularly common in Mexico [ 1 , 2 ]. Excess adiposity causes diabetes, but persistent hyperglycaemia in diabetes can itself cause pathological weight loss, distorting the observed associations of adiposity with prevalent diabetes and with cause-specific mortality [ 3 ]. Previous analyses of the Mexico City Prospective Study (MCPS)—a cohort of 150 000 Mexican adults recruited 20 years ago—found that hyperglycaemia in diabetes was common and associated with a quadrupling in all-cause mortality at ages 35–74 years [ 4 ]. Subsequent analyses found that, among individuals without diabetes, the association between body mass index (BMI) and mortality was J-shaped (comparable to that observed in other populations [ 5 ]), with each 5-kg/m 2 higher BMI above 25 kg/m 2 associated with a 30% higher all-cause mortality [ 3 ]. However, among those with diabetes, BMI was inversely associated with mortality, likely due to reverse causality. Participants with diabetes were therefore excluded from the observational analyses of adiposity and mortality, but this exclusion may have resulted in underestimation of the full effect of adiposity on mortality by removing, at least in part, the impact of adiposity on mortality that is mediated through diabetes.

Mendelian randomization (MR) approaches can mitigate biases due to reverse causality and confounding that are inherent in observational studies and seek to estimate the effects of lifelong differences in exposures on disease risks [ 6 ]. Previous MR studies conducted mostly in populations of European ancestry support the causal relevance of adiposity to cardiometabolic diseases and all-cause mortality [ 7–9 ] and have identified individual diseases most strongly associated with adiposity [ 10 , 11 ]. However, evidence from non-European populations with admixed ancestry remains scarce. To address this gap, we used MR approaches to estimate the causal relevance of lifelong differences in BMI for cause-specific mortality among 125 000 Mexican adults with admixed ancestry previously enrolled into the MCPS [ 12 ].
The MCPS study design and methods have been described previously [ 12 , 13 ]. A detailed description of the exclusions, genetic instruments for BMI and diabetes, mortality follow-up procedures and outcomes, and statistical analyses used in the current paper is provided in the Methods section of the Supplementary Material . A brief summary of the statistical methods is given below.

An additive genetic model of inheritance was assumed throughout. The one-sample Wald ratio method was used to assess the causal relevance of BMI to cause-specific mortality [ 14 ], in which Cox regression was used to estimate the association between a trans-ancestry BMI genetic score (BMI-GS) [ 15 ] and mortality, and linear regression was used to estimate the association between the BMI-GS and BMI. Analyses were performed separately for men and women, with the inverse-variance-weighted average of the resulting log hazard ratios (HRs) used when combining men and women. The assumptions of MR are that: (i) the instrument is associated with the exposure; (ii) the instrument is not associated with genetic confounders; and (iii) the instrument does not affect the outcome except through the exposure. The first assumption was assessed by using analysis of variance to estimate the percentage of variance in the observed BMI explained by the BMI-GS and, also, by plotting the mean BMI across fifths of the BMI-GS. The second assumption was addressed by adjusting for genetic principal components. To examine the possibility of violations against the third assumption, we tabulated the mean levels of potential confounders across fifths of the BMI-GS and performed additional ‘two-sample’ MR approaches (including weighted median and MR–Egger) [ 16 ].

To explore the extent to which the effect of genetically predicted BMI on mortality could be mediated by genetic diabetes liability, the direct causal effects of BMI were estimated in a mediation MR framework in which a trans-ancestry diabetes GS was constructed (from a set of genetic variants that did not overlap with the variants in the BMI-GS). A two-stage least-squares mediation MR approach was then used in which genetically predicted BMI and genetically predicted diabetes liability were jointly entered into a Cox model to estimate the causal effect of BMI on mortality not mediated by diabetes [ 17 ]. The proportion mediated was estimated by subtracting the log HR of the direct effect from the log HR of the total effect and then dividing by the log HR of the total effect. Bootstrap resampling (with 1000 resamples) was then used to provide a bias-corrected 95% confidence interval (CI) for this proportion.

Sensitivity analyses included: restriction to participants unrelated to the third family degree; use of a relaxed ‘clumping’ threshold when constructing the BMI-GS; excluding those with pre-existing diabetes or other chronic disease when estimating the association between the BMI-GS and BMI; alternative use of a BMI-GS derived from a large European ancestry population published by the GIANT consortium; analyses of mortality at younger versus older ages, by residential district, by proportion of Indigenous American ancestry, and by levels of physical activity and smoking status; and use of non-linear MR (both residual and doubly ranked methods [ 18 , 19 ]) to explore the log-linearity assumption between genetically predicted BMI and mortality risk. Non-linear MR analyses with the ‘negative controls’ of age and sex were also performed to explore the exclusion restriction assumption of MR.

Analyses were conducted by using STATA (version 17), SAS (version 9.4), and R (version 3.3.0).
### Study population and baseline characteristics

Of 159 755 participants recruited, 25 845 (16%) were excluded from all analyses. These comprised 21 244 (13%) without quality-control (QC) acceptable genetic data (see Methods section of the Supplementary Material ), a further 729 (0.4%) aged ≥90 years at recruitment, a further 1617 (1%) with missing or implausible height or weight measurements, and a further 2255 (1%) with uncertain mortality linkage. Of the remaining 133 910 participants, 125 003 were aged 35–74 years at recruitment [mean (SD) age 50 (11) years, 68% women] and 8907 were aged 75–89 years at recruitment. Of the 125 003 aged 35–74 years, the average ancestry proportions were 67% Indigenous American, 28% European, 3% African, and 1% East Asian, and 71 513 (57%) were unrelated to the third family degree. The baseline characteristics of the 125 003 participants aged 35–74 years at recruitment are shown in Table 1 .

### Genetic instrument for BMI

The BMI-GS created from the trans-ancestry meta-analysis comprised 724 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). The per-allele effects of these SNPs on BMI in MCPS were generally consistent with the estimates provided by the trans-ancestry meta-analysis ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). The BMI-GS explained 3% of the variance in measured BMI in both men (F-statistic 1178) and women (F-statistic 2866). A 1-SD higher BMI-GS predicted a 0.70-kg/m 2 higher BMI in men and a 0.94-kg/m 2 higher BMI in women ( Supplementary Figure S2 ). In both men and women, these slopes were slightly shallower in older participants and in those with the highest proportion of Indigenous American ancestry. Across fifths of the sex-specific BMI-GS distributions, BMI increased from 27.1 ± 4.0 to 29.0 ± 4.5 kg/m 2 in men and from 28.4 ± 4.8 to 31.0 ± 5.4 kg/m 2 in women ( Supplementary Table S1 ). In both men and women, the mean systolic blood pressure increased by an average of 2 mmHg across fifths of the BMI-GS, while the prevalence of diabetes increased by 5 percentage points. Other characteristics did not vary much by the BMI-GS.

### Genetically predicted BMI and all-cause, vascular-metabolic, and non-vascular-metabolic mortality

During a median of 20 years of follow-up, a total of 13 066 deaths occurred at ages 35–74 years, including 7111 vascular-metabolic deaths (3451 vascular, 2034 renal, 1069 hepatobiliary, and 557 acute diabetic crises) and 5955 non-vascular-metabolic deaths (2107 cancer, 2050 respiratory, 811 infective, and 987 external, other, or ill-defined; see Supplementary Table S2 for the International Classification of Diseases Tenth Revision codes used). An increase of 5 kg/m 2 in genetically predicted BMI was associated with nearly a doubling in all-cause mortality (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.63–2.00) ( Figure 1 ). For the composite of all vascular-metabolic deaths, the HR per 5-kg/m 2 increase in genetically predicted BMI was 2.15 (95% CI 1.87–2.48) while, for the composite of all non-vascular-metabolic deaths, it was 1.47 (95% CI 1.27–1.71). Estimates were similar in men and women.

Sensitivity analyses in which a less stringent clumping threshold was used, or in which those with diabetes or other chronic disease were excluded from the estimated association of the BMI-GS with BMI, or that were based on a BMI-GS derived from the GIANT consortium genome wide association study (GWAS) gave broadly similar estimates ( Supplementary Figures S3–S5 , though the HRs when using the GIANT consortium GWAS were a little higher). Two-sample MR analyses also gave broadly similar results, albeit with slightly weaker HR estimates ( Supplementary Table S3 and Supplementary Figure S6 ). Use of the residual and doubly ranked non-linear methods supported the plausibility of the associations between the genetically predicted BMI and all-cause, vascular-metabolic, and non-vascular-metabolic being continuous and log-linear ( Supplementary Figure S7 ); however, the same methods applied to age and sex revealed non-zero associations ( Supplementary Figure S8 ), illustrating the importance of fully controlling for the effects of age and sex in the main analyses.

### Genetically predicted BMI and specific causes of death

Of the individual causes of death studied, genetically predicted BMI was particularly strongly related to renal death (HR per 5-kg/m 2 higher genetically predicted BMI 3.59, 95% CI 2.76–4.67) and acute diabetic crises (HR 2.70, 95% CI 1.64–4.44) ( Figure 2 ). The HR was 1.68 (95% CI 1.32–2.14) for cardiac death and 1.70 (95% CI 1.11–2.60) for cerebrovascular death. Three-quarters of cardiac deaths were due to acute myocardial infarction (HR 1.58, 95% CI 1.19–2.10), with heart failure the second-most common cardiac cause (HR 1.57, 95% CI 0.77–3.21) ( Figure 3 ). For all vascular deaths combined, the HR was 1.75 (95% CI 1.43–2.14). Of the non-vascular-metabolic causes of death, genetically predicted BMI was particularly strongly related to respiratory death (HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.59–2.67) and infective deaths (HR 2.61, 95% CI 1.73–3.92), but it was not positively related to cancer (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.67–1.09), overall or for specific sites. When analyses were rerun in the subset of participants unrelated to the third degree, associations with particular causes of death were marginally weaker, albeit with wider CIs ( Figure 2 ).

### Impact of other characteristics

The relevance of genetically predicted BMI to all-cause mortality was somewhat greater at younger ages compared with older ages (HR 2.43, 95% CI 2.01–2.93 at ages 35–59 years versus HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.17–1.74 at ages 70–74 years) and marginally greater in those with a higher proportion of inherited Indigenous American ancestry (HR 2.01, 95% CI 1.69–2.39 in those in the top third of Indigenous American ancestry versus HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.30–1.89 in those in the bottom third) [ Supplementary Figure S9a : use of sex- and subgroup-specific estimates of the BMI-GS-to-BMI association gave nearly identical results ( Supplementary Figure S9b )]. The relevance of genetically predicted BMI to all-cause mortality was similar irrespective of residential district, smoking, and physical activity status. Among all 133 910 participants aged <90 years at recruitment, the all-cause mortality HR associated with 5-kg/m 2 higher genetically predicted BMI at ages 75–89 years was 1.40 (95% CI 1.22–1.60) ( Supplementary Figure S10 ).

### Mediation through genetic diabetes liability

As noted above, the prevalence of diabetes increased strongly across fifths of the BMI-GS. Figure 4 shows estimates of genetically predicted BMI with cause-specific mortality by using the two-stage least-squares (2SLS) method—rather than the Wald ratio method—before and after adjustment for genetic diabetes liability. As expected, the HRs from the 2SLS-based analyses were similar (albeit marginally weaker) to those from the Wald ratio method. Adjustment for genetic diabetes liability reduced the magnitude of the all-cause mortality log HR associated with the genetically predicted BMI by more than half [from ln(1.68) to ln(1.25) for all-cause mortality—a 56% reduction in magnitude (95% CI 35% to 94%)]. For vascular-metabolic mortality, the reduction in the log HR ratio on the adjustment for genetic diabetes liability was about two-thirds while, for the composite of all non-vascular-metabolic mortality, it was just under half.
In this large admixed Mexican population with high levels of obesity, we found strong evidence supporting a causal relationship between BMI and death from vascular, renal, diabetic, respiratory, and infective causes. Each 5-kg/m 2 higher genetically predicted lifelong BMI conferred more than a doubling in the risk of vascular-metabolic mortality, including more than a trebling in risk of renal mortality. For all-cause mortality, there was a clear trend towards larger proportional effects at younger ages and a suggestive trend of larger proportional effects in those with a higher proportion of Indigenous American ancestry. Effects were similar in men and women, however.

The present MR analyses aim to estimate the lifelong causal effect of BMI on mortality risk. By contrast, previous observational analyses from the same cohort estimated the relationship between measured BMI during middle age and cause-specific mortality [ 3 ]. In those analyses, individuals with diabetes at recruitment (as well as deaths during the first 5 years of follow-up) were excluded in order to reduce the reverse-causality bias caused by persistent hyperglycaemia in diabetes resulting in weight loss prior to BMI measurement at recruitment. After such exclusions, a J-shaped association between BMI and mortality was observed in which each 5-kg/m 2 higher BMI above 25 kg/m 2 was associated with 30% higher risk of all-cause mortality and 40% higher risk of vascular-metabolic mortality (which is consistent with that seen in other populations worldwide) [ 3 , 5 ]. However, although the exclusion of individuals with diabetes in our previous analyses was deemed necessary to limit reverse causality, it follows that the lifelong effects of BMI on mortality that are mediated ‘through’ diabetes would not have been fully captured in that analysis. This may well explain the larger relative risks of all-cause mortality associated with higher genetically predicted BMI in the current report. Indeed, the mediation analyses in the current report for the effect of BMI on mortality ‘not’ mediated through diabetes are consistent with our previous observational analyses [ 3 ]. Taken together, the results suggest that BMI may be an even more important cause of death in Mexico than previously estimated.

The magnitude of the associations reported in the current analysis of this Mexican population is somewhat greater than reported in previous MR studies conducted in European ancestry populations. For example, in a meta-analysis of 14 prospective studies and randomized trials, and four consortia enriched for coronary heart disease (CARDIoGRAMplusC4D), stroke (METASTROKE), diabetes (DIAGRAM), and lipids (GLGC) [ 11 ], each 4.6-kg/m 2 higher BMI was associated with a 36% increase in the odds of coronary heart disease and 98% increase in the odds of diabetes, but only a 9% increase in the odds of stroke. Likewise, analyses of 14 cardiovascular diseases in 370 000 UK Biobank participants found that each 5-kg/m 2 higher genetically predicted BMI was associated with about a 40% increase in the odds of coronary artery disease and 16% increase in the odds of stroke, with the strongest vascular associations observed for deep vein thrombosis (61% increase), heart failure (76% increase), and aortic stenosis (84% increase) [ 10 ]. A subsequent meta-analysis of MR studies plus de novo analyses of the FinnGen cohort confirmed the associations previously reported for diabetes and other cardiovascular diseases, but also demonstrated associations with several other diseases [ 20 ]. For example, in that study, each 1-SD higher genetically predicted BMI was associated with a 64% increase in the odds of gallstone disease, 81% increase in the odds of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and 65% increase in the odds of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, as well as an increase in the odds of several cancers [ 20 ]. Positive associations between genetically predicted BMI and disease risk have also been reported for infections at multiple sites, at least at BMI levels of >20 kg/m 2 [ 21 ].

Established mechanisms through which higher BMI increases cardiovascular and other diseases include insulin resistance, blood pressure, dyslipidaemia, and inflammation [ 22 ]. Mechanisms for the increased risk of infections associated with obesity include insulin resistance, but may also include immune function and adaptive responses [ 23 ], while pathways for the increased risk of chronic lung disease are less well understood. Causal associations between higher adiposity and adverse effects on glycaemia, blood pressure, and lipids have been confirmed by MR studies [ 11 , 24 ], while randomized trials of weight loss have demonstrated that these adverse effects can be reversed [ 25–27 ]. Clinical guidelines, both in Mexico and elsewhere, have prioritized the avoidance of excess weight (among other risk factors) for preventing premature cardiovascular events [ 28 , 29 ]. The findings of the present study provide strong support for recommendations prioritizing adiposity (and diabetes) control for the prevention of cardiometabolic diseases in Mexico.

The chief strengths of the present study include the large size, prolonged follow-up, and the fact that it was conducted in a previously understudied ancestry group with high levels of obesity and diabetes. The availability of genetic data in all participants allowed the use of a ‘one-sample’ MR approach. One advantage of this approach over alternative ‘two-sample approaches’ is that the instrument-to-BMI and instrument-to-mortality associations are estimated in the ‘same’ underlying population. The use of a single allele score in preference to each genetic variant acting as a separate instrumental variable (as done in the sensitivity analyses) also helped to reduce any weak-instrument bias. The primary instrument was derived from a trans-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis and, consequently, there was no overlap between MCPS participants and participants in the studies used to identify the SNPs used in the instrument or determine their weights. However, it did not include much Hispanic population representation, which may explain why the instrument explained only a fairly small proportion of BMI variance. Nonetheless, the strength of association between the instrument and BMI in the current study was clear, consistent, and broadly similar among different types of individuals. Limitations of the present study include the potential for some horizontal pleiotropy, although sensitivity analyses involving a range of alternative MR approaches yielded consistent results. Beyond mediation through diabetes, we have not yet explored other potential pathways, while the recruitment of participants aged ≥35 years means that we cannot explore the role of BMI on diseases at younger ages. The study population arises from just two districts of Mexico City and so the participants are not representative of adults throughout Mexico (or even Mexico City). However, prospective studies of non-representative cohorts of individuals can provide reliable evidence about the associations of risk factors with disease that are widely generalizable [ 30 , 31 ]. Finally, a lack of information on non-fatal outcomes means that the conclusions apply directly only to causes of death.
This large study of an admixed Mexican population implicates a strong causal relevance of higher genetically determined lifelong BMI with risk of death from vascular, renal, diabetic, infective, and respiratory causes, with a substantial proportion of the effect mediated through the effects of BMI on diabetes. Population-wide reductions in BMI as well as optimal diabetes control should remain key priorities for the prevention of premature death in Mexico.
Ethics approval was obtained from the Mexican Ministry of Health, the Mexican National Council of Science and Technology (reference 0595P-M), and the University of Oxford (reference C99.260). All participants provided written informed consent.

The authors explicitly justify their choice of MR as a method to overcome limitations of observational studies—particularly reverse causality and confounding—by leveraging genetic variants as instrumental variables. The study design includes detailed methodological decisions: use of a one-sample Wald ratio approach, construction of a trans-ancestry BMI genetic score, sensitivity analyses (e.g., two-sample MR, MR-Egger, weighted median), mediation analysis to disentangle direct and indirect effects through genetic diabetes liability, and extensive checks for validity assumptions (e.g., instrument strength, pleiotropy, linearity). These choices reflect a deliberate and principled selection of causal identification strategies. The passage also discusses how the study design addresses key challenges such as population stratification (via principal components), weak instrument bias (via allele score aggregation), and generalizability (via subgroup analyses). The focus is not merely on reporting associations but on establishing causal pathways, which aligns directly with Topic 3. While the topic 'Protection effectiveness, waning, reinfection & immune escape' is unrelated, and 'Measurement & bias handling' and 'Real-Time Debiasing & Delay Adjustment' are not central, the core of the paper is the methodological framework for causal inference—making Topic 3 the most appropriate and richest source for generating multi-step inference questions (e.g., 'Why might the exclusion of diabetic individuals in observational analyses underestimate the true causal effect of BMI on mortality?'; 'How does mediation MR help distinguish between direct and indirect causal pathways?').

ori_question.Question: In this study, what methodological choice best supports the inference that lifelong differences in BMI causally influence mortality risk, particularly in light of potential confounding and reverse causality?
Evidence: Passage: 'Mendelian randomization (MR) approaches can mitigate biases due to reverse causality and confounding that are inherent in observational studies and seek to estimate the effects of lifelong differences in exposures on disease risks.'

Passage: 'An additive genetic model of inheritance was assumed throughout. The one-sample Wald ratio method was used to assess the causal relevance of BMI to cause-specific mortality... Analyses were performed separately for men and women, with the inverse-variance-weighted average of the resulting log hazard ratios (HRs) used when combining men and women.'

Passage: 'The present MR analyses aim to estimate the lifelong causal effect of BMI on mortality risk. By contrast, previous observational analyses from the same cohort estimated the relationship between measured BMI during middle age and cause-specific mortality... After such exclusions, a J-shaped association between BMI and mortality was observed... However, although the exclusion of individuals with diabetes in our previous analyses was deemed necessary to limit reverse causality, it follows that the lifelong effects of BMI on mortality that are mediated ‘through’ diabetes would not have been fully captured in that analysis.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to evaluate the methodological justification for causal inference. Evidence 1 establishes that MR is specifically designed to address reverse causality and confounding—key limitations in observational studies—by using genetic variants as instrumental variables. This directly connects to the topic of causal effect estimation. Evidence 2 details the specific methodological implementation: the use of a one-sample Wald ratio approach with a trans-ancestry BMI genetic score, which allows for the estimation of causal effects within the same population, reducing potential bias from population stratification. This choice strengthens internal validity. Evidence 3 contrasts the current MR approach with prior observational analyses that excluded diabetic individuals to avoid reverse causality (e.g., weight loss due to hyperglycemia), but notes that this exclusion likely omitted the causal pathway from adiposity to mortality via diabetes. The current MR design, by not excluding individuals with diabetes and using lifelong genetic predisposition, captures both direct and indirect (mediated) effects. The correct inference is that the use of MR—specifically a one-sample approach with a genetic instrument—enables estimation of the total lifelong causal effect of BMI on mortality, including pathways mediated through diabetes, which observational methods cannot fully capture. This requires combining knowledge of MR’s strengths, the study’s design, and the limitations of prior analyses. External domain knowledge, while rich in drug-disease associations, does not provide relevant information about study design, causal inference, or the methodological advantages of MR over observational methods. Therefore, it was not incorporated.

choices.Option: Using a two-sample Mendelian randomization approach to compare genetic associations with BMI and mortality across independent populations, reducing the risk of population stratification
Applying a linear regression model to the observed BMI and mortality data to estimate the causal effect of BMI on mortality, adjusting for age, sex, and smoking status
Stratifying the analysis by age at recruitment to assess whether the causal effect of BMI on mortality varies across life stages
Excluding individuals with diabetes from the analysis to prevent reverse causality and ensure a clean estimate of the direct effect of BMI on mortality
Using a one-sample Mendelian randomization approach with a trans-ancestry genetic score to estimate the total lifelong causal effect of BMI on mortality, including effects mediated through diabetes

paragraph:
The potential outcomes framework is the dominant causal-inference framework in epidemiology [ 1–6 ]. Generally, under this framework, causal effects are defined as a contrast of outcomes that would happen among study participants if they were exposed (i.e. their potential outcomes if exposed) with outcomes that would happen among those same participants if they were unexposed (i.e. their potential outcomes if unexposed) [ 1 , 7–9 ]. Textbook guidance generally considers at least three assumptions key for estimating causal effects: (i) exchangeability, (ii) positivity, and (iii) consistency, our focus, which is that an individual’s outcome under the exposure they actually receive equals their potential outcome under that exposure [ 10 , 11 ]. Different, interrelated terms refer to the conditions under which consistency is met (e.g. the stable unit treatment value assumption) [ 12 , 13 ]. In epidemiology, the terms ‘well-defined intervention assumption’ [ 14 ] and ‘treatment variation irrelevance’ [ 15 ] are commonly used to describe ways consistency can be obtained.

Consistency is violated when there are multiple versions of the same exposure that have different effects on the outcome for the same individual [ 12 , 14 , 15 ]. Such exposures do not meet the well-defined intervention assumption [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Consider a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of an antidepressant in which participants are assigned to treatment arms clearly defined in all facets relevant to the outcome (e.g. dosage, duration, manufacturer); here, the well-defined intervention assumption would be satisfied. In contrast, consider an RCT in which there are different manufacturers who use varying formulations for what is labelled the same antidepressant, and the different formulations produce different treatment effects for some individuals. Here, some participants would have multiple potential outcomes for what is labelled a single treatment. Moreover, the estimated overall treatment effect in the study would be an average of the (potentially heterogeneous) effects of the different treatment versions in the sample [ 17 , 18 ]. Articulating a well-defined intervention would require specifying the manufacturer for each participant or including only one of the manufacturers. Alternatively, if there were no variation in the formulations’ effects, the well-defined intervention assumption would be satisfied because of treatment variation irrelevance, i.e. there may be treatment variation, but such variation is not relevant for the treatment’s effects on the outcome [ 15 ].

To satisfy the well-defined intervention assumption, textbooks and guidelines advocate conceptualizing exposures as treatments in hypothetical RCTs, even in observational settings [ 10 , 19 , 20 ]. Thus, when the well-defined intervention assumption is satisfied (along with other assumptions), causal effects can be interpreted as intervention effects: the effect an exposure would have on an outcome if it were modified by the hypothetical intervention [ 1 , 14 , 21 ]. This framing has several purported advantages. First, it encourages careful definition of exposures and causal contrasts, aiding satisfaction of consistency and estimation of precise causal effects [ 1 , 14 , 21 ]. Second, it enhances the potential for falsifying results of observational studies in actual RCTs, the ostensible gold standard for causal inference [ 1 , 22 ]. Third, it facilitates predicting the effects of actual interventions, making findings policy relevant [ 1 , 14 , 23 ]. For the latter two reasons, proponents encourage conceptualizing humanly feasible hypothetical interventions, although feasibility is not required [ 1 , 14 ].

According to textbooks and guidelines, specifying how an exposure would be intervened upon is key for estimating intervention effects, because different ‘hows’ can have different health effects [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Thus, failing to specify and operationalize the ‘how’ can cause consistency violations [ 1 , 14 , 22 ]. For example, consider a study aiming to estimate the effect on cognition of an intervention to increase physical activity by 2 h weekly over 10 years. In such a study, specifying how physical activity is increased would be key. Indeed, increasing it via boxing matches may have different effects on cognition than increasing it via running [ 25 , 26 ]. Alternatively, cogent arguments using theory, prior research or sensitivity analyses about why the ‘how’ would not matter for the intervention’s likely effects on the outcome (i.e. arguments for treatment variation irrelevance [ 15 ]) may suffice [ 16 , 27 ].

As the interventional framing and well-defined intervention assumption become more widely adopted, ‘causal effects’ and ‘intervention effects’ become synonyms [ 5 , 21–23 , 28 , 29 ]. Nonetheless, as with any new approach or framework, there may differences between what guidelines advise and what researchers do in practice [ 10 , 11 , 30–34 ]. Additionally, applying the interventional framework in epidemiology may present unique challenges, as epidemiological studies are frequently observational, analysing non-interventional exposures. Moreover, epidemiological datasets often lack sufficient detail from which to operationalize well-defined interventions (e.g. datasets may contain information on respondents’ duration of physical activity but lack information on activity type). In such settings, satisfying the well-defined intervention assumption can be challenging. Because of these challenges, best practices require transparent discussion of researchers’ reasoning regarding satisfaction of causal inference assumptions, including the well-defined intervention assumption [ 16 ].

In summary, although the well-defined intervention assumption has been widely accepted as key for estimating causal effects, satisfying the assumption can be problematic in common epidemiological settings. However, to our knowledge, no studies have systematically evaluated adherence to best practices regarding the assumption in epidemiological research. Thus, we investigated how epidemiologists using g-methods or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) [ 10 , 35–37 ] interpreted and addressed the well-defined intervention assumption in their observational studies. Our overall objective was to assess whether researchers who aimed to estimate the effects of hypothetical interventions followed best practices regarding the well-defined intervention assumption [ 10 ]. Specifically, we examined: (i) whether authors articulated explicitly causal objectives; (ii) whether authors stated their exposure contrast of interest in terms of a hypothetical intervention; (iii) if so, whether authors specified well-defined interventions supported by their data; (iv) whether authors discussed key causal inference assumptions, particularly consistency; and (v) how authors interpreted their findings, particularly given their discussion of assumptions.
### Article selection

We searched PubMed on 22 February 2021 for articles that: (i) were published from 2000–21 [ 38 ], (ii) were in the six general epidemiology journals with the highest 2020 impact factors [ 39 ], and (iii) included terms in their titles or abstracts related to g-methods or TMLE. Figure 1 displays our specific search criteria and terms.

We imported articles from PubMed into Covidence, a systematic-review data management tool [ 40 ]. Two reviewers (J.E.G. and K.L.K.) screened and included articles for data extraction if they: (i) were original research articles presenting findings from an observational study, (ii) used g-methods or TMLE, either as a primary aim or an emphasized secondary aim, and (iii) focused primarily on substantive research (not methodological development). We focused on studies using g-methods or TMLE because: (a) they often aim to estimate causal effects, for which the well-defined intervention assumption is relevant, and (b) g-methods and TMLE were developed using the potential outcomes framework as a foundation, making such studies particularly likely to consider the assumption. Figure 1 displays specific inclusion/exclusion criteria.

### Data extraction

The two reviewers independently extracted article data using a Google Forms tool. Reviewers focused on the primary study aim when extracting data, unless only a secondary aim used g-methods or TMLE, in which case reviewers focused on that aim. We organized the tool by manuscript section. If the answer to a question was unavailable in the designated section (e.g. Methods) but available in a different one (e.g. Results), reviewers answered the question using information from that section. Reviewers generally only used information explicitly provided by study authors to answer questions (i.e. they avoided inferring information on behalf of authors).

Reviewers extracted article metadata, including journal, publication year, title and subject area; each article could be assigned multiple subject areas.

From the Introduction, reviewers categorized the study’s objectives as: (i) ‘clearly causal’, when authors used explicitly causal language to describe the exposure-outcome relationship (e.g. ‘…the causal/interventional effect of…’), or (ii) ‘not clearly causal’, when authors used non-causal language (e.g. ‘…the association between…’) or a mix of causal and associational language [ 32 ].

From the Methods, reviewers first assessed whether authors stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention. Then, among studies in which this was the case (‘intervention-effect studies’), reviewers assessed if authors stated how the exposure would be intervened upon or changed. Among studies that provided a ‘how’, reviewers assessed if the stated intervention: (i) likely produced consistency, (ii) was practicably ‘actionable’ [ 1 ] or ‘feasible’ [ 1 ], (iii) could be implemented and tested in an RCT, and (iv) was supported by the data (i.e. the analytical variable matched the description of the hypothetical intervention [ 1 ]). Among studies in which authors did not provide a ‘how’, reviewers assessed if the ‘how’ mattered for the exposure’s or intervention’s likely effects on the outcome (i.e. if it mattered for consistency). As elsewhere, when assessing adherence to consistency, reviewers relied—when possible—on information regarding the assumption provided by authors; when authors did not provide such information, reviewers relied heavily on discussions in the epidemiological methods literature regarding consistency in studies of certain exposures [e.g. body mass index (BMI)] [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Reviewers also extracted the specific analytical method used.

From the Results/Discussion, reviewers first assessed if authors mentioned (i.e. at least listed as a condition for causal inference) the assumptions of consistency (or related terms), exchangeability and positivity. Next, reviewers assessed if authors discussed their findings in terms of intervention or policy relevance, and if authors stated predictions about what would happen to outcome burdens if their specific exposure contrast was applied in the real world. Subsequently, among intervention-effect studies, reviewers assessed if authors discussed intervention feasibility. Finally, among intervention-effect studies, reviewers assessed if authors explicitly interpreted their estimates as corresponding to the effects of a hypothetical intervention (versus a non-interventional causal effect, association, or otherwise).

Finally, considering all extracted data, reviewers assessed if intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions. Recognizing that no study is perfect, all causal effects are vague to some degree and we are not experts in all subfields, we concluded a study had a well-defined intervention if: (i) authors specified a ‘how’ that reasonably adhered to consistency, or (ii) when authors did not specify a ‘how’, they cogently argued for treatment variation irrelevance or, more generally, why consistency was likely satisfied or why consistency violations were likely inconsequential. In the absence of (i) or (ii), reviewers relied heavily on the epidemiological methods literature to inform their assessments.

### Conflicts

We resolved conflicts via discussions between the two primary reviewers, and when necessary, co-author consultation.

### Analysis

We tabulated the distribution of responses to each question, including separately for intervention-effect and non-intervention-effect studies. We did not calculate confidence intervals for our estimates because we did not aim to generalize beyond our sample. Our data and code are available at [ https://osf.io/knuc3/?view_only=bf24f8fb4f4947be86148e4b90d00e1a] , which contains the list of reviewed articles.
### Search and screening

Our PubMed search yielded 362 articles, 216 of which did not meet inclusion criteria, leaving 146 for review ( Figure 1 ).

### Data extraction

Supplementary Table S1 , available at IJE online, contains examples of extracted data and reviewers’ assessments.

Most included studies were published in American Journal of Epidemiology (67/146, 46%) or Epidemiology (35/146, 24%) ( Table 1 ). The median publication year was 2016. The most common subject areas were mortality (53/146, 36%) and social determinants (38/146, 26%).

We categorized 20% of studies (29/146, Table 2 ) as intervention-effect studies because they stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention ( Supplementary Table S2 , available at IJE online, contains details). Among them, 90% (26/29) had clearly causal objectives, compared with just 45% (53/117) of non-intervention-effect studies. Most intervention-effect studies used the parametric g-formula/g-computation alone to estimate their exposure contrast (22/29, 76%), whereas most non-intervention-effect studies used inverse probability weighting (IPW)/marginal structural modelling (MSM) alone (87/117, 74%).

Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ). In this study, the ‘how’ adhered to consistency, as the hypothetical intervention compared the effects on child growth and mortality of narrowly defined antiretroviral treatment strategies. Moreover, the ‘how’ was ‘feasible’, could be implemented in an RCT and was supported by the data. The absence of a specified ‘how’ in other intervention-effect studies is notable because we concluded that in most (18/28, 64%), the ‘how’ mattered for consistency, i.e. for the exposure’s likely effects on the outcome.

Of the three causal-inference assumptions, studies mentioned exchangeability most frequently (134/146, 92%); a minority mentioned consistency (62/146, 42%) or positivity (66/146, 45%) ( Table 2 ). However, intervention-effect studies mentioned all assumptions more frequently [28/29 (97%) mentioned exchangeability, 23/29 (79%) mentioned consistency, and 15/29 (52%) mentioned positivity]. Just 34% (40/117) of non-intervention-effect studies discussed results’ intervention or policy relevance, compared with 59% (17/29) of intervention-effect studies. Only 41% (12/29) of intervention-effect studies discussed intervention feasibility, and few studies of either type (≤10%) stated predictions about what would happen to outcome burdens if their exposure contrast was applied in the real world. Finally, authors explicitly interpreted their estimates as corresponding to hypothetical intervention effects in 45% (13/29) of intervention-effect studies.

Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85). Of the 10 most common subject areas among intervention-effect studies, occupational studies and/or cancer studies most frequently had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). Only one study had a well-defined intervention because it articulated an intervention ‘how’ that adhered to consistency ( Table 3 ). The other 10 had well-defined interventions—without articulating a ‘how’ — because of treatment variation irrelevance. In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was (e.g. reduce an exposure to a regulatory limit) and discussed why the mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘how’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome. In such cases, when possible, we deferred to the authors’ subject-area expertise in concluding the studies had well-defined interventions. For example, one study aimed to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce diesel-exhaust exposure on lung-cancer mortality among miners ( Table 3 ). According to the authors, reducing exposure through an intervention that improves ventilation would likely have similar effects on lung-cancer mortality as an intervention that reduces it via cleaner fuel or otherwise.

In contrast, no intervention-effect studies of obesity/BMI, substance use, health behaviours, nutrition and/or physical activity had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was, but did not discuss why the various mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘hows’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome. In such cases, when possible, we deferred to the methods literature in assessing the plausibility of treatment variation irrelevance and the well-defined intervention assumption. For example, one study aimed to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce BMI on all-cause mortality, but neither specified a ‘how’ nor cogently argued for treatment variation irrelevance ( Table 3 ). However, exercise-induced weight loss likely has different mortality effects compared with weight loss from medication, diet, illness or otherwise. Further, BMI (like many other exposures we classified as ill-defined) is a prototypical example of an exposure that often produces consistency violations [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Thus, when studies of such exposures simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely), we concluded they had ill-defined interventions.
### Summary

Evaluating 146 articles in top epidemiology journals, we investigated how researchers using g-methods or TMLE interpreted and addressed the well-defined intervention assumption in their observational studies.

Most studies had clearly causal objectives. However, despite the interventional framework’s growing prominence, only 20% (29/146) of studies stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention. Of these intervention-effect studies, only 3% (1/29) detailed ‘how’ the exposure would be intervened upon. Of those that did not provide a ‘how’, we concluded the ‘how’ mattered for consistency (i.e. treatment variation irrelevance likely did not hold) in 64% (18/28) of studies. Thus, we concluded just 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions.

We also observed concerning findings regarding studies’ adherence to best practices for causal inference more broadly. For example, although intervention-effect studies most often mentioned causal-inference assumptions, 21% (6/29) did not mention consistency and 48% (14/29) did not mention positivity. Notably across studies, consistency, exchangeability and positivity were often not robustly discussed, but rather simply listed as requirements for causal inference. For example, some intervention-effect studies (including those that lacked a well-defined intervention) stated consistency was required for estimating causal effects, but: (i) did not discuss the likelihood the assumption held, or (ii) acknowledged probable consistency violations without discussing how they might affect findings. This defies best practices of being transparent about a study’s assumptions and arguing for their satisfaction (or explaining the implications of violations for inference) [ 16 ].

### Explanation of findings

One explanation for non-adherence to best practices for addressing the well-defined intervention assumption, even when using methods designed to enhance causal inference, is the lag between the development of new approaches and their appropriate use in applied research. Indeed, recent reviews have observed nonadherence to best practices in the use of directed acyclic graphs [ 33 ], alignment between study goals and the variable selection methods used to address them [ 32 , 41 ], reporting of interaction [ 42 ], and assessment of mediation-analysis assumptions [ 43 ], among other areas [ 44 ].

Our findings may also reflect the well-defined intervention assumption’s contested status. For example, critics have argued the assumption restricts the field’s purview to narrowly defined exposures that can be conceptualized as treatments in hypothetical RCTs, marginalizing research on exposures not directly manipulable by biomedical or public-health interventions, including research on socio-structural factors [ 2 , 45–47 ]. In response, some proponents have downplayed the importance of intervention feasibility [ 48 ] and even implied that articulating the ‘how’ is unnecessary as long as there is ‘consensus’ that the ‘how’ would not matter for consistency [ 49 , 50 ].

In this context, applied epidemiologists may have recognized the difficulty of adhering to the assumption but lack knowledge of alternative causal-inference frameworks. Our findings suggest they have largely continued researching the causal effects of socio-structural factors and other challenging exposures (e.g. BMI), while circumventing or overlooking the specifics of the well-defined intervention assumption. In our review, this typically manifested in two approaches. In the more common approach, particularly for those with socio-structural exposures, studies avoided using the interventional framework altogether but did not explicitly adopt alternatives, even though non-interventional causal interpretations have been proposed for such exposures [ 51 , 52 ]. As evidence, whereas ‘social determinants’ was the second most common subject area of reviewed studies overall, it was rare among intervention-effect studies (12th most common of 22, eAppendix 2 available at IJE online). Instead, authors often stated their aims were to estimate ‘associations’ or ambiguous ‘effects’, yet occasionally still evaluated the validity of the well-defined intervention assumption (or related assumptions) in Discussion sections, implying intervention effects were of interest, despite signalling otherwise. That almost no study explicitly aimed to estimate non-interventional causal effects, like aetiological effects or realized effects [ 51–55 ], suggests the need for exposure to alternative non-interventional causal-inference frameworks in epidemiological training. In the less common approach, studies aimed to estimate intervention effects but failed to either: (i) articulate a ‘how’, let alone one that was well-defined, or (ii) cogently argue for treatment variation irrelevance. Thus, whereas using the interventional framework may help researchers explicitly state their objectives, articulate their estimands and acknowledge the assumptions underpinning findings’ validity, researchers’ engagement with the framework’s specifics—particularly the assumptions—is often rote and uncritical.

### Recommendations

Minimally, researchers aiming to estimate intervention effects should specify a ‘how’ that adheres to consistency and is supported by their data (or at least cogently argue for treatment variation irrelevance) [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Indeed, carefully specifying a ‘how’ is often key for adhering to consistency and anticipating the effects of hypothetical interventions [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Moreover, a core argument for articulating well-defined interventions is that specifying a ‘how’, particularly a feasible ‘how’, makes findings policy-relevant [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 23 ]. Following guidelines, like those outlined in the target-trial framework, may facilitate this process [ 31 ]. Conversely, researchers aiming to estimate alternative causal effects should be explicit about their estimand of interest and the assumptions required for causal inference, which may not include the well-defined intervention assumption [ 17 , 31 ]. For example, in a study in which the assumption is violated—but exchangeability and positivity hold—the estimated overall exposure effect will correspond to the effect the exposure actually had in the sample, averaged across the different ways that participants came to be exposed [ 17 , 18 ]. This realized causal effect may be an internally valid estimate of the exposure effect in the sample, but does not correspond to an intervention effect and will not predict what the effect of an intervention on the exposure would be [ 17 ]. This effect is often of interest, e.g. when aiming to identify the causes of population patterns of disease over a given period [ 51–53 ]. Thus, non-interventional causal-inference frameworks may merit more frequent use, particularly given the challenges of adhering to the well-defined intervention assumption. Finally, researchers aiming to estimate associations should be similarly explicit about their aims and assumptions [ 16 , 32 , 56 ]. Our recommendations align with recent studies highlighting the need for improved clarity of objectives and application of causal-inference approaches in epidemiology [ 32 , 33 , 56 ].

### Limitations

In our review, we generally only extracted information explicitly provided by authors to limit the influence of reviewer subjectivity, and two reviewers extracted all information, arriving at consensus. However, our assessments of whether studies had well-defined interventions were subjective and sometimes required subject-area expertise, and we are not experts in all subfields. Nonetheless, when possible, we relied on information provided by authors regarding satisfaction of consistency, although such information was often not provided. Without such information, we relied heavily on the methods literature to inform our assessments. An additional limitation is that some extracted data may have been influenced by journal requirements (e.g. Epidemiology discourages discussing results’ policy relevance [ 57 ]) and thus not reflect researchers’ predilections alone.
We found substantial deviations between guidelines regarding meeting the well-defined intervention assumption and researchers’ application of the guidelines, with intervention-effect studies rarely having well-defined interventions. We call for more careful treatment of the assumption in epidemiological research.
This study was exempt from IRB review and informed consent requirements.

It details how researchers using advanced statistical methods—g-methods and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE)—interpret and implement this assumption in observational studies. The study systematically reviews 146 articles from top epidemiology journals to assess whether researchers explicitly define interventions, justify consistency, and discuss key causal assumptions. This involves critical evaluation of study design, analytical choices, and the alignment between research objectives and methodological rigor. The core of the passage is not about a specific disease, exposure, or outcome, but rather about the validity, implementation, and challenges of a foundational methodological principle in causal inference. This aligns perfectly with Class 5, which encompasses the evaluation of analytical methods, study design, bias handling, and causal effect estimation. Multi-step inference questions could explore how violations of consistency affect causal estimates, how different methodological choices (e.g., g-formula vs. IPW) interact with the well-defined intervention assumption, or how the absence of a specified 'how' undermines the policy relevance of findings—requiring integration of methodological principles with empirical study characteristics.

The study investigates how researchers using advanced causal methods (g-methods and TMLE) in observational studies define their causal estimands, particularly whether they articulate a clear hypothetical intervention and satisfy the consistency assumption. The core of the analysis lies in evaluating whether researchers properly align their study design, exposure definition, and effect measure with the requirements of causal inference. Thus, Topic 3 is most appropriate, as it captures the central theme: the careful selection and justification of study design and causal effect definitions in observational research, especially in the context of complex causal frameworks like the potential outcomes model.

ori_question.Question: In a study aiming to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce exposure to a specific environmental pollutant on lung-cancer mortality, which factor would most critically determine whether the estimated effect can be interpreted as an intervention effect rather than a realized effect?
Evidence: Passage: 'Consistency is violated when there are multiple versions of the same exposure that have different effects on the outcome for the same individual [ 12 , 14 , 15 ].'

Passage: 'In such cases, when possible, we deferred to the authors’ subject-area expertise in concluding the studies had well-defined interventions. For example, one study aimed to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce diesel-exhaust exposure on lung-cancer mortality among miners ( Table 3 ). According to the authors, reducing exposure through an intervention that improves ventilation would likely have similar effects on lung-cancer mortality as an intervention that reduces it via cleaner fuel or otherwise.'

Passage: 'Thus, when studies of such exposures simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely), we concluded they had ill-defined interventions.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to determine what distinguishes an intervention effect from a realized effect. Evidence 1 establishes that consistency—the core condition for interpreting a causal effect as an intervention effect—is violated when different versions of an exposure (e.g., different methods of reducing pollutant exposure) produce different outcomes. This sets up the central issue: if multiple ways of achieving the same exposure level have different effects, the estimated effect is not a true intervention effect. Evidence 2 provides a concrete example from the passage where researchers argued that different methods of reducing diesel-exhaust exposure (e.g., improved ventilation vs. cleaner fuel) would have similar effects on lung-cancer mortality, and this argument was accepted as sufficient to satisfy the well-defined intervention assumption. This illustrates that the key factor is not just the exposure level, but whether the method of achieving it matters. Evidence 3 reinforces this by showing that when researchers fail to justify why different methods would not matter (i.e., fail to argue for treatment variation irrelevance), the intervention is deemed ill-defined, and thus the effect cannot be interpreted as an intervention effect. The external domain knowledge, while rich in associations between pollutants and lung cancer, does not provide information about how different intervention methods might affect outcomes or the conditions under which consistency holds. Therefore, it is not relevant to the reasoning chain. The question requires synthesizing the concept of consistency, the role of intervention method (‘how’), and the necessity of justifying treatment variation irrelevance—none of which is directly stated in any single piece of evidence. The correct answer must be that the ability to justify that different methods of achieving the exposure would have similar effects (i.e., treatment variation irrelevance) is the critical factor, which is not a direct restatement of any one evidence piece but emerges only through their integration.
