paragraph:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the leading cause of respiratory mortality globally, leading to over 3 million deaths per year. 1 Smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD and, historically, has been largely focused on as part of the control of COPD. 2 However, there is a growing realization that a large proportion of COPD cannot be explained by smoking, and that there may be important secondary risk factors. 3

There is mounting concern about the possible impact of pulmonary tuberculosis on long-term lung health. 4–7 Several studies have reported persistence of airway obstruction as well as chronic or recurrent symptoms after individuals recover from tuberculosis. 6 , 8 Tuberculosis may result in significant lung impairment; however, whether residual lung damage due to tuberculosis results in clinically significant outcomes has not been well studied. Although tuberculosis has been mentioned in some COPD guidelines, there is limited evidence of an association. 2 Few studies have assessed the relationship between prior tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD. Most of these studies have assessed tuberculosis diagnoses retrospectively or through self-report, and have been located in settings with a low burden of COPD, limiting generalizability. 9–14 Furthermore, whether an association between tuberculosis and subsequent development of COPD is independent of smoking status, a risk factor for both diseases, is not well elucidated. 2

China is going through large-scale health transitions. 15 , 16 An estimated 100 million people in China are estimated to have COPD, accounting for approximately 25% of total cases worldwide. 17 , 18 Tobacco use and an aging population are considered leading risk factors for this increasing COPD burden; however, risk factors for COPD beyond these, in China and more broadly, are not well understood. 2 , 3 , 13

To attempt to improve our understanding of the risk of COPD after developing tuberculosis, we used the Chinese Electronic Health Records Research in Yinzhou (CHERRY) study, a large, ambispective, population-based, observational cohort of participants in a setting with a high burden of COPD. 19 We assessed the association between tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD, adjusted for a range of potential confounders. We then evaluated whether important secondary characteristics, such as smoking status, modified this relationship.
### Study design and data source

We performed a longitudinal cohort study using the CHERRY, a population-based electronic health database established in 2006 and containing 98% of permanent adult residents in Yinzhou ( Supplementary Figure S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). 19 This database has been used extensively in our previous epidemiological studies. 20–22 The CHERRY is based on the Yinzhou Health Information System (YHIS) that contains comprehensive information, such as health check information, inpatient and outpatient electronic medical records, chronic disease surveillance system and death certificates. These databases are inherently linked to each other by a unique and encoded individual identifier. 19 In Yinzhou district in Ningbo, 96% of permanent residents are covered by the health insurance system. Residents of all ages are covered by the system; however only adults above 18 years of age on 1 January 2009 are included in the CHERRY Study. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.

### Identification of study cohort

In order to bypass the integration and preliminary test period of the system and to allow for full coverage of the regional population, we recruited residents who had registered in the CHERRY during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. Exclusion criteria included age <35 years, participants with a previous history of COPD or with a previous history of cancer and participants with missing values of covariates. We excluded younger participants because the vast majority of COPD occurs >35 years of age. The cohort was dynamic and therefore participants could enter at different time points if they had the exposure at baseline or during follow-up.

### Identification of tuberculosis and COPD

The exposure of interest was tuberculosis, from the health insurance database. In China, tuberculosis care is provided by the national government special funds and has a wide and comprehensive coverage rate. Tuberculosis events were recorded based on the Chinese National Disease Reporting system which includes all diagnosed tuberculosis cases at the city, provincial and national levels. 23–26 The definition of pulmonary tuberculosis disease and all tuberculosis was based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Due to the dynamic nature of the cohort, persons could contribute to the unexposed and, if they were diagnosed with tuberculosis during follow-up, also to the exposed ( Supplementary Table S2 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

We identified participants with the outcome as those diagnosed with COPD, defined by ICD-10 codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) during the study period (1 January 2009 to 30 September 2021). 27 The diagnostic date of COPD was defined as the endpoint date for persons developing COPD.

### Measurement of covariates

Demographic characteristics were collected as part of the baseline survey and included lifestyle factors, socioeconomic status, comorbidities and use of medications. Demographic characteristics included age, sex and marital status. Lifestyle factors were recorded at baseline, including smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and body mass index (BMI). We dichotomized weight into a group that was either overweight or obese (≥24 kg/m 2 and over) or normal and underweight (<24 kg/m 2 ). 28 , 29 Smoking intensity was defined as the average number of cigarettes smoked per day. Current alcohol drinking was defined as drinking at least 100 grams of any alcohol per week during the past year. Education level was measured at the baseline visit and included illiterate, primary school, middle school and high school and above. Important factors related to COPD were also considered, including diabetes, hypertension, asthma, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, arrhythmia, ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, heart failure, depression, anxiety, osteoporosis and the use of COPD medications ( Supplementary Tables S1 and S3 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

### Statistical analysis

We used Cox proportional hazards survival time regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of tuberculosis or pulmonary tuberculosis with risk of subsequent COPD. For COPD incidence, time-to-event data were constructed at first date of study recruitment and/or the date of tuberculosis diagnosis. Participants could have entered the study as unexposed (no history of tuberculosis) and then become exposed over follow-up upon developing tuberculosis. In the analysis, once COPD occurs, participants could no longer contribute to follow-up, regardless of their exposure status. We excluded 126 new cases of tuberculosis after a COPD diagnosis. Follow-up was censored at death or end of follow-up. The time to event in exposed and unexposed groups was defined as the time interval between the date participants were registered in the YHIS (or the time of TB diagnosis if diagnosed during follow-up) to the date of the earliest of COPD outcome (defined in the outcome measurement), death or the end of the study period (30 September 2021). Incidence rates for COPD were compared using two-sample Poisson tests. We defined three distinct regression models. In the first model, we adjusted for age and sex. Model 2 further adjusted for marital status, education level, smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for comorbidities and use of medications. Models 2 and 3 are the primary multivariable models in our analysis. One provides all potential confounding variables into the model (Model 3), and the other (Model 2) provides a simpler model (with less variables) which is less likely to be over-adjusted. In each of these models, we treated age as a continuous variable. We used Schoenfeld residuals to test for proportional hazard assumption ( P > 0.05).

We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD. Smoking status was categorized into current smokers if they smoked ≥1 cigarette per day for >1 year, former smokers if they had quit smoking for >1 year and never smokers for all others. Smoking intensity was divided into never smoking, <10, 10–20, ≥21 cigarettes per day. 30 , 31 Number of pack-years, representing cumulative dose, was calculated as (cigarettes per day/20) × smoking duration in years, and categorized into never smokers, <13, 13–24, ≥25 pack-years. 30 , 31 We combined former and current smokers when calculating smoking intensity and cumulative dose.

We also performed subgroup analyses to assess whether the associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD varied by age (35–49, 50–64 and ≥65 years), sex, smoking intensity, alcohol drinking, BMI (<24 or ≥24 kg/m 2 ), physical activity (<1 or ≥1 time/week) and education level. To evaluate whether an interaction was present, we used multivariable regression models with a multiplicative interaction term between each characteristic of interest and pulmonary tuberculosis. Then, we determined statistical significance for the interaction based on the maximum likelihood χ 2 from a nested model with and without the interaction term. 32

We calculated the population attributable fraction (PAF) of pulmonary TB and COPD using standard formulas 33 .

We conducted several sensitivity analyses. First, we excluded participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) as possible pre-symptoms of COPD. 34 Second, we further excluded incident COPD cases that occurred within the first year of follow-up or within 1 year of diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis and tuberculosis, to minimize reverse causation. Third, we used multiple imputation via chained equations (MICE) to impute missing values of covariates. Fourth, we altered the end of follow-up to 31 December 2019, in order to exclude the potential influence of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on outdoor physical activity, hospital visits and air pollution 22 . Fifth, we also excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline. Finally, we calculated E-value to assess the potential effect of unmeasured confounders. 35

All statistical tests were two-sided; 95% confidence intervals were considered to assess statistical significance.
We recruited 477 046 residents who had registered in the CHERRY study during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. We excluded 244 831 participants aged <35 years, 1552 participants with a previous history of COPD, 1008 participants with a previous history of cancer and 30 773 participants with missing values of covariates. Finally, we included a total of 198 882 participants in this study aged >35 years ( Figure 1 ). Median age of the study population was 46.5 [interquartile range (IQR), 40.5–56.2] ( Table 1 ); 51% of subjects were men.

Overall, a total of 1414 participants was identified with pulmonary tuberculosis, of whom 1413 were incident cases. The median follow-up time was 9.9 years (IQR, 8.8–11.1) and a total of 16 449 cases developed COPD during the study period ( Supplementary Table S4 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Median follow-up times between enrolment and incident tuberculosis diagnosis, as well as tuberculosis and COPD diagnosis, were 3.1 (IQR, 0.8–6.2) and 3.1 (IQR, 0.9–6.2), respectively. In the full cohort, the cumulative incidence of COPD was 8.3%, among individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis this was 23.6% ( Figure 2 ). When using a secondary exposure classification of all tuberculosis, cumulative incidence of COPD was 16.5%. The association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD was present in all multivariable models. Hazards ratios, derived from multivariable models measuring the association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD, ranged from 2.63 (95% CI, 2.36–2.93) in Model 1 to 1.77 (1.59–1.97) in Model 3 ( Table 2 ). For the association between all tuberculosis and COPD, the HR ranged from 1.71 (1.51–1.94) in Model 1 (adjustment for age and sex) to 1.18 (1.04–1.34) in Model 3 (adjustment for all demographic and clinical variables). When using differing classifications of smoking ( Supplementary Table S5 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) in model adjustments or a three-category variable for tuberculosis ( Supplementary Table S6 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online), results were similar. Using estimates of Model 2 and Model 3, the PAF for COPD due to pulmonary TB was 1.1% (0.9–1.3) and 0.5% (0.4–0.7), respectively.

When we further stratified our results to assess for interaction ( Figure 3 ), the relationship between pulmonary tuberculosis and increased risk of COPD was present across most but not all subgroups. An increased hazard of COPD was seen among persons aged 50–64 (aHR, 1.83; 1.56–2.15) and 65 years and above (aHR, 1.80; 1.50–2.16), but a weaker association was seen in those 35–49 years old (aHR, 1.40; 1.08–1.82). Associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD were observed among participants with poor education [less than high school: aHR, 1.90 (1.69–2.13); P interaction <0.001). We did not find evidence that smoking intensity, sex, alcohol use or physical activity were effect modifiers ( P interaction >0.05) ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). When we restricted our analysis to all tuberculosis; only smoking intensity did not modify the association.

Sensitivity analyses did not meaningfully change our findings ( Table 3 ). When excluding participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses, the aHRs were 1.91 (1.68–2.18) and 1.31 (1.13–1.52) for pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis exposure classifications, respectively. We also further excluded incident COPD cases occurring within the first year of follow-up, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.69 (1.51–1.90) and 1.18 (1.04–1.35), respectively. When using MICE to impute missing values of covariates, the corresponding aHRs were 1.76 (1.59–1.95) and 1.15 (1.02–1.30), respectively. Upon restricting follow-up duration to 31 December 2019, the corresponding aHRs were 2.04 (1.79–2.33) and 1.27 (1.09–1.49), respectively. In further sensitivity analyses, we excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.86 (1.66–2.08) and 1.24 (1.09–1.41), respectively. E-values were 2.94 and 1.64 for the associations of pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis with risk of COPD, respectively.
In this large, population-based cohort study, we found that persons who developed tuberculosis were at severely elevated risk of subsequently developing COPD. This relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent COPD was present even after accounting for smoking intensity (i.e., smoking did not confound, modify or interact with the relationship) and remained after several sensitivity analyses and after adjusting for a large selection of potentially relevant lifestyle, demographic and clinical confounders. This finding supports and extends prior work demonstrating lung impairment after a tuberculosis episode, 6 , 36 , 37 showing subsequent severe clinical chronic lung disease as a result. This work provides empirical evidence that tuberculosis is an important and underrecognized risk factor for COPD. The relationship was larger when considering pulmonary tuberculosis rather than all tuberculosis, supporting the hypothesis that pulmonary activity and damage during disease may be one mechanism of subsequent elevated COPD risk. We further found that certain subgroups of participants (participants who were older and with lower education, BMI and physical activity) were at highest risk of developing COPD after tuberculosis, which may suggest that targeted follow-up after recovery from tuberculosis may be a pragmatic and meaningful intervention to prevent severe lung disease.

Although lung damage due to smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD, there has been a growing push to recognize other routes or groups of patients that do not smoke who are also at high-risk. 2 , 3 Alternative risk factors may represent contributions to future COPD cases and may provide more amenable intervention strategies. The World Health Organization currently does not recognize tuberculosis as a risk factor for COPD. Our findings suggest that tuberculosis patients have increased risk of COPD, after controlling for the smoking variable, and that a proportion of COPD is attributable to tuberculosis. The results highlight the push for tuberculosis to be included. 9 There is growing realization in the tuberculosis field that post-disease sequalae and morbidity are immense. 4 , 6 , 7 , 38 Recent estimates suggest that there are approximately 155 million survivors of tuberculosis globally 39 ; our results indicate this population must be prioritized or, at a minimum, followed to prevent further lung damage. 38 , 40

Importantly, we found subgroups of participants that were at highest risk of developing COPD after a tuberculosis episode, including persons with low education, low BMI and not as physically active. Prior studies have either not identified important subgroups of persons with prior tuberculosis that are at particularly high risk of COPD, or shown heterogeneous results. 9 , 41 Groups at high-risk of COPD in our study may be an overlapping population, representing populations with low socioeconomic status (i.e., persons with low socioeconomic status may have low BMI, education level, etc.), suggesting that post-tuberculosis lung damage leading to COPD may be concentrated in the most at-need populations. Pathways explaining how these secondary variables accentuate the relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent tuberculosis cannot be ascertained with our data; however we hypothesize that low BMI may represent a severe form or more advanced stage of tuberculosis. 42

Our study has several strengths, including the large sample size with a wealth of demographic and clinical information on included participants. Second, distinct from most other databases of this kind, important individual-level, lifestyle risk factor information was available, including extent of physical activity, smoking intensity and alcohol use, among others. Our results are subject to less recall biases, as participants were administered surveys at multiple time points and were followed over time through a comprehensive health insurance system that detected diagnoses rather than self-reported prior tuberculosis. The CHERRY study, like large health insurance system datasets in many European countries, covers almost the entire district population (>99% of area inhabitants), thereby minimizing chances of missed tuberculosis diagnosis. 19 Last, tuberculosis diagnoses were assessed and confirmed through ICD-10 coding rather than through retrospective diagnosis or recall through self-report, as seen in prior studies. 12–14 This allows for direct confirmation of tuberculosis diagnosis and reduces potential exposure misclassification.

There are limitations to our analysis. First, despite the strengths of the comprehensive health system that the CHERRY study provides, tuberculosis cases that are never diagnosed and subsequently resolve are not covered, leading to underdiagnosis of tuberculosis. 43 Second, we did not measure household socioeconomic status or smoke exposures (e.g., use of biomass fuels), potential confounders that may impact on both tuberculosis and COPD. Third, although we stratify our analysis by whether the tuberculosis episode was pulmonary, the type, severity and drug-resistance profile of tuberculosis was not recorded. Future studies should further refine specific features of tuberculosis that are more likely to lead to COPD. Fourth, residual or unmeasured confounding is possible. For example, we did not measure characteristics at the time of tuberculosis diagnosis. Despite this, the high observed E-values suggest that any unmeasured characteristics would need to be heavily influential to affect our findings. Last, an underlying lung damage or susceptibility prior to the development of both COPD and tuberculosis, not available within our cohort, may be the cause of both diseases.
In conclusion, in our study of almost 200 000 participants within a population-based cohort study of an entire district area in eastern China, we found a markedly higher risk of COPD among persons with a tuberculosis episode. Importantly, this relationship remained after accounting for participant smoking status and intensity and was more pronounced among people with pulmonary tuberculosis. These results suggest that a prior tuberculosis episode should be considered an important risk factor for COPD and that prevention of tuberculosis may have indirect, downstream individual- and population-level health benefits.
The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.

category.Description: Explains how exposure arises across settings, covering behavioral, environmental, occupational, and social determinants; delineates canonical transmission routes and contact structures; interprets exposure-response with attention to measurement methods, units, detection limits, and thresholds; and situates risks within One Health interfaces involving reservoirs and vectors.
category.Rationale: The passage investigates the association between a prior episode of tuberculosis (a key exposure) and the subsequent development of COPD (a health outcome), with a strong focus on identifying and evaluating a non-smoking risk factor for COPD. The study is designed to assess the causal role of tuberculosis as a determinant of COPD, adjusting for major confounders such as smoking, BMI, physical activity, and socioeconomic status. The analysis includes detailed measurement of exposure (pulmonary vs. all tuberculosis), use of robust statistical methods (Cox regression, interaction testing, sensitivity analyses), and evaluation of effect modification by demographic and lifestyle factors (e.g., age, education, BMI). The findings suggest that tuberculosis—particularly pulmonary tuberculosis—is an important, underrecognized exposure contributing to COPD risk, independent of smoking. This aligns with Class 3’s focus on identifying and characterizing exposures, their measurement, and their relationship to disease outcomes, including how exposure-response relationships are shaped by measurement precision, confounding, and effect modification. The passage also situates this exposure within broader public health contexts (e.g., global TB survivors, health transitions in China), reinforcing its relevance to environmental and social determinants of disease. Multi-step inference questions could explore how different types of tuberculosis exposure (pulmonary vs. extrapulmonary) differentially affect COPD risk, how residual confounding might alter the observed association, or how social determinants (e.g., education, BMI) may mediate or modify the exposure-outcome relationship—making this class the most appropriate for generating complex, reasoning-based questions.

topic.Description: Integrates individual behaviours with environmental, occupational, and social/structural conditions that shape exposure probability and inequities.
topic.Rationale: The passage centers on identifying and analyzing the association between prior pulmonary tuberculosis and subsequent development of COPD, with a strong emphasis on how social, structural, and contextual factors influence this relationship. The study explicitly investigates how socioeconomic status (e.g., education level), BMI, physical activity, and other social determinants modify the risk of COPD after tuberculosis. Notably, the findings reveal that individuals with lower education, lower BMI, and less physical activity are at higher risk, suggesting that structural inequities amplify the long-term health consequences of tuberculosis. The study’s design—using a large, population-based cohort in a high-burden setting (China)—is explicitly chosen to capture real-world disparities and contextual exposures. Furthermore, the discussion highlights that these high-risk subgroups may represent populations with low socioeconomic status, linking the biological outcome (COPD) to broader social determinants. This focus on how social and structural conditions shape exposure to disease sequelae (i.e., COPD after TB) and contribute to health inequities makes Topic 1 the most appropriate. It supports multi-step inference questions about how poverty, education, and access to care may influence both tuberculosis outcomes and long-term respiratory health, going beyond simple associations to explore mechanisms of health disparity.

external_info:
An outbreak of pneumonia occurred in Viet Nam and Indonesia on March 12, 2003, with 305 confirmed cases and 5 deaths. Pneumonia is classified as a lung disease. Numerous drugs are associated with pneumonia, including amiodarone, asbestos, formaldehyde, cocaine, and various antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, chloramphenicol, and doxycycline. Additionally, arginine is implicated in the disease's pathogenesis. 

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is characterized by symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, cyanosis, fatigue, and hypoxia, and is associated with exposure to air pollutants, tobacco smoke, asbestos, and particulate matter. Drugs linked to this condition include corticosteroids, theophylline, salbutamol, and roflumilast, with arginine playing a role in its pathogenesis. It is categorized as an obstructive lung disease and resembles idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Asthma presents with symptoms including dyspnea, cough, wheezing, chest pain, and sleep disorders, and is associated with allergens such as ovalbumin, pollen, and environmental pollutants like ozone and nitrogen dioxide. Drugs used in its management include inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene antagonists, and beta-agonists, with the pathogenesis involving the chemokine CX3CL1. Asthma is classified as a bronchial disease and resembles atopic dermatitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Hypertension is associated with symptoms such as headache, dizziness, edema, and sleep apnea, and is linked to drugs including losartan, ramipril, and spironolactone, with several compounds such as prostaglandins A and phosphatidylinositols implicated in its pathogenesis. It is categorized as an artery disease and resembles abdominal obesity-metabolic syndrome 1, obesity, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Diabetes mellitus is classified as a glucose metabolism disease and is associated with drugs such as metformin, pioglitazone, and antipsychotics, with alanine and pyrimidine playing roles in its pathogenesis. It is also linked to environmental exposures such as pesticides, heavy metals, and air pollutants.

Cancer is categorized as a disease of cellular proliferation and is associated with drugs such as cyclophosphamide, temsirolimus, and various environmental carcinogens including pesticides and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, with amines and glycine implicated in its pathogenesis.

Tuberculosis and pulmonary tuberculosis are both classified as tuberculosis and are associated with drugs such as isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol, with lopinavir, phosphorus, and phosphates involved in pathogenesis. Tuberculosis is also categorized as a primary bacterial infectious disease.

Bronchiectasis is classified as a bronchial disease and is associated with antibiotics such as amoxicillin and tobramycin, with the aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption pathway implicated in its biology.

Congestive heart failure is categorized as a heart disease and is associated with drugs such as lisinopril, metoprolol, and digoxin, with hypoxanthine involved in its pathogenesis.

Osteoporosis is classified as a bone resorption disease and is associated with drugs such as bisphosphonates, calcium, vitamin D, and raloxifene, with amino acids and methotrexate playing roles in its pathogenesis. It is linked to pathways including osteoclast differentiation and mineral absorption.

COVID-19 is classified as a coronavirus infectious disease and is associated with drugs such as remdesivir, lopinavir, ritonavir, hydroxychloroquine, and baricitinib. It is also linked to the coronavirus disease - COVID-19 pathway.

ori_question.Question: In this cohort study, which factor most strongly suggests that the observed association between tuberculosis and subsequent COPD is influenced by broader social and environmental conditions rather than solely biological mechanisms?
Evidence: Passage: 'We further found that certain subgroups of participants (participants who were older and with lower education, BMI and physical activity) were at highest risk of developing COPD after tuberculosis, which may suggest that targeted follow-up after recovery from tuberculosis may be a pragmatic and meaningful intervention to prevent severe lung disease.'

Passage: 'Groups at high-risk of COPD in our study may be an overlapping population, representing populations with low socioeconomic status (i.e., persons with low socioeconomic status may have low BMI, education level, etc.), suggesting that post-tuberculosis lung damage leading to COPD may be concentrated in the most at-need populations.'
Passage: 'Despite this, the high observed E-values suggest that any unmeasured characteristics would need to be heavily influential to affect our findings.'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to infer that the association between tuberculosis and COPD is shaped by contextual determinants beyond biological mechanisms. Evidence 1 identifies a subgroup (older individuals with lower education, BMI, and physical activity) at highest risk of COPD after tuberculosis, suggesting that non-biological factors may amplify the risk. Evidence 2 explicitly links this subgroup to low socioeconomic status (SES), directly connecting the observed risk pattern to social and structural conditions such as education, nutrition (reflected in BMI), and access to health-promoting environments (reflected in physical activity). This transforms the interpretation from a purely biological association to one influenced by social inequities. Evidence 3, which reports high E-values, indicates that unmeasured confounding would need to be extremely strong to explain the association, thereby reducing the likelihood that residual confounding from unmeasured individual-level factors (e.g., diet, stress) alone accounts for the results. This strengthens the argument that the observed pattern is not due to hidden individual-level variables but instead reflects broader structural conditions. The external domain knowledge, while rich in associations between diseases and environmental exposures (e.g., air pollutants, tobacco smoke), does not provide specific information about socioeconomic determinants of tuberculosis or COPD outcomes. Therefore, it does not substantively inform the reasoning chain and was not incorporated. The question requires multi-step reasoning: one must first identify the subgroup pattern, then interpret it through the lens of social determinants, and finally use the E-value evidence to rule out alternative explanations, concluding that structural conditions are key drivers. The question is not answerable from any single piece of evidence and avoids direct references to 'social determinants' or 'inequity' in the stem, ensuring it requires inference rather than recall.

paragraph:
Household-based studies are often used to identify risk factors for tuberculosis (TB) infection transmission and evaluate the efficacy of TB preventive therapies. Typically, these studies define the earliest diagnosed TB patient within a household as the index patient and subsequently monitor their household contacts (HHCs) for incident TB disease. This design assumes that HHCs who develop TB disease are likely to have been infected by their respective index patients. However, this assumption may be challenged, as some HHCs likely acquire TB infections from community sources, introducing the non-differential misclassification of TB outcomes [ 1–5 ].

In principle, such non-differential misclassification biases study results toward the null, underestimating the true magnitude of the associations. Nevertheless, when unexpected or strong associations emerge, questions regarding the robustness and validity of the findings frequently arise. These concerns become particularly important in high-TB-burden settings, in which higher levels of community-based TB exposure may increase the potential for misclassification, thus weakening the conclusions derived from household-based studies [ 6 , 7 ].

To better understand the impact of community-acquired TB infections on household-based transmission studies, it is necessary to quantify the proportion of genetically linked index–HHC pairs, as these are likely the result of within-household transmission. In this study, we address this question in two ways. First, we assess the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs that are genetically linked by using data from a longitudinal household study that we previously conducted in Lima, Peru. We then incorporate the findings from this study into a systematic review of other studies that have applied molecular genotyping methods to index–HHC patient pairs. By synthesizing evidence across diverse epidemiological contexts and combining it with our primary data, we aim to rigorously evaluate the robustness and validity of household-based study designs across settings with different TB burdens. By clarifying the extent to which household transmission can be distinguished from community-acquired infection, this work also informs the design and interpretation of contact investigations, preventive therapy trials, and vaccine studies across settings with different TB burdens.
### Study setting and design

We conducted a prospective cohort study in 20 districts of Lima, Peru (population ∼3.3 million). The study design and methodology have been described previously [ 5 ]. Between September 2009 and August 2012, we enrolled incident pulmonary TB patients aged ≥16 years from 106 health centers and confirmed diagnoses by using sputum smear and culture. At enrolment, we collected sociodemographic and clinical data by using a structured questionnaire. Within 2 weeks of an index diagnosis, we invited HHCs to participate; consenting HHCs underwent TB symptom screening and, if positive, were referred for further evaluation. HHCs without TB at baseline were followed for 1 year, with visits at 2, 6, and 12 months. We classified HHCs diagnosed within 14 days as co-prevalent patients and those diagnosed between 14 and 455 days as secondary TB patients. Sputum samples were obtained whenever possible at enrolment or follow-up.

### Genotyping, whole-genome sequencing, and genetic distance analysis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) isolates from culture-positive index and HHC patients were genotyped by using 24-locus mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit–variable number tandem repeat (MIRU–VNTR) typing and sequenced by using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on the Illumina HiSeq platform. The read lengths ranged from 100 to 150 base pairs, with a minimum coverage of 20-fold. Raw WGS reads were mapped to the Mtb H37Rv reference genome by using the BWA-MEM algorithm [ 8 ]. We identified variants, including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), by using an alignment-based approach [ 9 , 10 ]. Isolates with <95% genome mapping coverage were excluded. We considered nucleotide calls missing if the valid depth of coverage was <10% of the mean coverage of the isolate, the mean read-mapping quality was <10, or the alternative allele frequency was <85%. Variants within the PE/PPE gene family and previously identified high-error regions were excluded [ 11 , 12 ]. Index–HHC pairs in which at least one isolate showed evidence of mixed infection were excluded from the analysis [ 13 ].

### Assessment of within-household transmission for index–HHC patient pairs

As a proxy for within-household transmission, we estimated the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs who were genetically linked by using MIRU–VNTR genotyping and WGS genetic distance analysis. A genetically linked transmission event was defined using MIRU typing as an index–HHC pair with ≥23 matched loci out of 24. In the WGS analysis, a genetically linked transmission event was defined as a genetic distance of ≤12 SNPs between Mtb isolates from the index–HHC pair [ 14 ]. We reported the overall proportion of genetically linked pairs, then stratified by co-prevalent versus secondary HHCs. Because many household studies focus on child contacts, who are more likely than adults to be infected by the index patient, we also reported matching proportions for pairs with a child contact [ 15 ]. Finally, we evaluated the associations between index and HHC characteristics and within-household transmission among index–secondary patient pairs by using a modified Poisson generalized estimating equation to account for correlation between pairs from the same households.
Among 12 676 HHCs exposed to a microbiologically confirmed index patient, 692 (5%) developed TB, of whom 246 (36%) were confirmed by using culture.

### MIRU genotyping matching

Among the 246 culture-confirmed HHC patients, 192 (78%) were successfully genotyped by using MIRU–VNTR, with data available for 168 index–HHC pairs. Twenty-three (14%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 145 pairs. Of these, 81 [56%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 47%–64%] were genetically linked. Twenty-six of 51 (51%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 55 of 94 (59%) index–secondary pairs were genetically linked. The HHC patients of 28 pairs were children. Of these, 4/5 (80%) co-prevalent and 15/23 (65%) secondary pairs were linked.

### WGS matching

Of 190 index–HHC pairs with WGS data, 15 (5%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 175 pairs from 152 households. Overall, 109 pairs (62%) were genetically linked. Transmission was observed in 34 of 66 (52%, 95% CI: 39%–64%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 74 of 109 (68%, 95% CI: 58%–77%) index–secondary pairs, with most secondary pairs (72/74) differing by up to five SNPs. When restricting to the 33 pairs with a child HHC, we noted 5/8 (63%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 19/25 (76%) index–secondary pairs ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Secondary pairs with female contacts were more often linked than those with male contacts (79% vs 54%, P = .008), while the Mtb lineage was not associated with genetic linkage ( P = .342).
### Search strategy and study selection

We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for papers that reported Mtb genotyping results for TB patients within the same household. We searched for papers published between 1 January 2006 and 20 June 2025, reflecting the time period following the widespread adoption of standardized 12-locus MIRU–VNTR [ 16 ]. Supplementary Table 2 describes the search strategy for each database.

### Screening

We performed an initial title and abstract review, excluding papers that did not discuss the household contacts of TB patients. For qualifying studies, we searched the full-text files for keywords related to Mtb molecular typing. Publications containing one or more keywords underwent full-text evaluation by two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. We excluded publications if they (i) did not involve original research on TB patients, (ii) did not include information on household membership, (iii) did not apply a qualifying genotyping method [spoligotyping, restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs), MIRU–VNTR, WGS] to Mtb samples, (iv) did not report Mtb genotype matching for household index–contact pairs, (v) enrolled fewer than five households, or (vi) obtained genotyping results for fewer than five index–contact pairs. We examined the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews for additional studies. A validation sample of 227 records was independently reviewed by a fourth reviewer, confirming the accuracy of the screening process.

### Data extraction

For qualifying studies, two reviewers extracted the following data: location and dates of patient enrolment, study design, eligibility criteria for index patients and contacts, procedure for identifying HHCs, definitions of household contacts, genotyping method(s), and the genotyping matching proportions for household patient pairs. We initially intended to extract individual patient data to assess the risk factors for genotype matching but this was unavailable in most studies. Instead, we extracted results based on the most stringent definition of matching of each study; when individual results were available, we calculated the proportion of identical genotypes. We reported the combined matching proportions for co-prevalent and secondary HHCs, and, when possible, separately for secondary HHCs as defined by the study authors. If the site-specific TB incidence was not reported in the publication, then we used WHO national estimates from the first year of enrolment or from 2000, whichever was later [ 17 ]. We also extracted individual-level metadata on age and gender when available.

### Quality assessment

We assessed the study quality by study design rigor and statistical robustness. Design rigor was scored (0–8) by using an eight-question framework on patient enrolment, household definitions, HHC follow-up, and genotyping completeness ( Supplementary Table 3 ). Statistical robustness was evaluated by the width of the Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs, with intervals of <40% considered robust.

### Modeling the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs

We modeled the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs by using a binomial generalized additive model with a logit link and spline term, with smoothness selected by using restricted maximum likelihood. For each incidence value, we estimated the fitted proportion and 95% CI on the probability scale.
The study selection process is shown in Fig. 1 . Out of 5910 unique citations identified from the search, we completed a full-text review of 231 publications. Two reviewed studies from Brazil were follow-up publications from an earlier and larger genotyping study, so we reported data from the larger study [ 18 ]. Ultimately, 22 articles met all inclusion criteria [ 18–39 ].

The 22 included studies, all published in English, evaluated within-household transmission between approximately 12 000 index patients and 2800 household contacts with TB, enrolled between 1995 and 2023 ( Table 1 ). These studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa (South Africa, Ghana, Uganda, the Gambia, Malawi), South America (Brazil, Argentina, Peru), Central and Western Europe (Poland, Spain, the UK), Southeast Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines), the USA, and China. Two studies [ 19 , 21 ] included co-prevalent household patients only, 5 studies [ 18 , 24 , 26 , 30 , 31 ] included secondary household patients only, and 15 studies [ 20 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 27–29 , 32–39 ] included both. Four studies focused their enrolment on patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis [ 27 , 29 , 30 , 32 ]. The included studies encompassed a wide range of TB-burden settings, with community incidence rates ranging from 6.7 to 845 TB patients per 100 000 person-years. The number of index–HHC pairs with genotyping data ranged from 6 to 344 per study, with a median of 17.5 pairs ( Table 2 ). Genotyping for one or more index–child HHC pairs was available for five studies and gender information for patient pairs was partially or completely available for eight studies ( Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 ).

### Quality assessment

Among the 22 studies from the systematic review, 10 studies (45%) [ 18–21 , 24–27 , 29 , 36 ] were scored as ≥5/8 for study design. The most common methodological gaps were the failure to report the proportion of eligible index patients who agreed to participate ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 2), the lack of active follow-up to detect incident TB among HHCs ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 7), and the prolonged interval allowed between the index patient’s diagnosis and the subsequent diagnosis of HHC TB patients ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 8).

Eleven (50%) reviewed studies reported matching proportions with a Clopper–Pearson exact 95% CI width of >40% [ 19–21 , 24 , 26–30 , 33 , 38 ]. Therefore, only 11 reviewed studies were considered statistically robust ( Fig. 2 ).

### Host factors and within-household transmission

Among the 11 reviewed studies that met our criteria for statistical robustness, three reported genetic linkage by age ( Supplementary Table 4 ). However, two of these studies [ 31 , 34 ] included three or fewer child contacts. In the third study [ 25 ], the matching proportion was 90% (26/29) in pairs with child contacts and 63% (20/32) in pairs with adult contacts. Three statistically robust studies reported gender information for comparison ( Supplementary Table 5 ). One study [ 37 ] reported 100% matching for all pair types and the two other studies [ 31 , 34 ] found matching proportions that were similar for female and male contacts, with slightly higher values in females (88% vs 81%, P = .656; 73% vs 70%, P = .999).
### All pairs (index–co-prevalent and index–secondary patient pairs)

Across 23 studies (22 from the review and our Lima study), the proportion of genetically matched index–HHC pairs ranged from 17% to 100%. Of six studies using multiple methods independently, five reported variability across the methods. No method universally yielded higher or lower proportions, though spoligotyping gave the highest proportions in three out of four studies. Eleven studies used MIRU–VNTR (with varying loci) and seven implemented WGS ( Table 2 ).

Among the 12 total studies with greater statistical robustness [ 18 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 31 , 32 , 34–37 , 39 ], 10 reported an overall matching proportion of ≥62% and two studies from the same cohort in Malawi reported proportions of 44% and 49%, respectively ( Fig. 2a ). The nine studies that reported a matching proportion of ≥62% were conducted in settings with a TB incidence of ≤276 patients per 100 000 person-years, while the studies from Malawi were conducted in an area with a TB burden of 386 patients per 100 000 person-years.

The spline regression model of all patient pairs suggests that, in study settings with an annual TB incidence of ≤250 per 100 000 population, at ≥61% (95% CI: 55%–67%) of household patients are genetically matched to their index patient, likely reflecting household TB infection transmission ( Fig. 2b ). However, estimates of the matching proportion in regions of exceptionally high TB incidence are limited by sparse data.

### Index–secondary patient pairs only

Eleven studies, including our study in Lima, reported a separate matching proportion for index–secondary patient pairs ( Fig. 3 ). Five studies were statistically robust, though all of these were conducted in settings of low or moderate TB incidence. Secondary matching proportions were equivalent to or higher than overall matching in all studies except for Robbins et al. , who reported a secondary matching proportion of 55% for exact spoligotype and RFLP matches. However, the inclusion of near genotype matches increases this proportion to 88%, highlighting the challenge of comparing across typing methods and definitions of concordance.
Here, we found that, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 cases per 100 000 person-years, the majority of index–HHC patient pairs are genetically matched, regardless of the genotyping method employed, suggesting that within-household transmission predominates at low to moderate TB incidence. However, substantial variation was observed in settings with higher TB burdens (>250 cases per 100 000 person-years), likely due to limited genotyping data and smaller sample sizes.

Genotyping tools differ in resolution: WGS offers the highest, RFLP and MIRU–VNTR moderate, and spoligotyping the lowest. Higher-resolution methods often yield lower matching proportions [ 40 ]. Within the same studies, the matching proportions varied, depending on the genotyping method used. Spoligotyping typically produced higher proportions, while no consistent pattern emerged with WGS, RFLP, and MIRU–VNTR. These inconsistencies may reflect the greater ability of WGS to detect mixed infections and its sensitivity to sputum quality, both of which affect matching calculations and contribute to discrepancies with RFLP and MIRU–VNTR.

Although all studies defined the earliest diagnosed TB patient in a household as the index or “source” patient, only four actively and prospectively followed HHCs to track incident TB disease. Most studies relied on national TB registries to retrospectively identify secondary patients, often diagnosed years after the index patient. In the studies from Malawi that reported matching proportions of <50%, the time between the index and contact patient diagnoses was allowed to be >10 years. This delay increases the likelihood that household cases are community-acquired rather than originating from household transmission. If these retrospective studies had limited the diagnostic interval between the index and secondary HHC patients to ≤2years, the reported matching proportions would likely have been higher. Thus, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 cases per 100 000 person-years, the actual proportion attributable to household transmission likely exceeds the estimated 61%.

Household contacts’ age and gender may also influence the within-household transmission dynamics. Many household-based studies, particularly clinical trials of TB preventive therapy, focus on child contacts to minimize misclassification, assuming that children have limited social interactions and are primarily infected by their index patient [ 5 , 41 , 42 ]. Our Lima study and Whalen et al. observed a trend toward higher matching proportions among pediatric contacts compared with adults, consistently with the rationale for child-contact study designs. Gender-based household roles may further shape transmission. Several systematic review studies indicate that women spend more time at home due to caregiving and domestic responsibilities [ 43–46 ], likely leading to increased exposure to infectious household members. This likely explains the higher matching proportions observed among female HHCs.

Our systematic review has limitations. First, despite a rigorous search strategy, we may have inadvertently missed relevant studies due to search-term constraints. Secondly, most included studies relied on data collected over a decade ago. Advances in diagnostics, community-based TB control, and expanded TB preventive therapy coverage may have altered the transmission dynamics, meaning that older findings may not fully reflect the current realities. Third, the limited sample size of index–HHC pairs in most studies precluded formal statistical testing; therefore, we presented descriptive analyses only, which restricts the extent to which we can draw statistical inferences. Fourth, we assumed that non-matched index–HHC pairs reflect community-acquired infection. In the absence of additional contact tracing or social network data, we cannot rule out the possibility that some of these pairs may instead represent unrecognized household transmission chains, which could lead to an overestimation of community-acquired infection.

In summary, our findings suggest that, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 per 100 000 person-years, 20%–40% of incident HHC TB patients may be misclassified as having had household transmission, with lower misclassification when analyses focus on child or female contacts. Its impact in high-incidence settings remains unclear. Because TB preventive therapy trials span countries with varying TB burdens, misclassification differences must be considered. Predictive modeling has been proposed to address community-acquired infections but standardized methods and validation are needed to better characterize household transmission in high-burden settings.
The Institutional Review Board of Harvard School of Public Health and the Research Ethics Committee of the National Institute of Health of Peru approved the study. All study participants or their guardians provided written informed consent and children <18 years of age provided assent.

category.Rationale: This passage is fundamentally focused on evaluating the methodological robustness and validity of household-based TB transmission studies, particularly in light of non-differential misclassification due to community-acquired infections. The core of the work involves a sophisticated methodological approach: combining primary data from a longitudinal cohort in Lima, Peru, with a systematic review of genotyping studies across diverse settings. The study critically assesses the impact of genotyping methods (MIRU-VNTR, WGS, spoligotyping) on the estimation of within-household transmission, addresses issues of study design (e.g., active vs. passive follow-up, diagnostic interval), and evaluates statistical robustness (e.g., confidence interval width). A key analytical contribution is the use of a binomial generalized additive model with spline terms to model the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of genetically linked pairs, which directly reflects advanced methodological modeling. The discussion also centers on bias handling—specifically, how misclassification affects causal inference in transmission studies—and proposes future directions such as predictive modeling to address community-acquired infections. These elements align precisely with Class 5, which emphasizes analytical methods, causal inference, bias assessment, and evaluation of study design and measurement. The passage is not primarily about surveillance (Class 1), outbreak investigation (Class 2), determinants (Class 3), immunity (Class 4), or forecasting (Class 6), but rather about rigorously evaluating and improving the methods used to infer transmission dynamics. This makes Class 5 the most appropriate for generating multi-step inference questions that require reasoning about study design limitations, bias correction, methodological trade-offs, and the validity of causal conclusions in epidemiological research.

topic.Rationale: The passage centers on the critical issue of non-differential misclassification in household-based tuberculosis (TB) transmission studies, where the assumption that all household contacts (HHCs) with TB were infected by their index patient may be invalid due to community-acquired infections. This misclassification biases estimates of household transmission toward the null, undermining the validity of study findings. The study systematically investigates this bias by using molecular genotyping (MIRU-VNTR and WGS) to distinguish true within-household transmission from community-acquired cases, thereby directly addressing measurement error in outcome classification. The analysis evaluates how genotyping method choice, time intervals between index and HHC diagnoses, and study design (e.g., active vs. passive follow-up) affect the accuracy of transmission attribution. It also discusses limitations such as sparse data in high-burden settings, potential overestimation of community transmission due to unmeasured household transmission chains, and the impact of outdated data. These elements reflect a deep engagement with measurement validity, misclassification, and the influence of study design on bias. While the study also touches on study design (Topic 3) and generalizability, its core focus is on identifying, quantifying, and mitigating measurement error and bias in transmission inference—making Topic 4 the most appropriate and richest source for generating multi-step inference questions that require combining genotyping data, study design features, and epidemiological principles to assess the robustness of transmission estimates.

external_info: Pulmonary tuberculosis is a form of tuberculosis, which itself is classified as a primary bacterial infectious disease. The condition is associated with a range of drugs, including aminosalicylic acids, arsenic, capreomycin, carbon monoxide, clarithromycin, cycloserine, dihydrostreptomycin sulfate, ethambutol, isoniazid, nitrogen dioxide, ofloxacin, pyrazinamide, pyridoxine, rifabutin, rifampicin, streptomycin, and the combination isoniazid/pyrazinamide/rifampin. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is also linked to several drugs, such as aminosalicylic acid, bedaquiline, capreomycin, cycloserine, entacapone, ethambutol, ethionamide, gatifloxacin, isoniazid, kanamycin, ofloxacin, pyrazinamide, rifampicin, tolcapone, and fluoroquinolones. The broader category of tuberculosis is associated with numerous drugs, including 9,9-dimethylcarbazine, amikacin, amithiozone, bedaquiline, chenodeoxycholic acid, ciprofloxacin, gentamicins, iron, kanamycin, menaquinone, OPC-67683, pitolisant, prednisolone, pyrroles, terizidone, tretinoin, verapamil, viomycin, isofon, and the combination isoniazid/pyrazinamide/rifampin. Additionally, certain drugs such as lopinavir, phosphorus, and phosphates are implicated in the disease’s pathogenesis. The condition is associated with the tuberculosis biological pathway. Furthermore, tuberculosis is linked to community-acquired infections, which are treated with a variety of antibiotics including amoxicillin, amoxicillin-potassium clavulanate combination, azithromycin, cefpodoxime proxetil, ceftobiprole, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, ciprofloxacin, clindamycin, co-trimoxazole, delafloxacin, doxycycline, erythromycin, flucloxacillin, linezolid, omadacycline, panton-valentine leukocidin, pristinamycin, solithromycin, sparfloxacin, teicoplanin, theophylline, trovafloxacin, vancomycin, and cefditoren pivoxil.

ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to answer the question. Evidence 1 establishes the general principle that non-differential misclassification—such as incorrectly classifying a community-acquired case as household-transmitted—biases results toward the null, reducing observed effect sizes. This sets the stage for understanding why accurate classification is critical. Evidence 2 provides context: in low-to-moderate TB incidence settings, most genetically linked pairs are consistent with household transmission, implying that genotyping can be a valid tool under these conditions. However, Evidence 3 introduces a key methodological flaw: allowing long intervals (>10 years) between index and secondary case diagnoses increases the chance that the secondary case was acquired from the community, not the household. This undermines the validity of the assumption that all HHCs with TB were infected by the index patient. The critical insight is that even with accurate genotyping, the study design—specifically, the time window used to define secondary cases—can introduce misclassification. Therefore, the validity of attributing cases to household transmission depends not just on genotyping accuracy, but on the temporal definition of secondary cases. The external domain knowledge lists antibiotics and drugs used in TB treatment, including those for community-acquired infections, but does not provide information relevant to study design, misclassification, or the temporal dynamics of transmission. Thus, it is not incorporated into the reasoning chain. The question requires multi-step reasoning: one must recognize that genotyping alone is insufficient, that study design choices (like diagnostic interval) affect misclassification, and that this in turn impacts the validity of transmission attribution—none of which is directly stated in any single evidence piece.
