paragraph:
Emerging evidence suggests that reproductive health factors in adolescence are associated with diabetes incidence in adulthood [ 1–3 ]. The onset of menarche, or the first menstrual cycle, indicates sexual maturation and is the first milestone in a woman’s reproductive history [ 4 ]. Epidemiologic data from high-income countries (HICs) show that younger age at menarche is associated with 1.5 times higher risk of diabetes incidence [ 5–10 ]. It is not clear whether these findings extend to women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) who exhibit different reproductive and metabolic profiles. On average, women in LMICs experience a later age at onset of menarche [ 11–13 ] and are less likely to be obese than women in HICs. India, a country with a high diabetes burden [ 14 , 15 ] and historically lower levels of obesity, offers an informative setting to evaluate the relationship between age at menarche and diabetes in the LMIC context.

Although the mechanisms underlying the link between early onset of menarche and type 2 diabetes are unclear, women with earlier onset of menarche are known to experience pronounced post-menarche adipose tissue accumulation [ 16 ] resulting in increased body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference in adulthood [ 17 , 18 ], which are important risk factors for development of diabetes [ 19 ]. However, the causal direction of the obesity-menarche association remains unclear as girls with childhood obesity experience rapid pubertal progression [ 17 , 20–22 ]. Genes controlling both age at menarche and glucose regulation also offer a possible explanation for this association [ 23 ]. Further, early menarche is associated with high levels of sex hormones and low levels of sex hormone-binding globulin, which in turn reduce insulin secretion and elevate blood glucose levels. It is hypothesized that with these hormonal features women with early menarche are therefore at higher risk of diabetes independent of adiposity [ 24–27 ].

To investigate the relationship between age at menarche and diabetes in adulthood, we estimated the longitudinal association between age at menarche and incident diabetes in women in the Cardiometabolic Risk Reduction in South Asia (CARRS) cohort. We also investigated the effect modification of this association by adult adiposity as it is a potential putative factor in this association from previously published studies.
### Participants

The CARRS study was established in 2010–12 as a multi-centric, community-based prospective study to identify risk factors for cardio-metabolic diseases among South Asians. The details of the CARRS study have been described elsewhere [ 28 , 29 ] and the cohort has maintained excellent retention at follow-up examinations [ 30 ]. Briefly, the cohort comprised of 12 271 adults aged ≥20 years from two cities in India (Chennai and Delhi) at baseline. Trained staff obtained informed consent and collected data using a standard validated questionnaire to record information on health-related behaviours and assessment of disease outcomes.

Of the original cohort at baseline, we excluded men ( n = 5868) and women with pre-existing diabetes ( n = 1543) (see Fig. 1 ). Of 4860 women free of known diabetes at baseline, we excluded 953 due to missing biomarker data to confirm diabetes status or missing age at menarche or age at menarche not within the range and subsequently another 144 due to missing other study covariate. Further, 109 women were lost to follow-up and censored from the analysis. For this analysis, the analytic cohort therefore comprised 3654 women who were diabetes-free at baseline and were followed until an incident diabetes event through 2021. While some statistical differences were observed (between women in the analytic sample and those excluded from the analysis) due to the large sample size, the standardized differences were <0.2 suggesting that these differences were unlikely to introduce bias in further analyses ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

The CARRS study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the Public Health Foundation of India (IRB00006658), Delhi; All India Institute of Medical Sciences (IEC/NP-17/07.09.09), Delhi and Madras Diabetes Research Foundation (MDRF/EC/EPI/2009/10), Chennai. Additionally, the study received approval from the Health Ministry Screening Committee of the Government of India.

### Exposure and outcome assessment

The exposure for this analysis was age at menarche, in years, or age at first menstrual period. It was ascertained at baseline based on self-report queried through a questionnaire. Given that there is no universally accepted definition for early menarche and there is no prior work from India, we considered age at menarche in years as a continuous measure. The outcome for this analysis was incident diabetes. Incident diabetes cases were defined as study participants who were diabetes‐free at baseline and who had fasting plasma glucose levels ≥126 mg/dl (≥7.0 mmol/l) or HbA1c levels ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol), or self‐reported medical diagnosis with prescription of glucose lowering drugs at follow‐up examinations [ 29 , 31 ]. On each of the biennial follow-ups, blood samples were collected for assessment of diabetes status whereas, participants were asked about physician-diagnosed diabetes at each annual follow-up visit. The date of onset of diabetes was considered as the date of most recent follow-up visit after the diagnosis of diabetes.

### Covariates

Participants reported information on socio-demographics (age, monthly household income, education, marital status, religion, and ownership of assets), lifestyle factors [ever-use of tobacco/alcohol, work-related vigorous physical activity [ 32 ], fruit/vegetable consumption (modified food frequency questionnaire)], first-degree family history of diabetes, medical history or presence of a chronic condition (hypertension, heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, dyslipidaemia), and reproductive history (number of pregnancies, menopause status) at baseline.

Physical measurements (blood pressure, height, weight, waist circumference) were recorded using standardized procedures [28]. Those with measured waist circumference ≥80 cm were grouped as women with central obesity. We calculated the BMI as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Although, literature supports the use of waist circumference as a more useful obesity index in the Indian population to assess the risk of cardiometabolic conditions, we included both the measures in our analysis [ 33 ].

### Statistical analysis

We accounted for the complex survey design in the statistical analysis and all estimates apply survey weights.

We summarized the participant characteristics as prevalence [95% confidence interval (CI)] for categorical variables and mean [standard deviation (SD) and 95% CI] for continuous variables for the overall sample and compared the same by incident diabetes status. The difference in the age at menarche by participant characteristics was also computed using the adjusted Wald test.

We next calculated the incidence rate of diabetes (95% CI) by the age at onset of menarche. In the absence of definitive age categories for menarche in the Indian population, we empirically established groups based on the distribution of menarche timing and diabetes incidence within our cohort. To achieve this, we computed available sample sizes and the number of diabetes events across each year of age at menarche. Drawing on this tabulation, we categorized menarche timing into four groups: ≤12 years, 13 years, 14 years, and ≥15 years. In our further analysis, age at menarche was analysed both, as a continuous and a categorical exposure.

We calculated person years of follow-up as the number of years from baseline to first diagnosis of diabetes, death, loss of follow-up, or end of follow-up (2021) whichever came first. We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age. We evaluated the proportionality assumption through the Schoenfeld residual test, which indicated no significant violation of the assumption ( P -value = 0.109). Based on the hypothesized causal pathways drawing on prior literature, we sequentially included five sets of covariates in separate models. The unadjusted model was followed by addition of baseline age of women (in model 1). We next included other socio-demographic variables (city, education, wealth index, marital status, religion), and family history of diabetes (in model 2), and lifestyle factors (physical activity, tobacco use, fruit/vegetable consumption) and presence of a chronic condition (in model 3). The final set of models incorporated adiposity measures as potential mediating factors: waist circumference as a measure of central obesity (model 4a) and BMI as a measure of general obesity (model 4b).

We assessed statistical interaction between age at menarche and obesity (BMI and waist circumference classifications, separately) using the P -value of the Wald test and also conducted Cox proportional hazards analyses stratified by obesity classification.

Lastly, we conducted an analysis restricting to women aged 20–45 years at baseline. This analysis addressed the higher potential for recall bias in the age at menarche among older women and allowed us to explore associations of interest in an age group that reported a younger age at menarche on average.

All analysis was performed using the STATA statistical package (StataCorp. 2019. Stata Statistical Software: Release 16 .1 College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC.).
Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of women. The mean age (SD) of 3654 women free of diabetes at enrolment was 37.7 (SD = 10.4; range: 20–85) years, 59.9% were from Chennai and 64.0% had high to secondary school education. More than 50% of women had waist circumference ≥80 cm and slightly over 70% had a BMI ≥23 kg/m 2 . Women who developed incident diabetes were, on average, older in age at baseline. A higher proportion of women residing in Delhi developed incident diabetes over follow-up. Additionally, women who developed incident diabetes were more likely to report menopause, had an existing chronic condition, a family history of diabetes and were obese at baseline.

The mean (SD) age at onset of menarche was 13.9 (SD = 1.3; range: 9–18) years in the total sample. Supplementary Table S2 shows mean age at menarche by demographic and health characteristics. Younger women (20–39 years: 13.7, 40–59 years: 140.0, and ≥60 years: 13.9 years; P <.001) and those having a family history of diabetes (13.7 vs 13.9 years; P = .001) had a significantly earlier age at onset of menarche compared to their counterparts. Although women with general and central obesity had an earlier onset of menarche compared to their counterparts, the difference was not significant.

The incidence rate of diabetes by groups of age at onset of menarche is shown in Table 2 . Over ∼11 years of follow-up (median: 9.2 years; range: 0.09–11.05 years), there were 390 incident diabetes cases. The overall incidence rate of diabetes was 12.4 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 11.23–13.69); cumulative incidence was 10.7% (95% CI 9.32–12.33). Diabetes incidence rate was highest among women with menarche onset at 13 years, 14.0 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 11.69–16.80).

Table 3 shows the Cox proportional hazards analysis of age at menarche with incident diabetes. We did not observe an association between age at onset of menarche in years (treated as a continuous measure) and incident diabetes in any of the models. The unadjusted association between age at menarche and incident diabetes was HR = 1.03 (95% CI 0.94–1.14). After adjusting for age, demographics, and other confounding factors ( Table 3 , model 4a), the HR was 1.04 (95% CI 0.95–1.14).

When menarche onset age was analysed as distinct categories ( Table 3 ), we found no significant associations between age at menarche and incident diabetes. After adjusting for age, demographics, and other confounding factors ( Table 3 , Model 3), compared to women who experienced menarche at age 12, women with age at menarche of 13 had HR = 1.26 (95% CI 0.80–2.01), those at age 14 had HR = 1.16 (95% CI 0.73–1.83), and those at age 15 or older had HR = 1.28 (95% CI 0.79–2.06). These HR estimates remained similar even when we accounted for central and general obesity measures (Models 4a and 4b).

Supplementary Table S3 shows models with continuous age at menarche stratified by waist circumference and BMI. The point estimates for the HR for the association between age at menarche in years and incident diabetes were consistently higher in women with waist circumference ≤80 cm vs >80 cm and in women with BMI ≥23 vs BMI <23, but none of these associations were statistically significant. Moreover, there was no evidence of statistical interaction between age at menarche with central obesity (Wald P = 0.145) or general obesity (Wald P = 0.138).

Sensitivity analyses restricted to women aged 20–45 years demonstrated that the incidence of diabetes was progressively lower for every one year later onset of menarche, HR = 0.97 (95% CI 0.88–1.07) (model 4a), though this was not a statistically significant finding ( Supplementary Table S4 ).
To our knowledge, this is the first prospective study of age at menarche and incident type 2 diabetes among women in India, a setting with rapidly rising diabetes in the last two decades [ 15 , 34 , 35 ]. Roughly one in 10 women aged 20–85 years newly developed diabetes over the 11 years of follow-up. On average, women in our cohort experienced menarche at 13.9 years, nearly one year later than the global average [ 5–7 , 18 ]. In contrast to findings in some populations [ 8 ], we did not find evidence of an association between age of onset menarche and incident type 2 diabetes in this setting. The null association remained unchanged after adjustment for and stratification by adiposity.

Although many studies have reported heightened risk of diabetes among women with earlier onset of menarche, the findings remain inconclusive, and associations appear to vary across race, ethnicity, and geography. The strongest and most consistent associations have been reported among white women and populations with an earlier average age of menarche [ 8 ]. While White women in the ARIC cohort had a higher risk of incident diabetes, no association was observed among African American women [ 7 ]. In a separate study of Chinese women, the risk of incident diabetes was higher among women those with an earlier onset of menarche, and the association was attenuated on adjustment for adult adiposity [ 36 ]. A recent analysis of the data from 262 368 women diabetes free at baseline in the UK Biobank cohort demonstrates that women with early menarche ( < 12 years) had a higher risk of incident diabetes (HR 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02–1.13) compared to women experiencing menarche at 13 years [ 3 ].

Beyond differences in racial and ethnic composition of study populations, the definition of early menarche varies, with some studies considering it as occurring before age 12, while others set the threshold at before 14 years. A meta-analysis of 14 studies found that women who experienced early menarche had a 22% higher risk of type 2 diabetes compared with women who did not experience early menarche [ 9 ]. A more recent meta-analysis of 28 studies reported very similar levels of excess risk (19% higher diabetes) in women with earlier onset of menarche [ 8 ]. In most of these studies, associations between menarche age and diabetes were attenuated after adjusting for adiposity [ 5 , 7 , 37 ]. Surprisingly, women in the earliest menarche group (≤12 years) in our study had the lowest incidence rate of diabetes, though the relative risk of diabetes was not statistically different between these women and women who experienced menarche at older ages.

While women in LMICs have historically reported later age at menarche onset than HIC counterparts [ 38 , 39 ], age at onset of menarche appears to be declining in the Indian population and globally [ 11 , 40 ]. Women in the 20–39 years age group in our cohort reported younger average age at menarche relative to the ≥40 year age group, providing additional evidence of earlier age of onset of menarche in more recent birth cohorts. Beyond genetic factors [ 41–43 ], earlier onset of menarche can be attributed to socio-economic development and the associated transition to more obesogenic lifestyles characterized by greater linear growth and relative weight gain in infancy and early childhood [ 44–52 ]. While it is understood that pubertal maturation is often preceded by rapid childhood growth and that girls with earlier onset of menarche tend to have higher BMIs [ 48 , 49 ], evidence also suggests that earlier onset of menarche can lead to post-menarche adiposity and insulin resistance, contributing to development of diabetes [ 20 , 53 , 54 ]. Given the ongoing nutritional and epidemiological transitions in India, the relationship between menarche onset and diabetes warrant additional research in younger women who are likely to experience differing environments from the CARRS cohort.

Primary strengths of this study include prospective data from large community-based representative sample of women with objective measures of glycaemic status to define diabetes over an 11 year follow up period. The key limitation of this study is the potential for recall bias in the self-reported age at menarche and the lack of information on health characteristics during childhood and adolescence such as BMI and lifestyle factors. Regarding recall bias, evidence suggests a high correlation between the menarche age assessed by recall during adulthood and that obtained prospectively in childhood [ 55 , 56 ]. Furthermore, our analyses restricted to younger women who would ostensibly be more likely to accurately recall age at menarche reinforced the findings in the full cohort. Regarding characteristics in childhood and adolescents, many of these factors are likely mediators which ought not to be adjusted for to derive unconfounded associations. We note that the differences in the characteristics of the analytic sample and the original cohort limit the potential generalizability of the findings to the population of urban women residing in the two study sites. We emphasize that the standardized difference in age at menarche is <0.1, suggesting sufficient covariate balance and therefore the potential for selection bias due to study inclusion criteria is low [ 57 ].

In summary, we did not observe an association between onset of menarche and risk of incident type 2 diabetes in a large population-based cohort of Indian women. Given the global trend towards earlier puberty timing, future longitudinal studies with younger populations and longer follow-up duration are warranted to further investigate the possible role of menarche timing in diabetes development.
The CARRS study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of the Public Health Foundation of India (IRB00006658), Delhi; All India Institute of Medical Sciences (IEC/NP-17/07.09.09), Delhi and Madras Diabetes Research Foundation (MDRF/EC/EPI/2009/10), Chennai. Additionally, the study received approval from the Health Ministry Screening Committee of the Government of India. This secondary data analysis was approved by the MSc Research Ethics Committee of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom.

category.Description: Describes who is susceptible and why, linking serologic measures to correlates of protection; evaluates effectiveness after vaccination or prior infection and its waning with reinfection, hybrid immunity, and variant escape, including the effects of vaccine dose number and intervals; and assesses severity risk using clinical and contextual prognostic factors.
category.Rationale: The passage investigates the relationship between age at menarche—a biological marker of reproductive maturation—and the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in adulthood, focusing on a cohort of Indian women. While the study is observational and not directly about immunization, its core focus is on identifying biological and developmental factors that influence susceptibility to a chronic disease (diabetes) later in life. The analysis centers on how early biological events (like menarche) may predispose individuals to disease through pathways involving metabolic dysregulation, adiposity, and hormonal changes—key elements of susceptibility. The study evaluates whether early menarche, a marker of altered developmental timing, increases susceptibility to diabetes, and explores potential mediating roles of adult adiposity, which is a known risk factor. The findings, though null, are interpreted in the context of biological mechanisms (e.g., insulin resistance, sex hormones, post-menarche adiposity) that shape individual susceptibility. This aligns with Class 4, which emphasizes understanding who is susceptible and why, including the interplay of biological, metabolic, and hormonal factors. Multi-step inference questions could explore the causal pathways from early menarche to diabetes, the role of adiposity as a mediator, the impact of age at menarche in different populations, and the implications of developmental timing on long-term disease risk—all requiring integration of biological plausibility, epidemiological evidence, and contextual factors.

topic.Description: Assesses risk of severe outcomes conditional on infection and stratifies prognosis by host factors.
topic.Rationale: The passage investigates the association between age at menarche and incident type 2 diabetes in adult women, with a focus on identifying whether early reproductive development is a predictor of future metabolic disease. While the study examines a biological and developmental exposure (age at menarche), the primary outcome is incident diabetes—a clinical condition that represents a severe health consequence in the context of cardiometabolic disease. The analysis explicitly evaluates how baseline characteristics, including adiposity (a key prognostic factor), modify the relationship between menarche timing and diabetes risk. The study uses Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios for diabetes incidence, adjusting for multiple confounders and stratifying by obesity status, which reflects a core epidemiological approach to assessing prognostic factors. Although the exposure is developmental, the outcome is a clinically significant, chronic disease with long-term morbidity, and the study’s goal is to determine whether early menarche is a risk factor for this adverse health outcome. This aligns most closely with Topic 4—assessing risk of severe outcomes (diabetes) and stratifying prognosis by host factors (e.g., adiposity, age, socioeconomic status). The null findings and sensitivity analyses further underscore the focus on prognostic modeling and risk stratification. While the topic of reproductive timing may seem related to susceptibility or life-course epidemiology, the central question is not about immune protection, vaccine effectiveness, or serological correlates, but rather about predicting a severe disease outcome based on early-life markers. Thus, Topic 4 is the most appropriate for guiding multi-step inference questions that require reasoning about causal pathways, effect modification, and the clinical significance of early-life exposures in predicting long-term disease risk.

external_info: Diabetes mellitus is classified as a glucose metabolism disease. It is associated with a range of drugs, including those that are commonly used in treatment such as Gliclazide, Glipizide, Nateglinide, Repaglinide, and Rosiglitazone, as well as compounds that play a role in disease pathogenesis such as Alanine, chemokine CX3CL1, and pyrimidine. The condition is also linked to various symptoms, including obesity, overweight, weight gain, weight loss, albuminuria, proteinuria, and microvascular angina. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, a subtype of diabetes mellitus, presents with additional symptoms such as acute coronary syndrome, gastroparesis, flushing, and overactive urinary bladder. It is associated with drugs like Acarbose, Linagliptin, Sitagliptin phosphate, and Pioglitazone, and its pathogenesis involves pathways including insulin secretion, PPAR signaling, pancreatic secretion, and the p53 signaling pathway. Type 1 diabetes mellitus 2 is recognized as a subtype of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Obesity, which is closely related to type 2 diabetes mellitus, is characterized by symptoms such as hyperphagia, hypoventilation, sleep apnea, and sarcopenia. It is associated with drugs like Lorcaserin, Phentermine, and Topiramate, and its pathogenesis involves pathways such as neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction and regulation of lipolysis in adipocytes. Obesity also resembles polycystic ovary syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Hypertension, which resembles abdominal obesity-metabolic syndrome 1, obesity, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, is associated with symptoms such as headache, dizziness, edema, proteinuria, and sleep apnea. It involves drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, and calcium channel blockers, and its pathogenesis includes involvement of prostaglandins A, phosphatidylinositols, and various other compounds. Dyslipidaemia is linked to drugs such as statins, fibrates, and resveratrol, and its pathogenesis involves creatinine and hydrocortisone. Kidney disease, a type of urinary system disease, is associated with drugs like vancomycin, gentamicins, and sodium selenite, and its pathogenesis involves calcium phosphate and glutamic acid. Heart disease, classified as a cardiovascular system disease, is associated with drugs such as amiodarone, statins, and resveratrol. Stroke is linked to drugs including aspirin, anticoagulants, and antithrombins, and its pathogenesis involves inositol and malonaldehyde.

ori_question.Question: In this cohort study, what would be the most appropriate method to evaluate whether the risk of developing diabetes differs by age at menarche among women with varying levels of central adiposity, while accounting for potential confounding?
Evidence: Passage: 'We also investigated the effect modification of this association by adult adiposity as it is a potential putative factor in this association from previously published studies.'

Passage: 'We assessed statistical interaction between age at menarche and obesity (BMI and waist circumference classifications, separately) using the P-value of the Wald test and also conducted Cox proportional hazards analyses stratified by obesity classification.'

Passage: 'The final set of models incorporated adiposity measures as potential mediating factors: waist circumference as a measure of central obesity (model 4a) and BMI as a measure of general obesity (model 4b).'
ori_question.Rationale: The reasoning chain requires integrating three distinct pieces of evidence to determine the correct analytical approach. Evidence 1 establishes the study's explicit aim to examine whether adult adiposity modifies the association between age at menarche and diabetes incidence—a key element of prognostic stratification. Evidence 2 reveals the specific statistical methods used: testing for interaction via the Wald test and conducting stratified Cox models by obesity status. This indicates that the study design included both interaction testing and stratification, which are standard approaches for assessing effect modification. Evidence 3 confirms that adiposity (specifically waist circumference) was included as a covariate in the final model, suggesting it was considered a potential mediator. However, the question is not about mediation but about effect modification—i.e., whether the risk of diabetes by menarche age differs depending on adiposity level. The correct method must therefore involve testing for interaction (not just adjusting for adiposity) and stratifying the analysis. The external domain knowledge lists obesity and diabetes as linked conditions and includes drugs and pathways related to both, but it does not provide information on statistical methods for effect modification or interaction testing. Therefore, it is not relevant to the reasoning chain and was not used. The question requires multi-step reasoning: one must recognize that the study aimed to assess prognostic differences by adiposity, understand that interaction testing and stratification are the appropriate methods for this, and distinguish this from simple adjustment for confounding. A reader who only sees evidence 3 might incorrectly conclude that adjusting for adiposity is sufficient, but the full answer requires combining all three to identify the correct methodological approach.

paragraph:
Lung development begins in utero and continues through adolescence [ 1 ], reaching peak volume by age 18 years for females and age 20 years for males [ 2–6 ]. Various factors, including body size, behavior (e.g. frequent inhalation and outdoor activities), and immature physiological systems, can influence lung development in childhood, making lungs more vulnerable to environmental exposures [ 2 , 7–9 ]. Accumulating evidence suggests that chronic exposure to air pollution during childhood can delay lung growth and accelerate functional decline into adulthood [ 2 , 10–12 ].

Air pollution, such as particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides, and ground-level ozone (O 3 ), can irritate airways through oxidative stress and lead to lung inflammation [ 13 , 14 ]. Long-term exposure to those air pollutants may result in declining lung function and bronchitic symptoms, including cough, phlegm, and chest congestion [ 13 , 14 ]. These chronic bronchitic symptoms have been recognized as phenotypes of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in adults [ 15 , 16 ] and are correlated with other lung diseases, e.g. lung cancer and asthma [ 17 ].

We previously showed that long-term childhood exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) and PM of ≤10 µm in diameter (PM 10 ) was associated with higher odds of adult bronchitic symptoms, independently of childhood respiratory conditions [ 18 ]. This suggests that childhood represents a susceptible period for long-term air-pollution effects. However, existing studies have not identified specific susceptible windows because air-pollution-exposure measurements over long pre-specified time windows (e.g. across several years as in previous studies [ 18 ]) are often not sufficiently temporally resolved to identify key specific ages of susceptibility. To address this gap, we leveraged high-temporal-resolution annual average exposure estimates of PM 10 , NO 2 , and O 3 from conception to age 16 years in the Southern California Children’s Health Study (CHS) to examine associations with self-reported adult bronchitic symptoms. We employed data-driven distributed lag models (DLMs) to identify susceptible air-pollution-exposure windows in childhood and investigated effect modification by sex.
### Study population

We focused on three waves of cohort recruitment of the CHS [ 18–20 ]: fourth-graders (ages ∼9–10 years) were recruited in 1992–1993 (Cohort ‘C’) and 1995–1996 (Cohort ‘D’) and kindergarteners and first-graders (ages ∼5–7 years) were recruited in 2002–2003 (Cohort ‘E’). A consistent recruitment protocol was used for all three cohorts and all were followed annually, biannually, or biennially with questionnaires through high school. Beginning in 2017, a subset ( n = 1444) was re-contacted for adult follow-up. After the exclusion of 79 participants with missing outcomes and one duplicate, 1365 participants were included ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Details of the follow-up study are published elsewhere [ 18 ].

All parents/guardians of participating children provided written informed consent during the childhood study and child participants provided written assent. During the adult follow-up assessment, participants provided electronic informed consent. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of the University of Southern California.

### Outcome definition

Adult bronchitic symptoms were identified as self-reported ‘yes’ to any of the following questions during the adult assessment: (i) During the last 12 months, have you had a cough first thing in the morning that lasted for as much as 3 months in a row?; (ii) During the last 12 months, have you had a cough at any other times of the day that lasted for as much as 3 months in a row?; (iii) Other than with colds, do you usually seem congested in the chest or bring up phlegm?; or (iv) During the last 12 months, have you had bronchitis? This approach is consistent with those of previous bronchitic symptoms assessments in the CHS [ 18 , 21–24 ] and in other studies [ 25 ].

### Exposure assessment

We assigned annual average ambient PM 10 , NO 2 , and O 3 concentrations to participants’ residential history from pregnancy to age 16 years. We did not include PM of ≤2.5 µm (PM 2.5 ) due to high missingness from limited monitoring data in the late 1980s and early 1990s in Southern California. Methods for constructing residential histories and exposure assessment were previously published [ 26 ]. The monthly average ambient air-pollution concentrations (24-h mean PM 10 , 24-h mean NO 2 , and 8-h maximum O 3 ) were estimated by using inverse-distance squared spatial interpolation, incorporating the US Environmental Protection Agency’s Air Quality System data [ 27 ] and supplemental CHS measurements [ 20 , 28 ]. Annual averages were estimated from monthly means, requiring ≥75% (9 out of 12 months) of data per age-year.

### Covariates

We included several childhood and adult variables as potential confounders based on prior work [ 18 ] and knowledge. Childhood variables included race/ethnicity, household income, maternal smoking during pregnancy, presence of smoker in the home, and presence of mold/mildew in the home. Sensitivity analyses included childhood bronchitic symptoms and asthma. Adult variables included age, highest educational attainment, body mass index (BMI), and current smoking status. We additionally considered community at study recruitment and CHS cohort (C, D, or E) to capture spatial and temporal variability in ambient air pollution. To assess sex-specific susceptibility, we stratified analyses by biological sex.

### Statistical methods

We first examined temporal correlations between air pollutants by using Spearman’s correlation. To explore susceptible windows, we fitted log Poisson DLMs with robust standard error estimators with a cross-basis of a log-linear exposure–response association based on prior work [ 18 ] and a lag–response association using a natural cubic spline smooth function. This approach identifies susceptible windows of exposure via the simultaneous estimation of air-pollution effects for each age-year while minimizing the potential bias from correlated exposures across the ages [ 29 ].

To fit the smooth function, we tested various knots numbers and placements ( Supplementary Table S1 ), guided by biological plausibility, age-specific models ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ), unconstrained DLMs, and quasi-information criterion minimization [ 30 ] (expanded in the Supplementary Methods ). Susceptible windows were identified when age-specific risk ratios (RRs) (per 10-unit increase in exposure) excluded 1. Sensitivity analyses tested knot choices, excluded potential non-confounders (i.e. adult smoking and adult BMI), and adjusted for childhood bronchitic symptoms and asthma to assess independence from early-life respiratory conditions.

Given the significant exposure and covariate differences between retained and excluded participants ( Supplementary Table S3 ), we assessed robustness to missing exposure data by analysing: (i) full exposure data (pregnancy-age 16 years), (ii) subsets with complete exposure data for selected age ranges, and (iii) imputed exposure (see Supplementary Methods ). NO 2 and O 3 analyses included the full ( N = 769), truncated (ages 1–12 years, N = 1124), and imputed ( N = 1332) samples. Due to the high missingness of exposure from pregnancy to age 16 years (87.84%), PM 10 analyses were limited to ages 3–12 years. Supplementary Fig. S1 illustrates the flowchart for analytic samples.

We applied Bayesian distributed lag interaction models (BDLIMs) [ 31 ] with the full sample to detect heterogeneity by sex ( Supplementary Table S3 ). BDLIM tests subgroup differences in sensitive windows, effect size, or both [ 31 ]. Based on the BDLIM findings, we then performed sex-stratified DLMs with the specified knots ( Supplementary Table S4 ).

Analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2 [ 32 ], with the dlnm [ 33 ] and regimes [ 31 ] packages.
The characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1 . Among those with full NO 2 and O 3 exposure histories, the average age at adult assessment was 33.7 ± 2.34 years. Participants in the NO 2 /O 3 (ages 1–12 years) and PM 10 subsets were younger, with mean ages of 32.0 ± 4.72 and 30.7 ± 5.04 years, respectively. Most participants were male (61%) and non-Hispanic White (51%–59%) or Hispanic (28%–36%). Approximately 30% reported childhood household incomes of between US$15 000 and US$50 000. Approximately 70% held a bachelor’s degree and 80% were nonsmokers. Twenty-two percent of participants with full exposure history reported bronchitic symptoms at adult assessment. This percentage was higher among the selected age-range (24%) and PM 10 (26%) subsets.

The median annual exposure to air-pollutant concentrations decreased at older ages, from a mean of 38.23 (pregnancy) to 23.64 (age 16 years) ppb for NO 2 , from 49.78 to 43.30 ppb for O 3 , and from 50.56 (age 3 years) to 39.06 (age 12 years) µg/m 3 for PM 10 ( Fig. 1 ). Correlations across different air-pollutant concentrations were higher at closer ages ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). Within each age, NO 2 and PM 10 had the strongest correlations (Spearman’s correlation coefficient range 0.49–0.82). NO 2 and O 3 were weakly correlated (–0.30 to 0.32), positive until age 11 years and negative from 12 to 16 years, whereas NO 2 and PM 10 were highly positively correlated, especially for ages 5–12 years (≥0.74) ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ).

The DLM results ( Fig. 2 ) showed that NO 2 exposure at ages 1–2 years was associated with a higher risk of adult bronchitic symptoms, with the largest associations observed at age 1 year [RR per 10 ppb = 1.12; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.01, 1.25]. O 3 exposure at ages 4–5 and 12–15 years was associated with increased risk and was the highest at age 14 years (RR = 1.51; 95% CI: 1.23, 1.86). Statistically significant inverse associations were observed for O 3 at ages 8–11 years and were the strongest at age 10 years (RR = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.71, 0.90). The single-pollutant model showed similar patterns, though NO 2 was non-significant in the full-exposure analysis ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ).

In secondary analysis (ages 1–12 years, larger sample), NO 2 showed similar patterns but attenuated associations, with susceptible windows extending to age 3 years ( Fig. 2 ). O 3 associations at ages 8–12 years became non-significant, while inverse associations at ages 1–2 years were significant ( Fig. 2 ). DLM using imputed exposure yielded similar trends but all CIs contained the null ( Fig. 2 ). Results remained consistent after excluding adult covariates or adjusting for childhood respiratory conditions ( Supplementary Figs S6 and S7 ).

BDLIM analysis suggested heterogeneity by sex in the effect size but not in the window for NO 2 and in the window only for O 3 ( Supplementary Table S3 ). However, sex-stratified analyses revealed overlapping lag–response patterns and CIs across ages ( Fig. 3 ). Results were robust to covariate changes ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ).

After adjustment for other pollutants, PM 10 models showed a downward risk trend ( Fig. 4 ). Borderline statistically significant inverse associations were noted at ages 9 and 10 years (RR = 0.93; 95% CI: 0.87, 1.00 and 0.92; 95% CI, 0.85–1.00, respectively) after adjustment for NO 2 . When adjusted for O 3 , susceptible windows appeared at ages 3–4 years, with the highest RR at age 3 years (RR = 1.13; 95% CI: 1.03, 1.25) ( Fig. 4 ). Additionally, in the sample restricted by PM 10 availability, we found susceptible windows at ages 3–4 and 11–12 years for NO 2 in the two-pollutant and three-pollutant models ( Fig. 4 ). Sensitivity analyses excluding adult covariates or including childhood respiratory conditions showed consistent results ( Supplementary Figs S9 and S10 ). However, given the high correlation between PM 10 and NO 2 , the multi-pollutant model results at older ages should be interpreted cautiously.
With 18 years of exposure history and adult follow-up in the CHS, this study is the first to have explored susceptible windows of childhood ambient air-pollution exposure with adult bronchitic symptoms. Data-driven DLM analyses suggested that early life (ages 1–2 years) might be a particularly susceptible exposure window for NO 2 and early adolescence (ages 12–15 years) for O 3 , while O 3 showed inverse associations in mid-childhood (ages 8–11 years). There was some suggestive evidence of an early-life (ages 3–4 years) susceptible window for PM 10 exposure.

Studies on the long-term effects of childhood air pollution on adult bronchitic symptoms are limited. Some have investigated related outcomes, such as asthma incidence [ 34 ], forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), and forced vital capacity (FVC) [ 35 , 36 ]. The Swedish BAMSE study of 2278 children followed from birth until 16 years of age found that exposure to traffic nitrogen oxides and PM 10 in the first year of life was associated with reduced FEV1 at age 16 years [ 35 ]. The Norway and Sweden RHINESSA study ( N = 3428) reported that O 3 exposure from ages 0 to 10 years was associated with lower FEV1 and FVC at age 28 years [ 36 ]. PM 2.5 and O 3 during ages 10–18 years were also associated with lower lung function [ 36 ]. No association with NO 2 was found, possibly due to the coarse temporal resolution from averaging exposure over 0–10 years, which may have masked the potential early-life effects of NO 2 . The Dutch PIAMA study with 3687 participants linked NO 2 , PM 2.5 , and PM 10 at birth to higher asthma incidence until age 20 years [ 34 ]. While these studies consistently associated childhood exposure to PM 10 , NO 2 , and O 3 with adverse adult respiratory outcomes, the susceptible exposure windows remain unknown. Few prior studies have focused on prenatal exposures, e.g. [ 37 , 38 ], limiting the ability to make preventive recommendations across childhood. Limited evidence may stem from methodological challenges, e.g. quantifying time-varying exposures, correlated exposure windows [ 39 ], and data limitations, such as insufficient temporal resolution and short follow-up periods. With high temporally resolved air-pollution estimates in the CHS and participants aging into adulthood, we had a unique opportunity to explore these associations.

Our findings for NO 2 align with those of a previous CHS study that reported NO 2 as a strong predictor for childhood bronchitic symptoms [ 22 ]. Our identification of the age of 1–2 years as a susceptible exposure window is consistent with suggestive evidence from PIAMA, BAMSE, and RHINESSA [ 34–36 ]. Findings were consistent across multi-pollutant models with varying age ranges and co-pollutant adjustments. The results for the single-pollutant model should be interpreted cautiously due to co-exposure with O 3 .

For O 3 , increased risks at ages 4–5 and 12–15 years were observed in the full age-range analysis, but these associations were not consistent in secondary or PM 10 analyses. Inverse associations at ages 8–11 years appeared only in the complete sample. A previous CHS study also found a statistically non-significant inverse association between O 3 and childhood bronchitic symptoms [ 22 ]. The long-term effects of ozone on respiratory health remain inconclusive [ 40–42 ]. Some primate studies suggest that O 3 may impair lung function [ 40 ], possibly leading to long-term respiratory symptoms. The observed inverse association may reflect unmeasured confounding, such as outdoor activities [ 43 , 44 ], or exposure misclassification due to indoor–outdoor differences, such as building filtration and air exchanges while people are staying indoors [ 45 , 46 ]. A study of adult asthma found protective associations with summertime O 3 only in single-pollutant models, underscoring the importance of multi-pollutant approaches [ 47 ]. Our age-based exposure metric limits direct parameterization of summertime O 3 . Future studies should explore seasonal O 3 measures to evaluate the persistence of this paradoxical effect.

In our study sample, PM 10 was highly correlated with NO 2 from age 5 years onward. After adjustment for NO 2 , some early-life susceptible windows for PM 10 remained, but the CIs widened, with some containing the null. Inverse associations at ages 9–10 years were inconsistent, possibly due to multicollinearity. Our previous study found the average childhood PM 10 (birth to 17 years) to be associated with increased odds of bronchitic symptoms in adulthood [ 18 ]. It is important to note that the present analysis required more complete age-specific exposure, reducing the sample ( n = 819) and ages examined (3–12 years) compared with those of the previous study ( n = 1204, birth to 18 years PM 10 exposure average). Other evidence also linked childhood PM 10 exposure to lung function decline. A CHS study reported non-statistically significant decreased FEV1 growth from ages 10–18 years [ 48 ] and the UK-MAAS birth cohort reported a 1.37% (2.52%, 0.23%) decrease in FEV1 with lifetime PM 10 exposure (birth to 11 years) [ 49 ].

Sex differences in the impact of air pollution on lung development have been reported, but the findings vary by developmental stages [ 37 , 50–53 ]. Some studies suggest greater male susceptibility in infancy [ 37 , 54 ]. For example, mid-gestation PM 2.5 exposure is associated with asthma by age 6 years in males but not in females [ 45 ]. Males also more frequently exhibit early-life respiratory symptoms, such as chronic cough, respiratory syncytial virus infection, and respiratory distress syndrome at younger ages [ 50 ]. Conversely, puberty-related studies suggest that estrogen may exacerbate, while androgens may alleviate, asthma symptoms [ 50–52 ]. In our study, we found no evidence of sex differences, possibly due to limited power in the sex-stratified analyses.

Our findings aligned with biological mechanisms. The alveolar stage of lung development (36 weeks’ gestation to age 10 years) is the longest [ 55 ], with peak alveolar multiplication (increasing lung size) at ages 1–2 years and completion by 8–10 years [ 1 , 55 ]. Air-pollution exposure during this stage, overlapping with our identified susceptible windows, may disrupt developmental programming, leading to reduced lung function and adult respiratory symptoms. Two primary hypothesized mechanisms are oxidative stress and inflammation. Air pollutants can induce reactive oxygen species and chronic inflammation [ 14 , 56 ], contributing to sputum production and respiratory symptoms such as daily cough, congestion, phlegm, and/or bronchitis, collectively known as bronchitic symptoms and phenotypes of respiratory dysfunction [ 57 ].

Our study has several strengths. First, by leveraging the long-term CHS cohort with detailed residential histories, we estimated the annual average residential air-pollution exposures from conception to age 16 years, capturing yearly exposure dynamics beyond fixed time windows. Second, long follow-up into adulthood allowed us to study the impact of childhood exposure on adult (>18 years old) respiratory outcomes. Only two cohorts (RHINESSA [ 36 ] and PIAMA [ 34 ]) have explored such an association. Rich follow-up questionnaire data enabled adjustment for various adult and childhood confounders. Third, we used a data-driven DLM approach to identify susceptible windows that have not been studied and applied in this context before. We note, however, that DLM results can be sensitive to parameter input such as knot selection and placement.

Our study also has limitations. First, bronchitic symptoms were self-reported based on recall of the prior 12 months, representing only a snapshot of adult respiratory health and potentially introducing outcome misclassification. However, as participants were unaware of their annual childhood air-pollution exposure when completing the questionnaires, any misclassification is likely non-differential. Symptom-based assessments have been used in multiple CHS investigations and have revealed associations with air pollution, particularly in studies of childhood bronchitis [ 18 , 21–24 ]. Second, missing exposure data—due to monitoring data gaps or residential histories—posed challenges, particularly for the DLMs. The significant differences in exposure and covariates between included and excluded participants suggest potential selection bias. We evaluated this by analysing additional models with restricted age ranges and imputed exposures. The results moved towards the null in the imputed exposure analysis, possibly from noise in the single imputations; however, we found consistent NO 2 results across the restricted age models. Third, exposures were assessed by using kriging, which has lower spatial resolution than advanced spatiotemporal models, potentially causing exposure misclassification. Fourth, we did not adjust for current air pollution, which could have confounded the results if correlated with childhood exposure and adult outcomes. However, the previous study investigating average childhood exposure and adult bronchitic symptoms in the same CHS data found little impact of current exposure adjustment on the association of childhood exposure with adulthood bronchitic symptoms [ 18 ]. Additionally, we adjusted for proxies of childhood and adult socioeconomic status and baseline residential towns, which account for some correlations between current and childhood exposures. Thus, current exposure is unlikely to be a major source of bias. Other unmeasured confounders, such as childhood antioxidant intake, may have introduced bias if correlated with exposures. Last, the limited sample size may have constrained generalizability beyond the study population.

In conclusion, our study provides new insights linking the timing of childhood air-pollution exposure to adult respiratory health. Our results highlighted that adult bronchitic symptoms are susceptible to NO 2 exposure during early life (1–2 years). Another susceptible window might be early adolescence (12–15 years) for O 3 and early childhood (3–4 years) for PM 10 , but more studies, especially with larger samples, are needed for robust conclusions. Our study emphasizes that reducing air-pollution exposure is critical for children with ongoing lung development.
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of the University of Southern California.

It systematically investigates how environmental exposures—measured with high temporal resolution from conception to age 16—impact respiratory health outcomes in adulthood. The study employs advanced statistical methods (distributed lag models) to analyze exposure-response relationships across time, explicitly addressing the timing and duration of exposure as critical determinants. The analysis accounts for measurement methods (e.g., kriging-based spatial interpolation, annual averages), exposure units (ppb, µg/m³), and challenges such as missing data and multicollinearity. The findings highlight distinct vulnerable periods (e.g., ages 1–2 for NO₂, 12–15 for O₃), which directly reflect the influence of developmental timing on exposure susceptibility. This aligns with Class 3’s emphasis on understanding how environmental exposures arise, are measured, and interact with biological vulnerability across time. The passage also situates these findings within broader public health contexts, including policy implications for air pollution reduction during critical developmental windows. Multi-step inference questions could explore how exposure timing interacts with lung development stages, how measurement limitations affect causal interpretation, or how co-exposure to multiple pollutants modifies risk—requiring integration of exposure science, developmental biology, and epidemiological methods.

external_info: Cough is a symptom associated with multiple conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, respiratory syncytial virus infectious disease, and lung cancer. It is also linked to a wide range of drugs that are either associated with its occurrence or used in its management, such as dextromethorphan, codeine, salbutamol, and corticosteroids. Environmental and occupational exposures, including air pollutants, particulate matter, tobacco smoke pollution, and various chemicals like arsenic, cadmium, and formaldehyde, are also associated with cough. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which includes cough as a key symptom, is classified as an obstructive lung disease and shares characteristics with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Asthma, another condition where cough is a prominent symptom, is categorized as a bronchial disease and resembles atopic dermatitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is associated with drugs such as montelukast, fluticasone/salmeterol, and theophylline, and its pathogenesis involves substances like we 201. Respiratory syncytial virus infectious disease, which can present with cough, is classified as a viral infectious disease. Lung cancer, which also features cough among its symptoms, is a respiratory system cancer and shares clinical and pathological similarities with malignant mesothelioma, mediastinal cancer, melanoma, and other malignancies. Lung carcinoma is recognized as a subtype of lung cancer. Bronchitis, another condition involving cough, is classified as a bronchial disease and is associated with drugs like amoxicillin-potassium clavulanate, theophylline, and salmeterol, as well as environmental agents such as nitrogen dioxide, smoke, and tobacco tar. Histamine has been implicated in the pathogenesis of bronchitis.

Passage: 'This approach identifies susceptible windows of exposure via the simultaneous estimation of air-pollution effects for each age-year while minimizing the potential bias from correlated exposures across the ages [ 29 ].'

ori_question.Rationale: The question requires multi-step reasoning that integrates three distinct pieces of evidence. Evidence 1 describes the statistical method used—distributed lag models (DLMs) with a cross-basis structure involving a log-linear exposure-response and a natural cubic spline for lag-response. This establishes the technical framework. Evidence 2 explains the purpose of this method: to identify susceptible windows by simultaneously estimating effects across age-years while reducing bias from correlated exposures. This is a key epidemiological principle—handling time-varying, correlated exposures without assuming a fixed window. Evidence 3 provides context: this study is the first to identify such windows due to its long-term, high-temporal-resolution exposure data. The reasoning chain is as follows: the study aims to determine when during childhood air pollution exposure has the greatest impact on adult outcomes. Standard methods using fixed time windows (e.g., average exposure from birth to age 5) cannot detect such dynamic effects. The DLM approach allows for continuous modeling of exposure effects across all ages, identifying specific periods (e.g., ages 1–2 for NO2) where risk is elevated. The cross-basis structure enables this by separating the exposure-response and lag-response components, allowing for flexible, data-driven identification of susceptible windows. The external domain knowledge lists conditions associated with cough and bronchitic symptoms (e.g., asthma, COPD, RSV), but it does not provide information about statistical modeling of exposure-response relationships or temporal dynamics of environmental exposure. Therefore, it is not relevant to the reasoning chain and was not incorporated. The question is not answered by any single evidence piece—without combining the methodological description (E1), its purpose (E2), and the study’s novelty (E3), one cannot understand how DLMs improve exposure-response interpretation. The correct answer must be an inference about the method’s role in identifying dynamic, time-specific effects, which is not explicitly stated in any one sentence.

paragraph:
The COVID-19 pandemic had substantial acute impacts worldwide, with more than 7 million deaths reported to the World Health Organization by December 2024 [ 1 ]. Mortality was particularly high in Brazil, representing 9.9% of all deaths worldwide in a country that accounts for 2.7% of the world’s population. This was due to a combination of unscientific political decisions, poor central coordination as different states and regions adopted variable approaches to prevention and case management, and conflicting public messages [ 2 ].

EPICOVID-19, a population-based serological survey carried out in four different waves during 2020 with a total of over 130 000 interviews in 133 Brazilian cities, showed that individuals with lower socioeconomic conditions, lower education, indigenous ethnicity, and black or brown skin colour were more likely to present antibodies against COVID-19 [ 3 ]. Other studies reported similar patterns in both high and low/middle-income countries [ 4 , 5 ].

Economic and social disruption due to the pandemic have profoundly impacted social, health, and economic outcomes among families, such as income reduction, unemployment, interruption of studies, and food insecurity [ 6 , 7 ]. During the pandemic, a six-country study (China, Japan, Italy, South Korea, UK, and USA) reported stronger impacts among individuals with low socioeconomic status [ 8 ]. In a systematic review, including studies from 27 countries, higher rates of dropouts and failures were reported among students from lower socioeconomic positions [ 9 ].

We aimed to describe how families were impacted by the pandemic in terms of income, employment, school attendance, food insecurity, and death of family members in a nationwide Brazilian population-based sample. Impact measures were stratified by socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, including indicators socioeconomic position and ethnicity. The rationale for stratification is provided by the importance of social determinants of health globally [ 10 ] and particularly in Brazil, which is one the most highly unequal countries in the world [ 11 ]. Our hypothesis was that the pandemic had a greater impact on population groups that were already more vulnerable at its onset, such as low-income families and households headed by women.
### Participants

Using the same sampling design as in the original 2020 study, 133 sentinel cities were selected throughout the country. The cities included Brasilia, 26 state capitals, and the largest cities in each of the country’s intermediate regions, as defined by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) [ 12 ]. In each city, a sample of 25 urban census tracts was drawn with a probability of selection proportionate to size, and 10 households were randomly selected in each tract. In each sampled household, all residents were listed, and one was randomly selected to be interviewed. If the sampled individual refused to be interviewed, a second one was sampled. If this individual also refused, the next household to the right was selected. A total of 33 250 participants were interviewed. Further details on the study methods have been described elsewhere [ 13 ]. Data were collected during May and June 2024.

### Outcomes

The following impact outcomes during the pandemic were studied: death of a family member due to COVID-19; decrease in family income; impact on work of a family member, defined as job loss (for those formally employed) or stopping working (for those in the informal sector); and impact on education, defined as any family member who stopped studying during the pandemic (analyses restricted to families with children or adolescents aged under 18). These three impact indicators referred to events or changes taking place during the pandemic. Household food insecurity during the pandemic was investigated using the Brazilian Food Insecurity Scale [ 14 ], which defines food insecurity at the household as one or more positive answers to eight questions. In addition, we analysed whether any household member had gone an entire day without eating due to lack of food. Food insecurity was assessed during the pandemic, rather than changes in food security compared to the pre-pandemic period.

### Procedures

The sampled individuals were invited to participate in the survey and informed about the objectives of the study, as well as its risks and advantages. Interviews were conducted only after the participant signed the free and informed consent form. The form was read when the selected individual was under 18 years of age; in this case, the child or adolescent either signed or fingerprinted the form, which a legal guardian also signed. The study represented minimal risk to health, being restricted to the application of a short questionnaire. Participants were informed that they could stop participating at any time during data collection.

### Data analysis

We used Stata 15 for the analyses. The prevalence of each outcome was described according to sociodemographic characteristics of the families, including region of the country, number and age distribution of family members, whether the family was headed by a woman, highest educational level of a family member, monthly family income, household wealth, and race/skin colour of the interviewee.

Household wealth was calculated through an index based on principal component analysis (PCA) of a set of household characteristics and assets (computer, internet access, colour television, air conditioning, motor vehicles, cable television, number of bathrooms, and number of residents per bedroom), similar to what is done for Demographic and Health surveys [ 15 ]. The first component of the PCA explained 37.8% of the total variance, and all variables had factor loadings above 0.4, except for internet access (0.24) and cable television (0.35). The wealth index was moderately correlated with reported monthly family income (Pearson’s correlation coefficient of 0.62), and both variables were retained in the analyses.

Information on race/skin colour—the official variable employed by the Brazilian classification—was not collected on each family member but only for the respondent. In consonance with the official classification used in Brazilian studies, the categories included (in Portuguese): branco, preto, pardo, amarelo, or indigenous; respectively white, black, brown, Asian, and indigenous [ 16 ]. Family income in the month preceding the interview was expressed in Brazilian minimum wages (∼US$250).

Proportions were compared using the Wald test. Prevalence ratios were estimated using Poisson regression. Sampling weights were employed to account for the sampling design (by using the ‘svyset’ command) and to reproduce the characteristics of the pooled set of 133 cities in terms of population size, sex, age, and race/colour, using the 2022 Census results [ 17 ]. All findings reported below resulted from the weighted analyses. Further details on weights are available elsewhere [ 18 ].

Equiplot graphs [ 19 ] were used to show inequalities in the outcomes according to wealth quintiles. The slope index of inequality (SII) was used to estimate the magnitude of income-related disparities [ 20 ]. The index ranges from −1 to +1, with negative values indicating higher levels of the outcome among the poor and positive values indicating the opposite.
Interviews were carried out in 33 250 households. Table 1 presents the distribution of households according to socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. Most households had a member with at least 9 years of schooling, a family income of up to three minimum wages, and were headed by a male.

Table 2 presents the five impact outcomes according to region, age, sex, wealth index, income, and race/skin colour. The death of a family member due to COVID-19 was reported in 14.7% [95% confidence interval (CI): 13.8%; 15.6%] of all households, being more common in wealthier and more educated families and in the North and Central-West regions. Reduced family income during the pandemic was observed in 48.6% (95% CI: 47.1%; 50.1%) of the households, with the highest prevalence in the North and Northeast and among families with current incomes of one minimum wage or less. About one of every three participants [34.9% (95% CI: 33.4%; 36.4%)] reported that they or someone in their household had lost their job or stopped working during the COVID-19 outbreak, this being more frequent in families whose income was three minimum wages or less. Concerning school attendance, 21.5% (95% CI: 20.1%; 22.9%) stated that a family member interrupted their studies during the pandemic. Food insecurity during the outbreak was reported in 47.4% (95% CI: 45.9%; 48.8%) of the families, and in 8.5% (95% CI: 7.7; 9.3), at least one adult failed to eat on one or more days due to lack of money (data not shown in Table). Food insecurity, work disruptions, and interruption of studies were more common among families earning one minimum wage or less, those led by women, and households with six or more residents. In contrast, white subjects were less likely to report food insecurity. Race/skin colour was not associated with the remaining outcomes. Table 3 describes outcomes according to race/skin colour stratified by family income.

Figure 1 shows that the widest absolute wealth inequality was observed for food insecurity, where prevalence in the poorest quintile was more than 30 percentage points higher than in the wealthiest quintile. For the death of a family member, the slope index of inequality (SII) was positive [0.08 (95% CI: 0.07; 0.10)], whereas for loss of income [SII: −0.16 (95% CI: −0.18 to −0.14)], impact on work [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.11 to −0.07)], school disruption [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.12 to −0.06)], and food insecurity [SII: −0.42 (95% CI: −0.43 to −0.4)], the slope index of inequality was negative, indicating greater disadvantage among the poorest. The lower SII estimate for food insecurity indicates that absolute wealth inequality was higher for food insecurity.
Our large nationwide, population-based survey in Brazil documented important impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, 4 years after the initial cases in 2020. The impact included high frequencies of family deaths, income reductions, food insecurity, work, and schooling disruptions. The stronger impacts tended to affect already vulnerable groups, as discussed below.

The literature extensively documents the pandemic’s impacts on income, work, and schooling [ 21 ]. Our findings quantify the magnitude of such impacts in Brazil, as well as confirm the importance of disparities associated with region of residence, educational levels, income, wealth, gender, family composition, and ethnicity. In sequence, we discuss in greater detail our findings on food insecurity, family composition, and regional disparities, as well as on the apparently paradoxical inequalities in mortality at the household level.

Food insecurity was particularly frequent in low-income and female-headed families, those with six or more members and with children, and among indigenous populations. Almost two-thirds of the low-income families reported food insecurity; the SII value of 0.42 indicates a wide prevalence gap of 42 percentage points between the poorest and wealthiest households. Due to our cross-sectional design, we cannot assert that the reported levels of food insecurity were fully attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic, because such shortages might have predated the arrival of the virus in the country. Nevertheless, the literature suggests that insecurity increased during the pandemic. A United Nations report published in 2020 showed increases in global food insecurity, with particularly severe effects in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This was attributed to increased unemployment, loss of income, and disruptions in supply chains [ 22 ]. In Latin America, a cohort study in Mexico showed increased food insecurity from 41.6% before the pandemic to 53.8% during the pandemic period [ 23 ]. In Brazil, the impact was amplified by pre-existing inequalities, with the most vulnerable families facing rising rates of food insecurity and undernutrition. Food insecurity was also attributed to the ineffectiveness of social policies during the crisis, leaving millions at risk of hunger and extreme poverty [ 24 ]. Food insecurity may have long-lasting effects, as affected individuals may be more likely to suffer from post-COVID conditions, as reported in a Brazilian cohort study [ 25 ].

There were important regional differences within Brazil. The North (Amazon) and Northeast regions were the most affected by reductions in income, interruption of studies, and food insecurity. These two regions were affected by the pandemic’s fastest initial escalation in Brazil. In our original EPICOVID-19 survey carried out in 2020, the highest prevalence of antibodies against SARS-Cov-2 was initially observed in 11 cities along the Amazon River, after which prevalence increased rapidly in the Northeast [ 26 ]. In addition to the well-documented socioeconomic disparities among the Brazilian regions [ 27 ], factors such as the structure and organization of health systems and management of the pandemic may have played a role. Race/skin colour may also have played a role, as indigenous people—who are concentrated in the Amazon area—were amongst those with the highest levels of infection, hospitalization, and deaths during the pandemic, accentuating their pre-existing vulnerability to acute respiratory diseases, even before the pandemic [ 28 ].

Earlier studies showed that the North region also had the highest case fatality among all five regions of Brazil, both in indigenous and non-indigenous people [ 28–30 ]. Baqui et al . [ 31 ] hypothesize that the regional effect is driven by the increased burden of pre-existing comorbidity in the poorest regions and among the indigenous, leading to increased COVID-19 susceptibility and severity, compounded by unequal access to health care, including intensive care. We also investigated gender-related issues. Because impact outcomes were measured at the household level, it did not make sense to break them down according to the sex of the randomly chosen survey respondent. Instead, we examined gender inequality by comparing families according to the sex of the head of the household. Families headed by women, which represented 40% of the sample, were disproportionately affected by higher rates of food insecurity, income reduction, and interruption of studies. These findings were consistent with those of other studies worldwide that reported on individual-level outcomes. Women were more likely than men to experience negative work outcomes, such as permanent job loss and reduced income, or reductions in total hours worked, both for paid and unpaid work, thus aggravating pre-existing gender gaps [ 32–36 ]. Increased childcare needs due to school interruptions were also reported to impact women’s work. Regarding food insecurity during the pandemic, an Ethiopian study also reported higher levels in female-headed households [ 37 ]. A systematic review focused on pregnant women from different countries found that food insecurity during the pandemic ranged from 11% to over 80% [ 38 ], while a survey in the Amazon Region reported a prevalence of food insecurity of 57% also among pregnant women, with higher levels in large families and in low-income households [ 39 ]. Our findings also showed increased risks in large families for income reduction, work and schooling disruptions, and food insecurity.

Taken together, our findings suggest that pre-existing disparities exacerbated the impacts of the pandemic and likely affected subsequent recovery in terms of food security, education, income, and employment. In many LMICs, households have turned to agricultural work to compensate for job losses in the services sector, and informal work has substantially increased among the poorest [ 7 ]. As an upper-middle-income country, Brazil’s GDP fell 3.3% in 2020, which represented a record low annual decline in recent history. On the positive side, this decline was reversed after the pandemic [ 17 ].

Similar impacts on inequality were seen in some high-income countries, like UK [ 40 ] and Korea [ 41 ], where the pandemic accentuated socioeconomic disparities, especially affecting low-income workers and other vulnerable groups. Lastly, the interruptions in schooling may also aggravate inequalities and social exclusion [ 9 , 42 ].

We found that deaths of family members were more commonly reported in wealthier and more educated families. This finding persisted even after adjusting for sex, age, region, and skin colour. This was a surprising finding as—despite having universal healthcare—poor Brazilians still have lower access to complex health services and shorter life expectancies than their better-off counterparts [ 43 ]. Our finding also contradicts the Brazilian literature on the relationship between COVID-19 mortality and socioeconomic factors, which is mostly based on ecological studies correlating routinely collected mortality data with census-based economic indicators. Most such studies found higher mortality in poorer or more deprived areas of the country [ 31 , 44–48 ]. However, we were unable to find any individual-level study from Brazil on this association. Two observations may help explain our paradoxical findings. First, due to differential life expectancy according to socioeconomic position, wealthier families were more likely than poor households to include elderly members before the pandemic, and these persons were at the highest risk of COVID-19 death. Our current post-pandemic analyses showed that 37% of all households in the poorest quintile and 46% of those in the wealthiest quintile had at least one member aged 60 or older. Similarly, these proportions were 35% and 45% for family income brackets below 1 and over 5 minimum wages ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Such variability in age composition helps explain why wealthier households were more likely to report a death from a disease that primarily killed elderly people. Further analyses also showed that the sharpest socioeconomic increases in mortality were observed for the deaths of the parents of the respondents than for younger relatives (Supplementary Table S2). Another possible explanation is the higher prevalence of non-communicable diseases among the poorest [ 49 ], which may have led them to attribute COVID-19-related deaths to other pre-existing conditions.

Our study’s strengths include its standardized survey methodology and its large population-based sample, including over 100 cities spread throughout a country with 8.5 million km 2 . Yet, some limitations should be acknowledged. First, the time elapsed from the peak of the pandemic to the data collection date poses the risk of recall bias. However, the outcomes under study are objectively defined major events, such as death or unemployment, which reduces the likelihood of poor recall. Second, our sample was restricted to large cities that usually have better access to health care, and 15% of the national population living in rural areas were not included. Third, the higher proportion of negative outcomes in female-headed families might result from the death of a male head of household during the pandemic. For two reasons, we do not think this is a likely source of bias. We found that the proportion of households led by women in our sample was very close to that reported in the 2022 National Census [ 17 ]. In addition, reported deaths in the family did not vary according to the sex of the head of the household ( Table 2 ), and lastly, exclusion from the analyses of households where a spouse died due to COVID-19 (Supplementary Table S3) led to very similar results to those reported above. Lastly, we could not collect information from households whose members were away during the attempted visit or refused to participate.

In conclusion, substantial impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil were documented in terms of mortality, nutrition, income, work, and education. The pandemic disproportionately affected population subgroups that were already vulnerable before the pandemic, such as low-income, female-headed, and indigenous households, thus contributing to exacerbate pre-existing disparities. Our findings underscore the importance of developing and expanding targeted policies to address the needs of the most vulnerable and will contribute to their recovery. Further research should focus on effective interventions to reduce these disparities, including food security programmes, and education support for children from low-income households, and on preparedness to face future epidemics.
The study was submitted to the School of Physical Education Ethics Committee at the Federal University of Pelotas [CAAE: 68382923.8.0000.5313].

category.Rationale: The passage is a comprehensive population-based study that investigates the social, economic, and demographic determinants of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on Brazilian families. It systematically analyzes how factors such as socioeconomic status, household wealth, income, education, race/skin color, region of residence, family composition (e.g., female-headed households), and household size are associated with disparities in outcomes like death, food insecurity, income loss, job disruption, and school interruption. These variables are central to the concept of 'determinants'—particularly social determinants of health—that shape exposure to risk and vulnerability during a public health crisis. The study explicitly links these structural factors to differential outcomes, demonstrating how pre-existing inequalities in society (e.g., wealth, gender, ethnicity) influenced exposure to pandemic-related harms. The use of stratified analyses, wealth quintiles, and inequality indices (SII) further underscores the focus on identifying and quantifying the role of social and structural exposures. While the passage includes elements of surveillance (e.g., mortality reporting) and susceptibility (e.g., age and comorbidities), the primary focus is on explaining *why* certain groups were more affected—i.e., the underlying determinants of exposure and risk. This makes Class 3 the most appropriate, as it supports multi-step inference questions about how social, economic, and geographic factors shape exposure to pandemic impacts, how these determinants interact, and how they might be modified through policy or intervention.
